limitations.takeaway: Useful, not magic. You still do the thinking.
points: The agent doesn't know what it hasn't been told. Until it has the context a decision needs, don't count on it to make projections for you.

You still do the work and put in the thinking. The agent primarily organizes it, like a scribe. But this scribe carries the RestoKit framework, which keeps it consistent in ways an agent without it can't cover for the trade. So it's still incredibly useful within these limits, and you can look into the framework itself to see what you can count on from it in the field.

What makes it work is traversal: it moves through the kit to find the situation and pulls together (synthesizes) what's relevant to read back to you. That's real, but it's not as much magic as people think.

Photo analysis is kept to a short list it does well: equipment, meter readings, rooms, and general progress. Appearance (moisture, wicking, shadows, textures, finishes) can't drive decisions or scopes without a meter reading or a person. Don't put full trust in everything. It's not a miracle solution. You still do your job.
Only Grok has been tested so far.

meta.description: Core knowledge structure for RestoKit, a field assistant for restoration work at any level (tech, lead, PM, or estimator) used by text or by voice. Separates foundational science from operational job flow. Built as a guide and a friend, not a boss. Written like a seasoned tech sitting next to you in the truck. Primary identity is a field memory system: it holds the rare edge-case lessons and tools that do not recur often enough to stay in active recall, then surfaces them when the situation finally reappears. It is a remembering tool more than a procedure manual.
meta.version_rule: This is the 1.1.4 release. Do not bump the version unless the owner says so.
meta.status: 1.1.4 (2026-11-20). Replaces 1.1.3 as the live kit. Weather-related water (wind-driven rain, storm water, roof and window leaks) is not Category 3 by how it got in: the category follows the inspection, and staining alone is not contamination or rot. The dry standard and drying goal are set and written at the first visit. The previous version stays downloadable for a while. Merging a new kit version to main publishes it to resto-kit.com automatically.

update_check.when: On first load in a session, before relying on the kit.
update_check.fallback: If that file cannot be fetched, read the version from the Loop in your agent section on https://resto-kit.com.
update_check.compare: Compare the published version to this file's meta.version.
update_check.if_newer: If the published version is newer, tell the user and give them the published kit URL from that file. Never auto-replace the loaded kit.
update_check.if_fetch_fails: If the check fails, say so briefly and continue with this file.

how_to_start.first_load: On first load in a session, run meta.update_check before relying on the kit.
load_order: 1. main_content.modules.answer_rules: how to answer, any level, text or voice.
2. main_content.modules.job_type_gate: confirm the job type before loading the water stack.
4. main_content.phases (phase0-phase4, plus hold_status when a job waits): the job flow. Follow each step's references into modules and base_science as needed.

5. main_content.modules.visit_note_cadence and main_content.modules.note_templates: on voice, job talk, or a visit, stage only the notes that visit earned, using the plain titles in note_templates and ending every output with the ◇ resto_kit footer. Offer and stage only. Never write Encircle.

6. Morning job talk, new intake, or catch-up: encircle_operations.job_file_review_workflow first, using note_templates.job_file_review (the same eleven questions). Then build or update Mitigation Scope from note_templates. Day Forward is scrapped; do not recreate it. After the meeting, the into-file note is delta only (encircle_operations.job_file_review_workflow.day_forward_plan.morning_note_delta). A company may still use its own review form; the kit writes plain titles and ends every output with the ◇ resto_kit footer.

7. When a topic depends on the state, use framework_scale.runtime_contracts.jurisdiction: ask once what state they work in, remember it for the company and session, then apply it. Until answered, stay state-neutral and say the rules vary by state.

on_request.rule: These stay off the job flow. Use them only when the user asks about the topic or term. Do not surface them during job-flow steps such as extraction.
on_request.glossary: Used when a term comes up or the user asks about one.
on_request.base_science: Background the framework was built from. Not for the tech to dive into unless asked. A phase step may still point to a section (psychrometry, water_movement_pathways); then use only that section.
on_request.daily_log_template: Loaded with the kit. Use it whenever the user logs the day; no separate template upload needed.

how_to_start.jurisdiction: When a topic depends on the state (licensing, hazard surveys, contracts, liens, record retention, building code), follow framework_scale.runtime_contracts.jurisdiction. Ask once, remember it, then apply it. Do not ask on first load. Do not assume Oregon or any other state.

standards_alignment.statement: RestoKit aligns with the principles of IICRC S500 and S520 but is written entirely in its own words. It does not reproduce IICRC text, signature language, or trademarks. The body of knowledge comes from field practice across restoration companies, including real-world operations the standards don't address. RestoKit is not an IICRC publication, is not affiliated with, approved, or endorsed by IICRC, and using it does not certify a job, a company, or a person.
do_not_say: meets the standard (as a claim about a job)
standards_alignment.say_instead: Our process aligns with the principles of IICRC S500 and S520. The job file shows what we did and why.
standards_alignment.citation_note: Page-level references for kit lines are kept outside this file. Kit lines are paraphrased and stand on their own; the kit body carries no source citations. When asked where a line comes from, give the kit section path.

tiers.required: law or regulation (or the product label).
tiers.informative: starting numbers or reference values that are not binding.

standards_alignment.scope: Restoration technical execution. Not legal advice, not medical advice, not an insurance-coverage opinion.
standards_alignment.citation_rule: S500, S520, and IICRC are named only in meta, in the legal_and_liability compliance lines (disclaimer_framing, must_not_claim), and in lines that say a practice aligns with the principles of IICRC S500 and S520. The kit body carries no source citations. No text is quoted from or attributed verbatim to S500/S520; kit lines are paraphrased.

meta.purpose: RestoKit exists because field jobs routinely miss hidden water migration, produce documentation that does not hold up under review, and make inconsistent remove-versus-dry calls. It pairs a linear job flow (phases) with physics-based decision support (modules) that works as an experienced guide rather than a checklist or a boss.

problems: Missed hidden water along baseplates, under vapor barriers, and into wall cavities or crawlspaces
Weak or inconsistent documentation that fails to support scope changes or defend against disputes
Inconsistent material removal decisions that either create callbacks (under-removal) or unnecessary cost (over-removal)
core_thesis.solution: Dedicated modules on water movement pathways, documentation discipline, and a category-dwell-material decision matrix, delivered as short lines during actual job execution.

meta.what_resto_kit_is: Not a replacement for real-world experience. Think of it as an experienced co-pilot: the tech, lead, or PM is still making the final calls; the kit feeds useful information, reminds you of what gets missed when you are tired or rushed, keeps the process consistent, and keeps the documentation clean. New techs get up to speed faster, average techs perform closer to your best, and seasoned techs get a reliable second brain for the edge cases.

framework_scale.purpose: Keep RestoKit usable as knowledge grows. Prevent dense modules from becoming unmaintainable or slow for voice/field use. Guide when and how to break modules into shallow trees.
framework_scale.core_principle: Phases stay linear and flat. Only support modules that accumulate edge cases get a shallow tree. Prefer clarity and speed over perfect hierarchy. RestoKit exists first as field memory for the eternal next-time: the rare tool, sequence, or lesson that would have saved massive labor but only appears infrequently.
triggers_for_tree: Module contains 5+ distinct decision or technique clusters
New edge cases keep landing in the same flat list
Voice retrieval starts returning too much irrelevant content
Techs or contributors can no longer quickly locate the right subsection
Cognitive load of the module exceeds what a field tech can hold while working

tree_design_rules.depth_counting: Depth counts dict levels below <module>.tree, or below the module root when a module has no tree. Lists and list items do not add depth.
tree_design_rules.depth_exception: Level 4 is allowed only for parallel rows: two or more siblings of the same kind (a material, an appliance, a pipe or wiring type, a case such as from_below/from_above, an option), each named by the item it describes in plain field words, ordered the way the field meets them or by severity. Rows of the same kind share a shape where they can. Anything at level 4 that is not a parallel row is a finding. Nothing goes past level 4. Volume note: use rows instead of a new branch when one level-3 node passes about 20 leaves.
known_exceptions: demolition.tree.access_prep.appliance_handling.practical_guidance is an object of per-appliance groups (level-4 children with different shapes), not a list of strings. Kept as is while level 4 is field-tested.

scope is allowed past the depth limits. Its matrix decisions reach level 5, and several lookup groups sit at level 4 without being parallel rows. When scoping, an agent pulls the whole scope object at once, so its depth does not slow navigation, and the object is small next to everything else passed in.
tree_design_rules.branch_naming: Use action or domain language a tech would actually say
tree_design_rules.content_placement: Each piece of existing content maps to exactly one primary branch. Cross-cutting notes can be lightly duplicated or referenced, but do not create deep cross-links
tree_design_rules.voice_priority: Every branch must be reachable with a short, natural request. Avoid forcing the tech through multiple clarifying layers
anti_patterns: Deep nesting beyond 3 levels, except parallel rows under depth_exception; never beyond hard_cap
Branches that only exist for organizational purity
Splitting a high-value single artifact (e.g. the material decision matrix) across multiple branches just for symmetry

single_home_plus_pointer.rule: Single home plus pointer. Each piece of knowledge lives in one place, its home. Anywhere else it is needed, a pointer names it by a short id instead of repeating it.
single_home_plus_pointer.how_it_works: framework_scale.pointer_index lists every id with the full path of its home, from the top of the kit file (most start at main_content). Every pointer value is one id or a list of ids, and every id must be in the index. When a home moves, only its index line changes; the pointers stay the same.
single_home_plus_pointer.pointer_fields: see, references, source, gathered_in, the scope decisions maps, and any other field whose value names a place in the kit. All of them use ids. Prose, web links, and outside labels such as sheet.ref stay as written.
single_home_plus_pointer.reading: Never show or speak an id to a reader. Agents and the website always expand an id to the full text of its home, inline, in the spot where the pointer sits.
single_home_plus_pointer.ids: Ids are short snake_case words, 5 to 15 characters, that read well aloud (cords, spider_box, backdraft). Billable catalog item ids may be up to 24 characters so they read clearly aloud (cross_contamination, containment_teardown); every other id keeps the 15-character limit. A whole module uses its module name as its id. One id per home, never reused.
why: No repeated text, so a fix lands in one place and copies cannot drift apart.
Agents and voice navigation can jump from a pointer to its home, so they can move through a kit bigger than one context window.
A reader never sees an id. The website and agents put the home's full text in its place.

restructuring_process: 1. Confirm the module has hit one or more triggers
2. Define 4–7 logical branches using field language
3. Map every existing subsection, note, and matrix into those branches
4. Keep the highest-leverage artifacts (material matrix, demo order, verification gates) intact and easy to reach
5. Update any phase step references that pointed at the old flat module
7. Document the change in the update notes file (meta.update_notes_file) and bump the relevant version
what_stays_flat: Core decision rules (category, remove-vs-dry principles, fixed-point monitoring, verification-before-teardown)
Base science modules unless they themselves become dense
High-value single artifacts such as the material decision matrix
current_candidates: safety_and_health, legal_and_liability, glossary, hvac_systems, answer_rules (thin, flat: watch only)
framework_scale.success_test: A tech can request the exact piece of guidance they need in one short phrase and receive only the relevant branch, not the entire dense module.

remembering_function.description: The highest-leverage use of the framework is retaining and retrieving rare, high-impact edge cases that individual techs and companies otherwise re-learn repeatedly. New notes of this type should be written as short voice notes inside the relevant module or Field Adaptations rather than forced into the phase sequence.
remembering_function.placement_guidance: Prefer field_adaptations, practical_judgment, or the module that owns the situation. Do not invent new top-level procedure steps for one-off lessons.

job_type_gate.note: Before water-module retrieval, confirm job type. See job_type_gate.
job_type_gate.voice_note: First: what kind of job is this? Don't load the water stack until you know.

runtime_contracts.purpose: Descriptive soft contracts for optional voice/runtime fields. Not a hard schema enforcer: retrieval and voice UX guidance only.

jurisdiction.name: session_state
jurisdiction.stated: The kit does not assume Oregon or any other state. The first time a session reaches a topic where the state matters, ask the user once, in plain words, what state they work in. Remember the answer for this company and this session, then apply it. Until the state is answered, give state-neutral guidance and say that rules vary by state.
jurisdiction.ask: What state do you work in?
jurisdiction.ask_once: Ask only the first time in the session that a state-sensitive topic comes up. Do not ask on first load of the kit. Do not ask again after the state is remembered, unless the user says the work is in a different state.
jurisdiction.remember: Keep the state for the company and the rest of the session. If the user names a different state later, update it and say so.
jurisdiction.until_answered: Give state-neutral guidance only. Say that licensing, survey, notice, contract, and lien rules vary by state. Do not apply Oregon, Washington, or any other state's specifics as the default.
when_state_matters: Hazard sampling and asbestos or lead survey rules
Work authorization, contracts, and lien documents
Building-code items such as crawlspace vapor barrier
jurisdiction.examples_are_not_defaults: State-specific text in the kit (for example Oregon and Washington in hazard_sampling.who_samples.examples_by_state) is an example for that state. Use it only when the remembered state matches. For other states, stay with the state-neutral rule and say the user should check local requirements.
jurisdiction.speakable: What state do you work in? I'll remember it for this session. Until I know, I'll stay general, because the rules change by state.

optional_voice_runtime_fields.voice_note: Short speakable summary for a module, branch, or step cluster.
optional_voice_runtime_fields.voice_line: Single speakable line on a phase step (preferred field name on sequence steps).
optional_voice_runtime_fields.voice_considerations: Thin speakable cue or object with tone/guards for field retrieval.
optional_voice_runtime_fields.references: Id or list of ids from framework_scale.pointer_index, the same system as see (a whole module uses its module name). The index holds each home's full path from the top of the kit file: never relative to the current module, never a list index; phase steps are addressed as phases.<phase>.sequence.<step id>. One key name for every machine-readable link, on steps, modules, or notes; omit when none apply. Expand each id to its home's full text inline before reading or showing it; never show or speak an id.
optional_voice_runtime_fields.board_stage: PM board column label for a step; must be in the union of phases.<phase>.pm_board_alignment.board_stages (plus phases.hold_status board_column when used).
optional_voice_runtime_fields.pm_board_alignment: Phase-level board column/stages map for PM tooling.
optional_voice_runtime_fields.reference_note: Optional short text next to references saying why the link matters.
optional_voice_runtime_fields.id: Stable snake_case id on each phase step; paths use it instead of list positions.
optional_voice_runtime_fields.hold_triggers: Phase-level list of known stall points; each item has trigger text and references to phases.hold_status. Not exhaustive.
optional_voice_runtime_fields.see: Id or list of ids from framework_scale.pointer_index. references, source, gathered_in, and decisions values work the same way. Says the knowledge lives at that home, so it is not repeated here. Every id must resolve in the index; the index holds the full path of each home. Expand the id to its home's full text inline before reading or showing it; never show or speak the id itself.

notes: Fields are optional; absence is valid.
Do not split high-value single artifacts (e.g. material decision matrix) for contract symmetry.
Empty references[] should be filled when the target is known, otherwise null/omit for cleaner retrieval.

phase0.name: Survey & Estimate
phase0.objective: Show up, investigate the loss, talk to the customer, explain what the job likely is, form a plan, and build the scope and estimate file the tech inherits. A survey is not authorization: Phase 1 starts at signed authorization.
principles: The surveyor does not lock scope. Initial scopes are almost always low: water hides behind baseplates, in interstitial spaces, and under flooring you can't read through. The file carries the assumption that scope grows.
Containment layout is a field-execution call. The surveyor marks wet areas and rough placement; the tech on site sets the plastic.
The structured scope is the source. The carrier PDF and the estimate entry are two outputs of it (Estimating: File Connection).
Same person, same visit: on small jobs the surveyor is the tech. Run Phase 0 and Phase 1 back to back; Phase 1's confirm steps then take seconds.

sequence.name: Arrival & Customer Conversation
sequence.description: Respond to the call and meet the customer. On interview, ask about the cause of loss if known, environment, house. Confirm what the work is (job-type gate) before loading water modules. Give the customer the lay of the project up front: what the job likely is, what to expect, and what the survey covers. A survey is not authorization.
sequence.voice_line: Tell me what happened and when. Here's what this kind of job usually looks like and what I'm going to check today.

sequence.name: Investigation & Wet-Area Marking
sequence.description: Walk the affected areas and mark where the water is: visible wet, staining, and suspected hidden paths. Marking is rough; the tech on site sets exact readings and containment from it. Make the first category call and write down why. Flag suspect materials; building age raises the bar but doesn't clear anything.
sequence.voice_line: Walking it now: marking visible wet, stains, and where it probably went that we can't see. First category call goes in the file with the reason.

sequence.name: Quick Photo Sweep
sequence.description: Take fast, broad photos of the affected areas and overall loss. Do it before anything is touched.
sequence.voice_line: I'm going to do a quick photo sweep of the whole affected area before we touch anything.

sequence.name: Crawlspace First Look
sequence.description: Size up the crawlspace at the hatch: odor, standing or sewage water, gas appliances, wiring. Run a 4-gas check only when there's a reason (sewage, a gas or fuel smell, a confined space) or when company liability tolerance requires it, not routinely (Crawlspaces: Safety & Access: Atmospheric Testing). Flag urgent issues for the crew.
sequence.voice_line: Hatch first: smell, water, sewage, gas, wiring. Run a 4-gas check only when there's a reason (sewage, a gas or fuel smell, a confined space) or when company liability tolerance requires it. Not routine.

sequence.name: Hazard Sampling (If Required)
sequence.description: Older home or suspect material, any age: sample or presume before any destructive work. Sample first and wait: results pending means no disturbing work. Who samples and how many: Hazard Sampling.
sequence.voice_line: Older home or suspect material: we sample or presume before we cut or demo anything.

sequence.name: Scope & Estimate
sequence.description: Draw all the line items for the scope, build the estimate sketch, and form the plan. Write what was assumed. Rough containment placement notes only: do not lock the plastic layout; that is the tech's call on site. Project the equipment from the job conditions and run or start the pre-setup power survey so you know whether a power box is needed before the truck is loaded.
sequence.voice_line: Line items, sketch, and plan, and I'm writing down what I assumed, because this scope will grow.

sequence.name: File Setup: Room Measurements & Documentation
sequence.description: Measure affected areas, create a simple diagram with room names and square footage, take overview photos from corners, and document any pre-existing damage. Record the category determination rationale and all survey findings. The file is what the tech inherits.
sequence.voice_line: Measuring the affected rooms and sketching a quick diagram with square footage. Also noting any pre-existing damage.

pm_board_alignment.notes: Phase 0 covers first assignment through scope. A bid is not authorization.

hold_triggers.trigger: Customer won't sign the work authorization.

phase1.name: Initial Response & Stabilization
phase1.objective: Starts at signed authorization. Get on site, stop the active loss if necessary, protect people and contents, remove free water quickly, document the situation, and establish initial drying conditions. Major demolition is generally avoided during this phase.

sequence.name: Verify Paperwork
sequence.description: On the phone or on arrival: Confirm work authorization is signed. This is the hard gate before any physical work. Work order review: walk the scope and collect biocide/antimicrobial consent here, low-key, with the rest of the paperwork; a 'no' can change the scope (Legal and Liability: Informed Consent Antimicrobials). Confirm with the customer what the survey found (cause of loss if known, environment, house), or ask now if there was no survey. Confirm what the work is (job-type gate) before loading water modules, not every job is a water job.
sequence.voice_line: First thing: work authorization signed and the work order reviewed, including whether they're okay with a biocide if we need one. Then confirm what kind of job this is before we load water modules.

sequence.name: Safety Assessment & Category Verification
sequence.description: On site: Perform a safety walkthrough. Verify or adjust the preliminary category, knowing the COL is key, and if you don't know it by now you're hunting for it. Flag suspect materials; building age raises the bar but doesn't clear anything. The category is set from what the inspection finds (source, path, dwell time, temperature, and signs of contamination), not from how the water got in.
sequence.voice_line: Quick safety walk and confirm the category. Anything look off: asbestos concerns, electrical, structural?

sequence.name: Confirm or Complete Survey Documentation
sequence.description: Confirm the survey photo sweep, room measurements, diagram, corner overview photos, and pre-existing damage notes are in the file. No survey? Do the quick photo sweep now before you touch anything, and complete measurements once the loss is stable.
sequence.voice_line: Survey photos and measurements in the file? If not, quick photo sweep now before we touch anything: measurements after it's stable.

sequence.name: Source Control (If Needed)
sequence.description: Shut off the water source if it is still actively leaking. Open a faucet and watch the pressure drain to confirm.
sequence.voice_line: If water is still running, shut it off at the source and verify it's actually stopped.

sequence.name: Bulk Water Extraction & Surface Cleaning
sequence.description: Floor protection as needed, then aggressively extract all standing and accessible water: extraction comes first on the vast majority of losses because the water is still spreading. Containment before extraction is the exception, only when the situation truly calls for it (Equipment Setup: Containment First Exceptions). On Category 2 or 3, clean and wipe the surfaces you will work across; any biocide follows the Day 1 decision (phase1 Verify Paperwork), and contaminated porous material comes out before treatment. Extraction comes before contents and plastic in every category; contents move first only if they block the water path. Sewage pump-out may need containment first (Equipment Setup: Containment First Exceptions). Cat 3 crawl: the hose breaks the hatch containment, so use heavier path protection along the hose route instead of relying on the hatch seal.
sequence.voice_line: Time to pull the standing water out hard: stop the spread first. Category 2 or 3 means we clean and wipe what we work across; biocide only if it was approved on Day 1.

sequence.name: Contents Protection (After Extraction; First Only If Blocking the Water Path)
sequence.description: Extraction comes before contents and plastic in every category. Move contents first only when they block the water path (extractor or hose cannot reach the water). After bulk extraction: move or elevate contents and furniture off wet floors and protect high-value or vulnerable items. See Scoping: Order of Work: Extraction First.
sequence.voice_line: Water out first. Only move what's in the way of the extractor; the rest of the contents come up right after.

sequence.name: Baseline Moisture Readings
sequence.description: Take initial moisture readings and psychrometric data in affected and unaffected areas. From the unaffected readings, set the dry standard for each affected material and write the drying goal into the file now, so every visit and the final check are measured against it (Base Science: Dry Standards).
sequence.voice_line: Baseline moisture readings and psychrometrics: affected areas plus clean unaffected reference points. The unaffected readings set the dry standard, and the drying goal goes in the file today.

sequence.name: Crawlspace Inspection
sequence.description: Confirm the survey's crawlspace notes, or size it up at the hatch now if there was no survey: odor, standing or sewage water, gas appliances, wiring. Run a 4-gas check only when there's a reason (sewage, a gas or fuel smell, a confined space) or when company liability tolerance requires it, not routinely (Crawlspaces: Safety & Access: Atmospheric Testing). Full entry: identify urgent issues and drop wet insulation to the ground if time allows.
sequence.voice_line: Quick look at the hatch: smell, water, gas appliances, wiring. Then I'm dropping into the crawlspace: wet insulation, staining, any hot spots.

sequence.name: Containment & Protection
sequence.description: Install floor protection and containment exactly where you anticipate it going for the duration of the project. You may have to adjust, but it generally stays where it goes. The surveyor marks rough placement; the layout is your call.
sequence.voice_line: Floor protection down first, then walls and/or doors, to reduce the air volume as much as possible to the affected area.

sequence.name: Equipment Setup
sequence.description: Before anything goes on the truck or into the room, run the pre-setup power survey: project the equipment, total the nameplate amps, map the nearby circuits, and use a power box only when the load exceeds the free capacity. Plan cord routing so doors are not left open. Set up and start dehumidifiers and air movers. On Category 2 or 3, run an air filtration device (AFD). Once the water is under control, isolate heavily contaminated (Category 3) areas and put them under negative pressure. On Category 2/3, start humidity control and AFD first; air movers go on after contaminated porous material is out (or for directed cavity drying), not across contaminated finishes.
sequence.voice_line: Power survey first, then equipment going in. Clean water: dehus and air movers. Category 2 or 3: dehus and AFD first: fans after the contaminated stuff is out.

sequence.name: Confirm Sampling Results or Hold
sequence.description: If sampling is pending, confirm results before any disturbing work. Results not back, or asbestos-containing (more than 1 percent) or presumed, means no disturbance: enter Hold if the job cannot progress. No survey and suspect material? Sample or presume now, before any destructive work.
sequence.voice_line: Sampling back yet? No results, no disturbing work. If we're stuck waiting, the job goes on hold.

sequence.name: Limited Targeted Access (Low-Risk Only)
sequence.description: On clean Category 1 losses, you may remove outlet covers and switch plates. In older homes or with suspect material, baseboard removal waits for asbestos results: asbestos-containing or presumed material is not disturbed (required; see Hazard Sampling).
sequence.voice_line: On clean Category 1 we can pull outlet covers and switch plates. Baseboards in older homes stay put until we have test results: sample-wait is the default.

sequence.name: End of Phase Documentation
sequence.description: Record all findings, readings, equipment locations, category, crawlspace observations, and sampling requirements.
sequence.voice_line: Wrapping Phase 1: logging category, readings, equipment placement, crawlspace notes, and any sampling we need.

pm_board_alignment.notes: Phase 1 runs from signed authorization through initial stabilization. The paperwork gate and category verification are the primary control points.

phase_collapse_note.description: On active high-volume sewage losses that require the pump truck, the detailed Phase 1 sequence yields to rapid mitigation. Authorization and Category 3 safety still apply. Bulk extraction and source control take priority so the plumber can repair. Full documentation, measurements, and selective access resume after the flow is stopped and volume is reduced.

hold_triggers.trigger: Source control waiting on a plumber.

phase2.name: Selective Demolition & Post-Demo Cleaning
phase2.objective: Open up the building, remove unsalvageable wet materials, thoroughly clean the structure, and properly set up drying equipment based on the new reality of the job.

sequence.name: Demo Planning & Scope Confirmation
sequence.description: Review the survey (Phase 0) and Phase 1 documentation, photos, readings, and category. Confirm hazards (asbestos results if pending; still pending means Hold). Decide on remove vs dry-in-place for each material type using Demolition: Decision Logic (material decision matrix and category/dwell criteria). Plan the demo sequence and identify hidden water chase priorities.
sequence.voice_line: Let's review what the survey and Phase 1 found and decide exactly what comes out versus what we try to dry. Check those asbestos results if we have them. Plan our attack order.

sequence.name: Pre-Demo Controls & Protection
sequence.description: Verify or upgrade containment and engineering controls for the demolition work. Set up or reinforce dust containment, floor protection, and any needed decon chamber.
sequence.voice_line: Before we start cutting, make sure containment is solid, and dust control is in place. Check for any plumbing or electrical issues we need to flag.

sequence.name: Execute Demo Order
sequence.description: Follow the standard physical removal sequence using top-down logic on walls and ceilings. On flooring, start where access is cleanest and easiest (transitions, under appliances, doorways, or natural edges), then work systematically while chasing hidden water. Work surgically around utilities, protect finished surfaces that remain, and expand scope as hidden moisture is revealed.
sequence.voice_line: Follow the demo order: trim, outlets, fixtures, and cabinets first. On flooring, start where it's easiest to get in clean and chase the water from there. Protect what stays and open up hidden spots as we find them.

sequence.name: Hidden Water Investigation & Scope Expansion
sequence.description: Actively investigate and document water migration into wall cavities, under floors (especially under vapor barriers or LVP), along base plates, behind cabinets, and in interstitial spaces. Expand the scope as needed until active moisture or water staining is no longer found in previously unopened areas. Document the progression with photos and notes.
sequence.voice_line: Keep hunting as we demo: base plates, under flooring, wall cavities, behind vanities. Open until we stop finding wet material or staining. This is normal; document every expansion so scope makes sense later.

sequence.name: Post-Demo Foundational Cleaning
sequence.description: Remove heavy debris, vacuum floors thoroughly, then knock dust from framing/wires/boxes with air blast (blower, or ULV with the liquid off) only inside controlled containment with HEPA capture running. Wipe down all exposed framing, plumbing, electrical, and horizontal surfaces. Final detailed vacuum focusing on corners and gaps. On Category 2/3, a biocide (pump or ULV) goes on only when a biocide line is approved: pre-cleaned surfaces, registered product, label allows the method (see ULV vs Hand-Pump Sprayer). Fog is never the default and never the cleaning. Consider pressure wash + extractor method on concrete slab Category 3 jobs with heavy contamination (never on a wood subfloor).
sequence.voice_line: Heavy clean now that it's open: debris out, vacuum, blow dust out of the framing only inside containment with HEPA running, wipe everything down, final vac on corners. Biocide only if it's approved for this job and the label allows it: fog isn't the default. This clean structure dries better and has fewer callbacks.

sequence.name: Drying Equipment Re-Setup for Opened Structure
sequence.description: Re-evaluate the now-exposed structure and reposition or add dehumidifiers and air movers for optimal airflow across newly exposed wet surfaces and into cavities. Set up local tenting for bound moisture in subfloors or under cabinets where appropriate. Direct airflow into wall cavities via flood cuts or access points. Re-confirm psychrometric goals and equipment sizing for the current conditions.
sequence.voice_line: With the walls and floors open, we reset drying for the real job. Aim air movers into cavities, set up tenting under subfloors or hard-to-reach spots if needed. Make sure the dehus are sized right for what's exposed now.

sequence.name: Crawlspace or Special Area Final Preparation
sequence.description: If crawlspace is affected: confirm all wet insulation has been dropped and removed or scheduled for removal, address any vapor barrier repairs practical at this stage, set proper airflow management (never push contaminated air into living space), and verify any localized drying or negative air setups are correct.
sequence.voice_line: Crawlspace check: wet insulation handled? Vapor barrier situation noted? Airflow set so we're not pushing bad air upstairs? Any localized tenting or negative air ready?

sequence.name: End of Phase 2 Documentation
sequence.description: Record all materials removed with justification and photos, updated scope of work, new equipment placement diagram, cleaning methods used, any remaining concerns or access limitations, and confirmation that the structure is now ready for active drying.
sequence.voice_line: Phase 2 wrapped: logging exactly what came out and why, new photos of the open structure, drying equipment map, cleaning notes, and any flags for monitoring. Ready to start the real drying work.

pm_board_alignment.notes: This is the primary 'In Progress' production phase. Scope expansion during water chase is expected and must be documented the same day.

hold_triggers.trigger: Scope grows past authorization: waiting on a supplement or change order.
Hidden asbestos or lead stops demo.

phase3.name: Active Drying & Monitoring
phase3.objective: Maintain proper drying conditions and adjust equipment daily until materials meet dry standards.

sequence.name: Daily Psychrometric & Equipment Baseline
sequence.description: Take consistent psychrometric readings (temperature, RH, GPP) in affected areas and unaffected reference points using the same locations and methods every day. Record dehumidifier inlet vs outlet grain depression. Compare current conditions and equipment performance against Day 1 baseline and established dry standard goals.
sequence.voice_line: Morning readings on the usual spots: affected and clean reference areas. Temp, RH, GPP. Check what each dehu is actually pulling. Are we holding the drying gradient we need?

sequence.name: Equipment Inspection, Repositioning & Adjustment
sequence.description: Physically inspect every piece of equipment: dehumidifier performance and condensate removal, air mover positioning and operation, AFD filter condition if running. Reposition air movers to maintain directed airflow across wet surfaces and into any open cavities. Add, remove, or re-duct equipment based on current moisture distribution and drying progress. Implement or adjust local tenting for stubborn bound moisture areas.
sequence.voice_line: Walk every machine. Dehu still pulling strong? Air movers aimed across the wettest spots and into cavities? Any areas lagging that need a tent or redirected air? Adjust now before we leave.

sequence.name: Fixed-Point Moisture Meter Survey
sequence.description: Take pin-type or non-invasive moisture readings at the exact same locations established on Day 1 and post-demo. Include subfloor, exposed framing, wall cavities where accessible, base plates, and any previously elevated readings. Record trends and flag any areas not showing expected improvement.
sequence.voice_line: Moisture survey on the fixed points: same places every single day. Subfloor, framing, cavities, base plates. Look for steady drops and call out anything that's stuck or getting worse.

sequence.name: Hidden & Commonly Missed Area Check
sequence.description: Specifically inspect high-risk missed areas: under and behind cabinets and toe kicks, subfloor beneath base plates, California corners, inside vanity kickboards, under shower pans and tubs (over a crawl, meter the underside of the subfloor from below, hammer probe recommended for subfloor over 3/4 inch; Crawlspaces: Inspection: Underside Subfloor Under Shower Pans), and any wall cavities opened during demo. Use access points to check for remaining moisture or new wicking. Address findings immediately with additional airflow, tenting, or further selective removal if justified. A particle-board, MDF, or compressed-wood cabinet bottom that sat wet is a removal, not more airflow (Demolition: Decision Logic: Material Decision Matrix: Cabinets).
sequence.voice_line: Check the usual hiding spots: under cabinets, base plates, corners, under tubs, vanity kickboards. Use every access we created. Anything still wet back there? We fix it now, not after we think we're done.

sequence.name: Containment, Controls & Safety Re-Verification
sequence.description: Re-inspect all containment integrity, negative pressure performance (if in use), floor protection condition, and engineering controls on every monitoring visit. Repair any gaps, re-tape seams if needed, and confirm makeup air paths are clear. Especially critical after any additional work or foot traffic in the space.
sequence.voice_line: Containment walk: plastic still tight? Negative pressure holding under load? Any new gaps or damage from traffic? Fix it before we go. Safety first, every time.

sequence.name: Progress Analysis & Intervention Planning
sequence.description: Analyze drying trend data. Expect steady moisture reduction; if progress stalls after 48-72 hours of proper conditions, investigate root causes (insufficient airflow across surfaces, hidden moisture sources, equipment undersized for current open volume, temperature issues). Plan targeted interventions such as additional cavity drying, local tenting, or equipment changes for the next visit.
sequence.voice_line: Are the numbers moving like they should? If it's been a couple days and moisture isn't dropping, we troubleshoot: airflow? hidden water? equipment size? Plan the fix for tomorrow: tent it, redirect air, or whatever it takes.

sequence.name: Daily Documentation & Trend Logging
sequence.description: Record all psychrometric data, moisture readings, equipment performance notes, adjustments made, photos of current conditions, and any new observations or concerns. Maintain clear trend documentation that demonstrates progress toward dry standards for defensibility and billing support.
sequence.voice_line: Logging everything: readings, what we moved or changed, photos, and notes on progress. Good trend data protects us and the customer when we say we're done.

pm_board_alignment.notes: Daily board column is usually 'Monitoring' or 'Drying'. Fixed-point discipline and trend logging are what make the job defensible when the adjuster asks questions.

hold_triggers.trigger: Drying stalls from an access issue or a structural or engineering question.

phase4.name: Verification & Closeout
phase4.objective: Confirm the structure is dry, complete final documentation, and close out the job professionally.

sequence.name: Pre-Verification Controls & Safety Gate
sequence.description: Before beginning final verification, confirm all containment, negative pressure, floor protection, and safety measures remain intact and functional. Verify no new hazards have developed. Do not proceed to equipment removal or teardown until final moisture verification has passed.
sequence.voice_line: Before we touch any equipment or start tearing down, let's confirm containment is still solid and there are no new safety issues. We don't pull anything until the numbers say we're dry.

sequence.name: Comprehensive Final Moisture Verification
sequence.description: Perform a full moisture survey using the same methods and locations as previous visits, plus any additional suspect or borderline areas identified during drying. Confirm that all affected materials have reached the established dry standard (within acceptable tolerance of unaffected comparable materials in the same building under current conditions). Document with timestamped readings, photos, and clear comparison to baseline.
sequence.voice_line: Final moisture verification: every fixed point plus anything that was borderline or hidden. The numbers have to show we're at dry standard or better. No 'feels dry': data only.

sequence.name: Structural, Cavity & Contents Inspection
sequence.description: Visually and physically inspect all opened wall cavities, subfloor areas, crawlspace (if applicable), under-cabinet spaces, and any other previously wet assemblies for remaining moisture signs, staining, microbial growth, or structural concerns. Confirm contents that were cleaned or stored on-site are in acceptable condition and properly returned or staged.
sequence.voice_line: Walk every opened area and the crawlspace one more time. Any missed moisture, staining, or issues? Check that contents we handled are good. Everything ready for the customer to see?

sequence.name: Controlled Teardown & Site Restoration
sequence.description: Only after verification passes, systematically remove drying equipment, air movers, containment plastic, floor protection, and any temporary supports. Clean any dust or debris generated during teardown. Return the site to as close to pre-loss condition as practical, protecting finished surfaces during removal.
sequence.voice_line: Verification passed: now we pull equipment and containment. Clean up after the teardown so the place looks sharp for the customer. Protect floors and walls while we work.

sequence.name: Customer Walkthrough & Education
sequence.description: Conduct a thorough walkthrough with the customer (or representative) of every affected area. Present before-and-after photos side-by-side. Explain in plain language what was done, why certain materials were removed or dried in place, what the dry standard means, and what signs to watch for that would indicate a problem returning. Provide written recommendations for any remaining repairs or preventive maintenance.
sequence.voice_line: Customer walkthrough time. Show the before photos next to what it looks like now. Explain what we did and why in normal words. Make sure they know what to watch for and that we're a phone call away if anything feels off.

sequence.name: Final Documentation Package Assembly
sequence.description: Compile the complete job documentation package: all pre-loss, during, and post photos with descriptions; daily moisture and psychrometric logs with trend analysis; equipment runtime and placement records; detailed scope of work with justification for all removals; category determination rationale; dry standard evidence; customer communications and sign-off. Ensure everything is organized, dated, and defensible for billing, insurance, and potential disputes.
sequence.voice_line: Final package: photos, logs, scope changes, dry standard proof, everything. Over-document rather than under. This protects everyone and makes billing and future reference easy.

sequence.name: Job Closeout, Warranty & Follow-Up
sequence.description: Obtain any required final customer signatures. Explain warranty coverage and duration clearly. Provide contact information for any post-job concerns. Secure the property, complete vehicle loading, and note any lessons learned or process improvements for the team. Confirm all billable items and time are accurately captured.
sequence.voice_line: Customer signs off, we go over the warranty, give them our direct number. Site locked up, truck loaded clean. Anything we learned on this job that the rest of the team should know? Job closed strong.

pm_board_alignment.notes: Nothing moves to 'Closed' until verification numbers pass. Teardown before dry standard is one of the fastest ways to create callbacks.

hold_status.name: Hold Status
hold_status.frequency: Common, occasional, usually brief but sometimes extended. Projects can go on hold at any time for a variety of reasons, this list is non exhaustive
hold_status.objective: Stabilize the loss at the absolute minimum level required to prevent immediate secondary damage while the job waits for insurance approval, abatement scheduling, plumber coordination, or other external constraints. Do only minimal hold actions: protect contents from standing water, flag safety hazards, and install minimal plastic containment if needed. Do not run unauthorized extraction, demolition, or full drying service until the hold is lifted. Any drying or air filtration equipment requires a direct customer conversation and stays at the smallest number justified by need and out-of-pocket affordability if insurance does not cover.

sequence.name: Verify Hold Reason and Timeline
sequence.description: Confirm with customer or PM exactly why the job is on hold (insurance claim pending, abatement scheduled, an issue with a material interested party, plumber coordination, or other constraint) and get the expected release date or trigger event.
sequence.voice_line: We're putting this one on hold: insurance approval, abatement, material interested party, or plumber coming in. What's the expected timeline before we can move forward? Hold stays minimal until that trigger clears.

sequence.name: Basic Safety, Contents Protection, and Minimal (but sufficient, to order) Containment
sequence.description: Move or elevate any contents sitting in standing water. Flag any immediate safety hazards. Install minimal plastic containment where it helps control the environment. Have a direct conversation with the customer about placing a minimal number of drying or air filtration units based on actual need and what they can afford out of pocket if insurance does not cover. Do not expand into unauthorized extraction or demolition. If hold gear is running, watch GPP delta for vapor management: do not chase tighter depression while on hold.
sequence.voice_line: Hold limits: contents out of water, safety flagged, a few sheets of plastic if needed. For equipment, talk about what's actually necessary and what you can cover if insurance doesn't come through: no unauthorized extract or full service on hold.

sequence.name: Documentation of Hold Status
sequence.description: Record the reason for the hold, expected release trigger, minimal actions taken, and any customer communications. Update the job file so the hold is visible to PMs and schedulers. Note start dwell clock / known wet time so the resume re-gate can use elapsed dwell.
sequence.voice_line: Logging the hold reason and expected release. This keeps it visible on the board until we're cleared to proceed.

hold_reasons.insurance_approval: Customer unsure if insurance will cover; waiting for claim filing, adjuster notes, and scope approval. Minimal work only to avoid billing the customer directly.
hold_reasons.abatement_scheduling: Known asbestos or other hazardous material present; licensed abatement company must complete work before restoration demo can begin. Job stays on the board until abatement confirms completion.
hold_reasons.plumber_coordination: Water heater, supply lines, or other plumbing must be moved or temporarily extended before demo can continue. Job waits for plumber to complete work and confirm reattachment is possible.
hold_reasons.material_interested_party: Homeowner death triggering probate/estate delays, mortgage company holding the insurance check, HOA or landlord-tenant dispute where no one will sign the work authorization, or contents evaluation hold where adjuster wants to inspect high-value or totaled items before allowing removal.
hold_reasons.other_constraints: Any external factor preventing full work: permit delays, landlord approval, equipment availability, or customer request to pause.

hold_status.minimal_actions_only: Basic contents protection from standing water, safety flagging, and minimal plastic containment only. No unauthorized extraction, demolition, or full equipment layout. Any drying or air filtration equipment must be discussed directly with the customer and limited to the smallest number justified by need and their out-of-pocket affordability if insurance does not cover. On hold, manage vapor with GPP awareness: do not chase tighter depression or expand scope until the hold lifts.
hold_status.when_to_resume: Insurance approval received, abatement company confirms work complete, plumber completes move or temporary extension and confirms reattachment possible, material interested party authorizes and signs, or other constraint resolved. Before returning to demo or active drying: re-verify category using elapsed dwell time plus current evidence (odor, discoloration, organic debris, visible growth); re-check PPE and engineering controls against the current category; document the hold period and the re-gate findings. Then resume the phase that was active when the hold was placed: do not skip the category/PPE re-gate after a long hold.

pm_board_alignment.notes: Jobs land here for insurance approval, abatement, plumber coordination, or material interested party issues. Minimal actions only.

hold_status.voice_note: Hold means minimal only: contents up, safety flagged, light plastic if needed. No unauthorized extract or full dry-out until we're cleared. After a long hold, re-check category, PPE, and controls against dwell time and what you see now before you jump back into demo or drying.
hold_status.resume_voice_line: Hold's lifted: before demo or drying, re-verify category with the elapsed dwell and what we see now, then match PPE and controls. Document that re-gate, then pick up the phase we were on.
hold_status.entry_rule: A job can enter Hold from any phase (0-4). Each phase lists its known stall points in hold_triggers.
hold_status.exit_rule: Record why and when the job stopped. Once the constraint clears, return to the phase the job left. If days have passed, re-verify readings (and category, PPE, and controls per When to Resume) before picking up the work.
hold_status.judgment_note: Whether a project pauses is mostly a judgment call worked out between the materially interested parties: the restoration company, the homeowner, and the insurance carrier. The kit labels common hold points; it is not an exhaustive checklist.

demolition.title: Demolition
demolition.description: Selective removal decisions, physical sequence, special assemblies, access prep, controls, and post-demo cleaning. Shallow tree structure for scale.

decision_logic.title: Decision Logic
decision_logic.description: Remove vs dry decisions, material matrix, water chasing, and category effects. Controlled removal of materials that cannot be reliably dried or that present unacceptable risk if left in place: strategic and minimal; only remove what is necessary to allow proper drying or eliminate unacceptable risk.
key_activities: Assess before cutting: check for asbestos, lead, hidden utilities, and structural concerns
Determine remove vs dry-in-place decisions using material type, category, and dwell time
Work top-down and outside-in when possible
Use surgical precision around electrical, plumbing, HVAC, and customer belongings
Protect all surfaces and contents that will remain
Set up dust and debris containment during demo
Proper bagging and removal of contaminated materials
Documentation of what was removed and justification
critical_decision_points: Remove vs dry in place? (Consider material type, category, dwell time, and drying feasibility)
How aggressive should removal be? (Category + dwell time are major drivers)
Can we use targeted methods (drill holes, flood cuts, access points) instead of full removal?
Do we need lead/asbestos testing before starting major demo?

material_decision_matrix.description: A structured reference for deciding whether to restore materials in place or remove and replace them. Organized by material type, water category, and approximate dwell time.
key_principles: Drying finish and porous materials in place is Category 1 only (Scoping: Equipment Timing: Drying in Place). On Category 2 or 3, porous and semi-porous finish materials come out. Structure that can't be removed as a finish (framing, slab, structural plywood subfloor, masonry, heavy timber, steel) is cleaned and dried, not a dry-in-place call.
Time + Category = Risk. Longer dwell time combined with higher category strongly pushes decisions toward removal of porous and organic materials.
Dwell bands (kit-wide): short dwell = ≤48 hours; long dwell = >48 hours in warm conditions. Matrix short_dwell / long_dwell cells use this clock.
Modern flooring systems (LVP, sheet vinyl, tile over liners) frequently trap water underneath, making removal or major intervention more common than with older construction.
When access for proper airflow is poor, even resilient materials may need to be removed.
When in doubt on Category 2/3 or long-dwell jobs, lean toward removal of high-risk materials.

drywall.category_1_short_dwell: Usually restore in place if it returns to dry standard with no musty odor or softening.
drywall.category_1_long_dwell: Often remove if significant wicking or hidden moisture is found behind the paper.
drywall.category_2_short_dwell: Remove affected sections (drying in place is Category 1 only).
drywall.category_3_any_dwell: Remove (gypsum board in Category 3 is unrestorable).
drywall.ceiling_note: Sagging ceiling board is a hazard and a removal: support it first.
drywall.cut_height_note: On Category 3, cut above the wet line and round up to the next 2-foot interval. There is no fixed cut height in inches. Cut above the highest wet reading, not the visible water line.

dimensional_lumber_framing.category_1_short_dwell: Almost always restore in place with proper drying and monitoring.
dimensional_lumber_framing.category_1_long_dwell: Usually restore in place unless significant checking or mold evidence exists.
dimensional_lumber_framing.category_2_short_dwell: Often restorable with good drying access and consistent monitoring.
dimensional_lumber_framing.category_2_long_dwell: Usually restorable with aggressive drying and monitoring.
dimensional_lumber_framing.category_3_short_dwell: Typically restorable with thorough cleaning, drying, and monitoring.
dimensional_lumber_framing.category_3_long_dwell: Restorable unless dry rot or structural compromise is present. Clean, dry, and monitor closely.

particle_board_mdf_osb.note: Typically if water touches this stuff, it’s toast. Harbors mold very well, and the water just breaks it down immediately. It’s so cheap, it’s almost always tossed even in a Cat 1 short dwell. But it depends on the customer too. Cabinet bottoms are not that call. They hold the box. See cabinets.
particle_board_mdf_osb.category_1_short_dwell: Sometimes restorable if caught very early with minimal swelling. Not cabinet bases or bottom panels: light Category 1 exposure can look fine, but meaningful dwell means replace. They swell, they hold the box, and the bottoms are cheap (Demolition: Decision Logic: Material Decision Matrix: Cabinets).
particle_board_mdf_osb.category_1_long_dwell: Usually remove: swelling is often permanent. Cabinet bottoms: replace.

closed_cell_spray_foam.category_1_any_dwell: Usually stays. Remove where you need to inspect behind it (see Inspection Rule).
closed_cell_spray_foam.category_2_short_dwell: Inspection-driven: probe the framing for wicking height, remove foam a margin above it, and check for growth.
closed_cell_spray_foam.category_2_long_dwell: Inspection-driven, with a wider margin; contamination on the face is cleaned or removed.
closed_cell_spray_foam.category_3_any_dwell: Inspection-driven; often comes off further because contamination behind it is likely. Contaminated foam is removed.
closed_cell_spray_foam.note: Closed-cell usually doesn't absorb, but it slows the dry of what is behind it.
closed_cell_spray_foam.inspection_rule: Removing spray or closed-cell foam is mainly an inspection step: the foam itself is rarely ruined. Probe the framing to find how high the moisture wicked, then remove foam above that line by a margin (a ways and then some) to look for growth behind it. Not a blanket keep or a blanket remove by category.

concrete_slab.category_1_any_dwell: Almost always restore in place with proper drying methods.
concrete_slab.category_2_any_dwell: Restore in place with enhanced airflow and dehumidification.
concrete_slab.category_3_any_dwell: Usually restore in place but with strong engineering controls and extended drying.
concrete_slab.note: A slab under hardwood or vinyl is a long dry confirmed by the flooring warranty test methods, not a pin meter. A falling reading on new concrete is hydration.

lvp_or_sheet_vinyl.category_1_short_dwell: Sometimes restorable if water is extracted quickly and edges can be lifted for drying. Category 1 only.
lvp_or_sheet_vinyl.category_1_long_dwell: High chance of needing removal or major intervention due to trapped moisture.
lvp_or_sheet_vinyl.category_2_any_dwell: Remove (Category 2/3 under a floating or sheet floor is a removal), then dry the substrate.

carpet_and_pad.category_1_short_dwell: Carpet sometimes salvageable; pad is usually removed.
carpet_and_pad.category_1_long_dwell: Pad almost always removed. Carpet often removed as well.
carpet_and_pad.category_2_any_dwell: Remove carpet and pad (drying in place is Category 1 only). The customer may elect to keep and clean the carpet in certain instances by signing a release of procedure.
carpet_and_pad.glue_down_and_woven: Cushion-backed glue-down may not come up whole. Woven carpet is secured on all four edges and dried from the top. Significant subfloor damage usually means the carpet goes.

tile_and_thinset.category_1_short_dwell: Often restorable if water is extracted quickly and weep holes or edge lifting can be used.
tile_and_thinset.category_1_long_dwell: Frequently requires removal or major intervention, especially with liners or uncoupling membranes.
tile_and_thinset.category_2_any_dwell: Remove tile, thinset, and liner on Category 2 (drying in place is Category 1 only). Thinset/mastic are asbestos-suspect: sample in Evaluate, hold until clear.
tile_and_thinset.category_3_any_dwell: Generally remove on Category 3: take out the tile, thinset, and liner. Contaminated water gets under the tile and into the thinset and substrate, where it can't be cleaned or verified in place. Tile on a concrete slab is the knock test first (Demolition: Special Assemblies: Flooring Insights: Tile Over Concrete: Knock Test): hollow on Category 3 comes out; solid usually stays. If a case looks different, write down why you left it.

fiberglass_insulation.category_1_short_dwell: Unfaced fiberglass wet only at the bottom can sometimes stay; otherwise usually remove. Collapsed insulation is a removal.

cellulose_insulation.any_category_any_dwell: Remove. Wet cellulose comes out on any category.

open_cell_spray_foam.any_category: Holds water. Category 2/3 or saturated: remove. Category 1 short: case by case; it slows the dry behind it. Removal also serves as the inspection behind it (see Demolition: Decision Logic: Material Decision Matrix: Closed Cell Spray Foam: Inspection Rule).

mineral_fiber_lay_in_tile.category_1: Replace if stained, sagging, or wet through (cheap; usually replaced).
mineral_fiber_lay_in_tile.category_3_any_dwell: Replace. Older ceiling panels are an asbestos check first.

plaster_and_lath.category_1: Usually stays and dries in place: slow saturation, slow dry (Class 4). Asbestos/lead check before disturbing.
plaster_and_lath.category_2_or_3: Remove (drying in place is Category 1 only). Asbestos/lead check before disturbing.

solid_hardwood_flooring.category_1: Often dryable; sudden leaks dry better than slow; never sand cupped boards early.
solid_hardwood_flooring.category_2_or_3: Removal, then dry the substrate, then the finish.

laminate_and_engineered_wood.any_category: Swollen laminate is unrestorable. Category 2/3 under it: removal.

wallpaper_and_paneling.category_3_any_dwell: Remove. Paneling over furring hides cavities.
wallpaper_and_paneling.category_1: Often a vapor lid: open or remove to dry the wall behind it.

cabinets.particleboard_category_1: On paper, Category 1 with light exposure can look salvageable: someone may say leave the bases. Dwell is what kills particle-board, MDF, and compressed-wood bottoms: they swell, lose strength, and they hold the whole cabinet. Prefer replace those bottoms when wet with meaningful dwell. The material is cheap, same class of call as drywall or insulation. Don't gamble on salvage.
cabinets.solid_wood_category_1: Category 1 only: usually dry in place: pull toe kicks and drill holes so the cavity dries (skip if trashed or moldy).
cabinets.note: Swollen compressed-wood boxes are discards. The bottoms call is particle board, MDF, and compressed wood. Solid-wood boxes can dry in place on Category 1 only.
cabinets.voice_note: Cat 1 with light exposure can look like you should leave the cabinet bases. Dwell is what kills particle-board bottoms: they swell, lose strength, and they hold the whole box. The bottoms are cheap, same call as drywall or insulation. Don't gamble. Replace them. Solid wood can dry in place on Cat 1 only.
cabinets.solid_wood_category_2_or_3: Not a dry-in-place: remove (salvage deconstruction billed separately from tear-out).

hvac_duct.note: Qualified HVAC contractor; contaminated system stays off.

structural_steel_and_fireproofing.any_category: Steel is restorable. Inspect the fireproofing; pre-1981 fireproofing is an asbestos check.

heavy_timber.any_category: Restorable; slow dry (Class 4). Clean if contaminated.

masonry_and_cmu.any_category: Usually restorable; slow dry. CMU loose-filled with vermiculite or perlite is an asbestos check.

multilayer_subfloor_and_gym_floor.any_category: Water under a multilayer floor is a removal of the wet layers. A dance or gym floor in Category 3 comes off.

fire_rated_assemblies.rule: Any opening is closed back to the rating. Required.

tack_strip.category_1: Cover exposed strip (puncture hazard); can stay if sound.
tack_strip.unsanitary_water: Remove with the appropriate protection and disposal.

electrical_components.submerged_breaker_or_panel: Replace / qualified electrician. Wet electrical stays off until cleared.
electrical_components.wet_nm_cable: Wet NM-B cable wicks along its paper wrap; dry-location cable is a replace per manufacturer and industry guidance. Document it and flag it: the electrician makes the cut. Detail: Electrical Safety: Electrical Extras: Wet NM Cable.

crawl_soil_and_vapor_barrier.rule: The dry is the structure, not the soil. Contaminated vapor barrier comes out; pulling it adds evaporation load. A biocide on the soil does nothing.

material_reconciliation.purpose: Shows where the kit matrix agrees with, is stricter than, or differs from the baseline on materials and assemblies, including the informative lines in Base Science: Material Behavior: Reference Lines. One artifact; the baseline's Category 3 removal lines sit on top of it.
agreements: Dimensional framing: usually restorable (clean and dry).
kit_stricter_or_different: Carpet Category 2: the kit default is to remove carpet and pad. The customer may elect to keep and clean the carpet in certain instances by signing a release of procedure.
Plywood Category 3 'usually restorable', not addressed in the baseline; kept as field practice with cleaning.
Tile and thinset: the Category 2 row follows the baseline (tile is a lid; the dry is the cavity). Category 1 and 3 rows are added detail.

Particleboard Category 1 short 'sometimes restorable' still applies off the cabinet, if caught very early with minimal swelling. Cabinet bases and bottom panels that sat wet are a replace: cheap, and they hold the box. Category 1 light exposure is not a leave-the-bases call. The baseline only addresses Cat 2/3 particleboard cabinets (replace) and swollen case goods (discard).
fixed_conflicts: Cellulose was grouped with fiberglass ('Cat 1 short can sometimes be dried'); baseline: wet cellulose comes out on any category. Split.
LVP/sheet vinyl Category 2 'usually requires removal or significant intervention'; baseline: Category 2/3 under a floating or sheet floor is a removal.

chasing_the_water.description: The common practice of progressively discovering and adjusting scope as hidden water is revealed during demo and investigation.
common_hidden_paths: Along the backside of baseplates and bottom plates
Interstitial spaces (wall cavities, behind cabinets, under toe kicks, inside vanities)
Under vapor-barrier flooring (LVP, hardwood over slab, tile)
Behind trim, baseboards, and quarter round
Into checks, end grain, and voids in wood framing
chasing_the_water.field_reality: On many jobs, especially Category 2/3 or with significant dwell time, you will need to expand the original scope as you chase water into hidden areas. This is normal and expected.
chasing_the_water.approach: Start with the known wet areas. As you demo, actively look for and follow water into hidden spaces. Continue expanding until you stop finding active moisture or water staining. Document the progression.
chasing_the_water.mindset: Be prepared for scope to grow during the job. 'Chasing the water' is part of doing the job correctly, not scope creep.
chasing_the_water.voice_note: Initial scopes are almost always low on these jobs. Water hides behind baseplates, in interstitial spaces, and under flooring you can't read through. Keep opening things up until you stop finding wet material.

category_specific_guidance.category_1: More conservative. Prioritize minimal removal and targeted drying methods when possible.
category_specific_guidance.category_2: Drying in place is Category 1 only: remove porous and semi-porous finish materials; clean and dry structure.
category_specific_guidance.category_3: Drying in place is Category 1 only: remove porous and semi-porous finish materials; clean and dry structure under engineering controls. Extended dwell increases hidden microbial risk.

decision_logic.voice_considerations: When deciding what stays and what comes out, look at the material, the category, and how long the water has been there. Particle board, insulation, and drywall on anything beyond clean short-dwell water are usually better removed. Particle-board cabinet bottoms are that same call: Category 1 can look light on paper, but dwell swells them and they hold the box. Prefer replace. The bottoms are cheap. Solid-wood boxes can dry in place on Category 1 only. Dimensional lumber and closed-cell foam give you more room to dry. Modern flooring systems with vapor barriers often need physical intervention. Document why you made the call.
field_practice: Use a knife on painted and caulked edges when removing finished materials so you don't rip the paint.
Assess before you cut: asbestos, lead, hidden utilities, and structure first.
When removing vanities or base cabinets, never cut the water supply lines. Cut the cabinet back panel around the pipe penetrations.
Protect what stays: Ram Board, heavy builder's paper, or plywood on finished surfaces, secured with low-adhesive blue tape.
On Category 3, cut above the wet line and round up to the next 2-foot interval. There is no fixed cut height in inches. Cut above the highest wet reading, not the visible damage line.
Cap opened water supply lines with pressure caps even if the valve is off.
On lath and plaster, expect chicken wire and mixed fasteners; a carbide multi-tool often beats a reciprocating saw. Plaster can often stay and dry (slow); it is an asbestos/lead check first.
Remove exposed fasteners, nails, and screws as you work.

Saw depth stops at the wallboard. In walls, get wet insulation off the framing so the framing is exposed and can dry, and bag it right away in 6-mil, especially when people live above or below. Anything crossing a clean area is double-bagged. Open the pockets of saturation. Crawlspaces follow Crawlspaces: Insulation Removal.
If removing sections of cabinets, shore the stone countertop temporarily (Demolition: Access Prep: Countertop Removal: Props).

Particle-board, MDF, or compressed-wood cabinet bottoms that sat wet: replace them. Category 1 with light exposure can look like a save. Dwell is what kills them, and the bottoms are cheap: same call as drywall or insulation. Solid-wood boxes can dry in place on Category 1 only: pull the toe kick and open the cavity.
Wood paneling in basements is often over furring strips: hidden cavities that need attention on Category 3.
common_mistakes: Starting demo without proper pre-assessment (asbestos, lead, utilities)
Over-cutting and removing more than necessary
Under-cutting on Category 3 or long-dwell jobs (callbacks)
Not setting up dust containment before starting demo
Not documenting what was removed and why
Working bottom-up or inside-out, which increases cross-contamination
Leaving particle-board cabinet bottoms because Category 1 looked light on paper. Dwell swells them. They hold the box, and the part is cheap: replace them.

physical_sequence.title: Physical Sequence
physical_sequence.description: Standard top-down order and flooring approach.

demo_order.name: Demo Order – Top Down with Practical Access
demo_order.description: Standard physical removal sequence that prioritizes safety, surface protection, and systematic investigation. Follow top-down logic on walls and ceilings. On flooring, start where access is cleanest and easiest, then work systematically while chasing hidden water and protecting finished surfaces.
steps: 0. Engineering controls before any demo: 6 mil and 4 mil plastic, HEPA negative air, floor protection, painter's plastic. Commonly missed. Exception: items the lead names (e.g. an appliance that won't fit out once the plastic is up) come out first (Scoping: Order of Work: Engineering Controls Before Demo).
1. Remove all trim (any time before drywall): door casing, window trim, baseboards, quarter round, and cove molding. Pull all protruding nails.
2. Remove outlet and switch covers, light fixtures, and any wall-mounted heaters.
3. Remove all wall-mounted fixtures and accessories: mirrors, towel bars, toilet paper holders, soap dishes, grab bars, etc.

4. Sink & Toilet Decision: Shut off water supplies. For sinks: disconnect water lines and drain, then install compression caps on the lines. For toilets: shut off water, flush to empty the tank, disconnect supply line, and plug the drain with a drain plug. Toilets come out before the flooring under them. Plumbing caps go on right after any water-line item comes out (dishwasher, fridge, toilet, sink).

5. Appliance Decision: Handle per Demolition: Access Prep: Appliance Handling. Appliances come out before cabinets, around the same time as countertops. Default pull order: refrigerator, range, dishwasher, washing machine, dryer, water heater. Cap water lines as each comes out.

6. Countertop Decision (with appliances, before base cabinets): per Scoping: Countertops: stone almost always off first; cheap top on a non-salvaged particle-board unit goes with the unit; on a salvage cabinet the top comes off first; tile tops ask about bullnose and backsplash. Remove backsplash if present.

7. Cabinet & Vanity Decision: Remove upper cabinets, lower cabinets, vanities, and full-height cabinets if affected material is behind or underneath them. Save undamaged cabinets and countertops for reinstallation. A particle-board, MDF, or compressed-wood bottom that sat wet is not a save: replace it (Demolition: Decision Logic: Material Decision Matrix: Cabinets). Solid-wood boxes can dry in place on Category 1 only. Salvage cabinets: pull the toe kick and drill holes so the cavity dries (skip if trashed or moldy). Salvage deconstruction bills separately from tear-out.
8. Tile & Tub Decision: Remove tile walls, tub surrounds, bathtubs, showers, or toilets if affected material is behind or underneath.

9. Walls usually before floors, often the same day; order depends on access and materials. Cut and remove wall and ceiling material (drywall, plaster, or tile wall), then pull all nails and screws from studs and ceiling joists.
10. Pull wet insulation.

11. Flooring Decision, top down: finish floor (carpet, laminate, vinyl, hardwood, tile, glue-down), then underlayment or pad and tack strip, then mud bed / thinset / self-leveler, then subfloor denail and scrape. Thinset, mastic and old self-leveler are asbestos-suspect: sample in Evaluate and hold until clear.
12. After all demo: framing cleanup and mold cleaning. Trash goes out as needed throughout, not only at the end.

physical_sequence.nail_removal: After removing trim, baseboards, drywall, or paneling, pull or hammer down all visible nails, screws, and staples. This is especially important around doorways, convex corners, and base plates where people will be walking or passing through. On floors, either remove completely or hammer flat and tape over. Reasonable thoroughness is expected, while there is always one more nail, the space must be made safe to walk through.

muck_out.title: Muck Out
muck_out.description: Muck out is demolition work. Crews often cut and roll up the vapor barrier with the muck.
muck_out.not_cleaning: Muck out is not cleaning: the area stays dirty until new visqueen or vapor barrier goes down.

closed_cell_foam_water_intrusion.title: Closed-Cell Spray Foam on Below-Grade Walls: Water Intrusion Decision Framework
closed_cell_foam_water_intrusion.description: Decision framework for closed-cell spray foam assemblies on below-grade walls. Distinguishes water entry from below versus from above. Foam removal is mainly an inspection step: the foam is rarely ruined; it comes off to see what's behind it. Removal height is driven by actual moisture readings plus a margin, rather than fixed arbitrary cuts.
core_principles: Closed-cell spray foam is non-porous and does not absorb or wick water through its matrix.
Water behavior depends on entry point: from below it wicks up the wood framing; from above it can run down the foam-concrete interface or micro-channels.
Once the face is opened, the remaining risk is primarily bound moisture in the double base plate and lower studs, plus any hidden mold at the wood-foam interface.
Do not drill the studs. Use standard hammer-probe or screw method to map the actual vertical extent of elevated moisture. Remove foam only to that height plus a safety margin.

from_below.behavior: Water wicks upward through the double base plate and lower framing. Foam itself remains largely unaffected except at the bottom interface.
from_below.recommended_default: Targeted height-based removal driven by moisture readings.
from_below.key_risk_zone: Double base plate and the measured height of elevated moisture in the studs.

from_above.behavior: Water can run down the back of the foam via micro-channels, the foam-concrete interface, or imperfections in the spray application.
from_above.recommended_default: Full removal of affected foam is the conservative and lower-risk approach.
from_above.key_risk_zone: Entire height of the foam assembly plus any areas water may have traveled behind it.

strategy_targeted_height_based.name: Moisture-Mapped Targeted Removal (Primary Method)
strategy_targeted_height_based.description: Open the face with a flood cut. Use hammer probe or screw method on the exposed wood to determine the actual height of elevated moisture. Remove foam only to that height plus a couple of extra inches for safety. Leave remaining foam in place. Dry the exposed wood face.
strategy_targeted_height_based.applicable_only_when: Water entered from below and there is no extensive visible mold or musty odor requiring broader cavity access.
steps: Establish fixed-point moisture readings on the exposed studs and double base plate using hammer probe or the screw method. Map how high the elevated moisture actually travels.
