Remove foam only to the highest reading plus a safety margin of a couple extra inches across the affected bays.
In any bay that already shows visible mold on the face, remove foam for the full height of that bay or until clean material is reached.
Perform a nose test in the newly exposed interface. If odor is present, continue removing foam upward until the cavity is clean.
Build an angled tent over the opened strip and pipe dry air to dry the exposed wood face and base plate.
Document the moisture map, the exact height of foam removed, inspection findings, and drying rationale.
advantages: Labor and material cost scale directly to measured damage instead of arbitrary full or fixed-height cuts.
Preserves the majority of existing R-value.
Avoids unnecessary invasive drilling of structural members.
Still verifies the highest-risk interface zone with real data.
Faster and less physically destructive than full removal.
limitations: Requires disciplined fixed-point moisture mapping and documentation to remain defensible.
Residual interface behind retained foam must be acknowledged.
Not appropriate when water entered from above.

strategy_full_removal.name: Full Removal of All Affected Bays
when_to_choose: Visible mold on the face of removed drywall or framing that may have penetrated the cavity
Insurance carrier or company policy requires complete removal
Category 2 or 3 water or long dwell time with elevated hidden mold concern
Owner or risk tolerance demands near-zero callback probability.
advantages: Near-zero hidden moisture or mold risk.
Simplest to defend under review or dispute.
disadvantages: Highest labor cost: full demo and disposal of all foam.
Highest material cost: full re-spray required later.
Complete loss of existing R-value in the affected area.

closed_cell_foam_water_intrusion.voice_considerations: On closed-cell foam below grade: first figure out if the water came from below or from above. From below we map the actual moisture height with probes or screws and only cut to that line plus a couple inches. From above, full removal of the affected bays is usually the safer call. Don't drill the studs: the readings already tell us what we need.

power_tool_option.description: Specialized closed-cell foam removal power tools exist. Most restoration companies do not carry them.
power_tool_option.when_to_consider: Large square footage or repeated jobs where the specialized tool pays for itself in labor savings.

subcontracting_option.description: Specialist contractors who focus on spray foam removal and replacement can be brought in for edge cases.
subcontracting_option.when_to_consider: One-off large jobs, lack of in-house equipment or experience, or when the labor hours would be economically inefficient for your team.

decision_notes.primary_method: Moisture-mapped targeted removal is the preferred default for water entry from below. It eliminates arbitrary cuts and makes cost scale exactly to the measured damage.
decision_notes.inspection_gate: The height of foam removed is determined by actual hammer-probe or screw readings plus a small safety margin. A nose test in the exposed strip remains a practical secondary check.
decision_notes.from_above_warning: When water enters from above, targeted height-based removal is not recommended. Water can exploit micro-channels or the foam-concrete interface and travel behind the foam, making full removal the lower-liability path.
decision_notes.no_drilling: Do not drill patterns into the studs. The standard RestoKit fixed-point methods (hammer probe or screws) already give the data needed without creating additional penetrations.
decision_notes.documentation_requirement: Document the moisture map (readings and locations), the exact height of foam removed, visible findings, and the reasoning for the selected approach. This protects the technician and the company under review.

belly_wrap_access.title: Belly Wrap Access: I-Cut Method
belly_wrap_access.description: When temporary access is needed through the black moisture barrier belly wrap on mobile homes without replacing material, cut a big I-shape that spans the entire bay between joists.
key_principles: One long vertical slit running the full width of the bay with short horizontal cuts at top and bottom creates wide flaps that peel open for full access
After work is complete, simply tape the I back together to reseal if no new material is needed
Prevents tearing or uncontrolled ripping of the belly wrap during access
belly_wrap_access.voice_considerations: On these old trailers, cut a big I in the belly wrap that spans the whole bay: vertical slit with little cross cuts at top and bottom so you can peel it open clean and just tape it back shut when you're done.

old_trailer_floor_assembly_note.description: Practical guidance for working with non-standard floor assemblies common in older mobile homes and trailers. Particle board, hardboard/Masonite, or similar material often serves as both subfloor and underlayment with no separate layer. Open crawlspace directly below joists.
key_principles: These older mobile homes frequently have non-standard floor assemblies. The visible particle board, hardboard, or similar material often functions as both subfloor and underlayment with no separate layer underneath. Walls and ceilings can also have combined or missing layers (paneling directly on studs, no drywall, etc.). Always verify what you are actually cutting through.
Cut affected subfloor in manageable sections back to sound, dry edges.
Once a section is removed, step down through the opening onto the crawlspace floor: this is standard efficient practice on this build.
Chase water immediately as you open each section; it frequently continues under adjacent runs of subfloor and along joists or baseplates.
Debris falls through into the crawlspace; keep the space usable as you work.
Do not over-barricade every new opening when actively using the crawlspace for access.
Work from supported perimeter areas or directly on joists once sections are open. Stay off center of spongy/taped sections until bad material is gone.
Cut in small controllable pieces (score first, then reciprocating saw or multi-tool set just above joist depth). Lift pieces up and out when practical.
Step down into each new opening. Use the holes as access points.
Continue until sound, dry edges or moisture readings stabilize.

decision_framework: Fast/sudden leaks give significantly better odds of saving hardwood than long/slow leaks.
Water coming from underneath (crawlspace, subfloor) is much harder to recover than surface water.
Never sand cupped hardwood too early: allow it to dry and flatten naturally first.
hardwood_floors.voice_note: On hardwood, sudden leaks are your friend. Water from below is the enemy. And never sand cupped boards too early: let them dry flat first.

tile_over_concrete.decision_guidance: On a concrete slab, knock the tile before the remove-or-leave call (Knock Test). Also weigh dwell time, whether the customer wants to save the tile, and the installation method (especially a liner or uncoupling membrane).
tile_over_concrete.knock_test: Knock the tile on a concrete slab. A hollow sound means voids or grooves in the mortar where water can sit; on Category 3, remove it. A solid sound usually means there is no space for water to go; removal is not required.
tile_over_concrete.voice_note: Tile over concrete: knock it. Hollow means voids or grooves in the mortar where water can sit: on Category 3, take it out. Solid usually means no space for water to go, so removal is not required. Still take it out if there's a smell, or the customer or the company is worried about health and welfare. If it was affected and stays, get a signed release. Don't push removal just to check a box. Write down why.

cement_board.title: Cement Board and Mortar Board
cement_board.description: Demolition of cement board or mortar board. Billed SF on the sheet.

access_prep.title: Access Prep
access_prep.description: Clearing the way so wet materials behind or under fixtures can be reached.

appliance_handling.description: Decision logic, safety steps, and field techniques for handling appliances during pre-demo prep and selective demolition. Appliance work is usually access prep (done so you can properly reach wet materials behind or under the unit), not pure demolition of the appliance itself.
key_activities: Appliances come out before cabinets, around the same time as countertops.
Identify every utility connected to the appliance (water, power, gas) before touching anything.
Shut off utilities at the source or local valve and verify they are actually off.
Disconnect lines cleanly. Cap every supply line right after each water-line item comes out (dishwasher, fridge, toilet): before moving to the next item.
On gas appliances (including water heaters): perform soap test on capped lines and connections before leaving the area.
Protect finished floors and surrounding surfaces before moving any appliance.
Document condition, connections, and surrounding area with photos before and after handling.
Decide remove vs protect-in-place based on access needs, scope, contamination level, and salvage value.
appliance_handling.voice_considerations: Before you start cutting around any appliance, shut off its utilities, verify the shutoff, cap the lines, and soap test if it’s gas. Protect the floor, photo everything, then decide: pull it for access or protect it and work around it. Appliance work is access prep, not demo. When in doubt on gas, stop and escalate.
critical_decision_points: Does this appliance need to move to access wet materials behind, under, or around it?
Is this appliance worth saving? (Especially garbage disposals, newer fridges, and dishwashers on clean or short-dwell losses.)
Is gas involved? If yes, extra verification and soap test are required.
Can we safely cap and test ourselves, or does company policy require a licensed plumber?

practical_guidance.mindset: Appliance handling is almost always access prep work. You are clearing the way so you can demo the actual wet assemblies. Do not treat it as core demolition: the goal is controlled removal or protection with minimal damage to the appliance and the finished space.
practical_guidance.removal_sequence: Appliances come out before cabinets, around the same time as countertops (Scoping: Order of Work: Appliances and Caps). Default pull order: refrigerator, range, dishwasher, laundry units, water heater; adjust to layout and water path. Plumbing caps go on right after each water-line item comes out (dishwasher, fridge, toilet), not at the end. Exception: an appliance that won't fit out once the plastic is up comes out before engineering controls, when the lead names it.
general_rules: Shut off and verify every utility before disconnecting.
Cap every open supply line, even if the valve is off. This is non-negotiable.
Protect salvageable and unaffected floors with Ram Board, moving blankets, or plywood before sliding or lifting any appliance.
Use proper moving equipment or two-person lifts on heavy units. Never drag appliances across finished floors.
Photo document before you touch anything: wide shots plus close-ups of connections and existing damage.
refrigerators_and_fridges: Unplug and secure the cord. Remove contents if the customer is not home or if the unit must be moved a significant distance.
These are heavy and top-heavy: always use help or an appliance dolly.
Usually worth saving unless heavily contaminated or long-dwell Category 2/3 with visible mold risk.
If leaving in place, protect the unit and the floor around it during any nearby demo.
dishwashers: Shut off the water supply valve (usually under the sink). Disconnect hot water line and drain hose.
Disconnect electrical (plug or hardwired under the unit).
Commonly removed because they sit directly in wet zones and block wall/floor access behind them.
Newer units on clean or short-dwell losses are often worth saving if they can be protected.

garbage_disposals.priority: High: try to save these whenever practical.
guidance: Disconnect electrical at the switch or outlet first.
Disconnect the drain plumbing (P-trap and dishwasher drain line if connected).
These are relatively easy to remove and reinstall. Strongly prefer saving over replacement unless the unit is old or visibly damaged.
If the disposal is out for more than a day, cap or plug the drain line temporarily.

core_rules: Shut off gas at the appliance valve or main gas shutoff. Confirm there is no gas smell.
Disconnect the gas line using proper tools. Immediately cap the supply line with an approved gas cap or plug.
Perform a soap test on the capped line and any remaining connections. Spray soapy water and watch for bubbles. No bubbles = good.
Document the soap test (photo or written note). This protects everyone on gas work.
Know your company policy: many require a licensed plumber for gas reconnection.
gas_appliances.soap_test_note: Use a spray bottle with dish soap and water. Any bubbling means gas is escaping. Do not leave the area until the test is clean.

additional_notes: Often located in garages, tight closets, or utility rooms. Measure your access path before attempting to pull the unit.
Shut off water supply and gas (or electric) power. Verify both are off.
Disconnect water lines and cap them. On gas models, cap the gas line and soap test.
These are heavy: use proper lifting technique or equipment and protect the floor while moving.
If occupants still need water, a temporary cold-to-hot bypass with a double-female hose adapter is sometimes possible. Notify the customer and document it.
Reconnection and gas/electrical work is typically handed off to a licensed plumber on most jobs.

liability_and_escalation: Gas line work carries real risk. If you are not fully comfortable or your company requires it, escalate to a licensed plumber before capping or testing.
Reconnecting gas, water, or hardwired electrical to appliances is often outside standard tech scope. Confirm your company’s rules.
Always document who performed shutoff, capping, and any safety testing.

countertop_removal.description: Stone and solid surface countertops are usually removed for access rather than because the material itself is damaged. Focus on controlled detachment to avoid cracking expensive slabs.
countertop_removal.props: Stone countertop props: 3 ft on center max. Posts at the seams, the sink, and the ends, with a top block.
key_principles: Remove brackets and clips from below first: this is the primary attachment on most cabinet-installed tops.
Cut perimeter caulk and sealant before attempting to lift.
On caulked or perimeter-glued tops, wood shims can provide even upward pressure across multiple points.
Watch stress points: inside corners of L-shaped tops and the corners around sink cutouts are the most vulnerable to cracking.
Always double-protect finished floors. Stone is heavy and will damage surfaces if it shifts or drops.
Always check if the backsplash is glued to the countertop.

Countertops are heavy, especially stone L-shapes. If you need extra help to remove it, fully prep the countertop the day before the crew arrives. Remove all brackets, cut all perimeter caulk, and remove the backsplash if it’s attached to the countertop. Don’t make the crew stand around while you’re still prepping.
When the stone stays up and cabinets come out under it, prop it: 3 ft on center max, posts at the seams, the sink, and the ends, with a top block.
countertop_removal.voice_considerations: Keep it practical. Most techs already know how to use shims once they hear the idea: don’t over-explain the distribution. Just flag the weak points (sink cutout corners and L-miters) and the need for floor protection.

plumbing_electrical.description: Practical field knowledge for plumbing and electrical considerations on water damage and restoration jobs. Focuses on safety, common issues, when to escalate, and real-world habits.
combined_considerations: Water + electricity is one of the fastest ways to get seriously injured or killed. Always treat it with extreme caution.
On older homes, both plumbing and electrical systems are often outdated and more hazardous when water is involved.
If you're unsure about the safety of the plumbing or electrical system, or if the work goes beyond basic equipment setup, escalate to a licensed professional early.
Document any plumbing or electrical concerns you observe. This protects everyone if issues arise later.
plumbing_electrical.voice_note: Find the main shutoff early and verify the water actually stopped. Polybutylene or old brittle CPVC? Shut the main first. Never assume power is off: verify it, and call the licensed trade when it's past basic equipment setup.
plumbing_electrical.reference_note: GFCI and breaker rules live in Electrical Safety.

door_removal.title: Door Removal
door_removal.description: Detach doors that are in the way of the work or at risk of damage.
door_removal.upper_scale_practice: Lay a rag between doors stacked against finished walls and between doors stacked against each other.

register_removal.title: Register Removal
register_removal.description: Removing registers is billable as demolition access prep.
register_removal.storage: Store removed registers somewhere safe: a drawer set aside for removed parts, another room, or just outside containment. No bagging rule.

controls_and_limits.title: Controls & Limits
controls_and_limits.description: Safety gates, asbestos limits, and limited-containment rules.

asbestos_demo_limits.description: Disturbing work stops on asbestos-containing (more than 1 percent) or presumed material. The three-linear-foot line is retired as a work permission.
asbestos_demo_limits.rule: Asbestos-containing material (more than 1 percent) or presumed asbestos stops the disturbing work. Suspect material is sampled or presumed. Licensed abatement. An owner survey does not clear demo. Pre-1978 lead and the renovation rule carry the same duty. Sample first and wait. If results are pending, treat as positive.
required_controls: These are controls for sampling and for work on material confirmed negative. They are not permission to cut asbestos-containing or presumed material.
HEPA vacuum at point of cut
Dust containment and careful debris handling
asbestos_demo_limits.when_to_escalate: Any disturbing work on asbestos-containing or presumed material. The old three-linear-foot line is a retired field note, not a work permission.
asbestos_demo_limits.voice_considerations: Older home or suspect material? Sample first and wait. If results are pending, treat as positive. Do not use the retired three-foot line as work permission. The Oregon small-repair example is in Hazard Sampling: Who Samples: Oregon Small Repair Note: use it only when the remembered state is Oregon.
asbestos_demo_limits.jurisdiction_caveat: Always verify local, OSHA, EPA, and state asbestos rules before cutting. Some states require a licensed inspector before any disturbance of presumed material. Oregon and Washington examples: Hazard Sampling: Who Samples: Examples by State. Do not treat those examples as the default. If the work state is not yet known, follow Kit Framework: Runtime Contracts: Jurisdiction.
asbestos_demo_limits.voice_note: Suspect material? Sample and wait. An owner survey does not clear the cut. Licensed abatement if it is asbestos-containing or presumed.
asbestos_demo_limits.age_note: Building age is a prompt, not a clearance. Asbestos can be present in any era; pre-1981 fireproofing and 9-inch tile are named checks. Lead: pre-1978 buildings fall under the EPA renovation rule.

limited_containment_demo.description: Guidance for investigative openings and very small, localized work in finished or semi-finished spaces with dust captured at the tool or behind a local barrier. Once the work is a mold removal scope, containment and the minimum negative come first (Containment: Mold Pressure); doing it with less is a written deviation (see Alignment Note).
when_appropriate: Investigative opening, or a very small isolated spot where the dust is captured at the tool (a removal scope otherwise needs full containment or a written deviation)
No significant red flags from the risk assessment
Total affected drywall removal expected to stay under 10 sq ft
engineering_controls: Run an AFD with intake pointed toward the work area
Place floor protection directly under the work zone
Use checkerboard cutting method: cut small sections, vacuum edges thoroughly, then carefully remove each piece
Never rip or break the drywall
Two-person technique preferred (one cuts, one vacuums)
limited_containment_demo.scaling_rule: If significantly more mold, moisture, or odor is discovered once the wall is opened, stop immediately and upgrade to proper containment.
limited_containment_demo.alignment_note: Use this for an investigative opening or a very small spot where the dust is captured at the tool (source capture or a local barrier is allowed for an intrusive opening). Once it is a mold removal scope, containment goes up and the minimum negative is set before disturbance (Containment: Mold Pressure). Doing a small removal with only capture at the tool is a written deviation with the reason. The 10 sq ft line is a field rule of thumb (EPA-style).

red_flags: Visible moisture or water staining beyond the immediate spot
Evidence of long dwell time or hidden water damage
Location in a basement, crawlspace, or high-humidity area
initial_risk_assessment.action: Any red flag: use full containment instead.

ppe.cutter: Respirator under the written program (full-face with P-100 preferred) + cutting gloves
ppe.helper: Respirator and gloves; HEPA vacuum at the cut

framing_treatment.finished_spaces: HEPA vacuum and wipe the framing, pipes, and wiring. Use a pump sprayer only if a biocide line is approved: no fog in finished, occupied spaces.

post_demo_clean.title: Post-Demo Clean
post_demo_clean.description: Foundational cleaning sequence after the structure is opened.

demo_final_cleaning.description: Foundational cleaning after demolition (any biocide is a separate, approved step) to remove dust, debris, and contaminants before drying begins. This step is critical for air quality, preventing callbacks, and preparing surfaces for drying equipment.
key_activities: Remove heavy debris
Vacuum floor
Blow medium particulates down top to bottom inside controlled containment with HEPA capture running (blower, ULV with liquid off, or a fan in a bind), then vac floor again
Wipe down all exposed framing, plumbing, wires, and electrical boxes, horizontal surfaces
Final detailed vacuuming (especially corners, base plates, and gaps)
Biocide application (pump or ULV) only when a biocide line is approved: pre-cleaned surfaces, registered product, label (see ULV vs Hand-Pump Sprayer)
Stain remover/sealer on exposed framing only when justified, after removal and cleaning, and with client approval (cosmetic)

alt.title: Pressure Wash + Extractor Method for Contaminated Sill Plates
conditions: Heavy contamination present (sewer backup with sludge or groundwater flood carrying dirt/silt)

demo_final_cleaning.voice_considerations: This phase is often rushed or skipped in the field. Emphasize that a clean, dust-free structure dries better and has fewer callbacks. The post-demo cleaning sequence should be treated as a repeatable checklist, not optional.
critical_decision_points: Is this a standard post-demo clean or a heavier Category 3 / mold decontamination?
Is a biocide line warranted and approved? If so, does the label allow fogging?
Has cleaning inside electrical boxes and hard-to-reach areas been completed?
practical_guidance: Dust collects behind outlets and switches where the vacuum can't reach: clean inside electrical boxes during the wipe-down.
Microfiber rags: fold in half twice for 8 clean faces per rag. Save and wash them.
The pressure wash + extractor method is for slab-on-grade framing, with the extractor running the whole time, then dehumidify to dry.
Ongoing cleaning during drying and monitoring visits as needed.
Many techs underestimate how much dust remains after demo. A thorough base clean improves air quality and cuts musty-odor callbacks.

voice_entry_points: demo decisions / remove vs dry / material matrix

crawlspaces.title: Crawlspaces
crawlspaces.description: Safety, inspection, insulation removal, airflow management, drying techniques, vapor barrier, and high-contamination protocols. Shallow tree for scale.

safety_and_access.title: Safety & Access
safety_and_access.description: Air check, PPE decisions, and basic access rules. Most crawls are routine work; know the few real hazards and keep moving.

atmospheric_testing.rule: Run a 4-gas check only when there's a reason (sewage, a gas or fuel smell, a confined space) or when company liability tolerance requires it, not routinely. It is not a routine standard-logic billable line (Scoping: Crawlspace Track).
atmospheric_testing.stop_condition: Hatch size-up only: gas or sewer smell, gas appliance or line, combustion equipment running, or no airflow with tight single egress means don't enter; stop and escalate to the PM.
atmospheric_testing.voice_note: Run a 4-gas check only when there's a reason (sewage, a gas or fuel smell, a confined space) or when company liability tolerance requires it. Not routine. Smell gas or sewer at the hatch, or there's combustion running down there? Stay out and call it up.

respirator.approach: Use professional judgment based on conditions.
respirator.recommended: Wear a respirator with a properly rated filter anytime there’s visible dust, disturbed insulation, Category 2/3 water, or musty odors.
respirator.situational: On a tall, clean, well-maintained Category 1 crawlspace with a fresh vapor barrier, many techs will skip the respirator for quick entries. The hazard assessment decides, and any respirator use is under the written program (29 CFR 1910.134).
respirator.voice_note: If it's dusty or dirty at all, I'm wearing a respirator. Clean crawl, quick look: the hazard assessment decides, not the clock.

other: Knee pads are highly recommended if you want to still be doing this job in ten years.
Headlamp with backup batteries is strongly recommended.
Gloves and coveralls are situational based on how dirty the crawlspace is.

rules: Don't work alone in a tight, contaminated, or hot crawl, or on a long job down there.
Have someone at the access point when the crawl is tight, deep, hot, or contaminated; on a quick look in a clean crawl, make sure someone knows you're down there.
Contain and AFD your access location if inside the house with high contamination risk.
Hand materials out: don’t throw them
Leave the crawlspace cleaner than you found it
Lay plywood or Ram Board from the hatch to the work area.
Stay on the joists when you can: don't crawl across insulation or the vapor barrier.

manpower.principle: Many hands makes light work, especially in crawlspaces.
manpower.voice_note: If you’ve got four guys on site and the crawlspace can use the help, get three of them down there. Pace yourself efficiently, don't burn yourself out.

confined_space.rule: Most residential crawls are non-permit spaces. Run a 4-gas check only when there's a reason (sewage, a gas or fuel smell, a confined space) or when company liability tolerance requires it, not routinely. It is not a routine standard-logic billable line (Scoping: Crawlspace Track).
confined_space.before_entry: Size it up at the hatch: smell, water, wiring, gas appliances, debris. Buddy topside when it's tight, hot, or contaminated. GFCI cords. Anything that looks permit-required (hazardous atmosphere, engulfment, entrapment) is out of standard logic: stop and escalate.
confined_space.voice_note: Look and smell at the hatch. Gas smell, get out. Live wiring in water, kill power first. Anything unusual, stop and call it up.

safety_and_access.real_hazards: Keep it brief: live wiring near water, sharp debris and fasteners, pests, sewage, heat. Gas smell = get out and call it in.

inspection.title: Inspection
inspection.description: What to look for on every crawlspace entry.
key_things_to_look_for: Water staining or discoloration on the underside of floor joists, subfloor, and sill plates
Damaged or collapsed storage (cardboard boxes, paper products, etc.)
Sagging or improperly supported HVAC ductwork
Disturbed or broken plumbing straps and hangers
Corrosion or dissolved sections on the underside of pipes (especially from drain cleaners like Drano)
Standing water or ponding on the ground
Condition of the existing vapor barrier (rips, pooling, mold underneath)

hot_water_line_breaks.description: Hot water supply line breaks in crawlspaces that have been leaking for an extended period. These create ideal conditions for rapid mold growth.
hot_water_line_breaks.why_high_risk: Hot water provides both consistent moisture and elevated temperature. Combined with organic material (wood, dust, insulation) in a confined space, this leads to very fast microbial amplification, often described as 'instant mold'.

check: HVAC returns and supplies (especially if the air handler or ductwork is in or connected to the crawlspace)
Plumbing cutouts and penetrations under cabinets and vanities
Floor gaps, register openings, and any other floor penetrations
Rim joist areas and other potential leakage points into wall cavities

hot_water_line_breaks.voice_note: Hot water line that's been leaking in the crawl for weeks or months? That's basically a mold incubator. Check everywhere air moves from down here into the house: HVAC, under-cabinet plumbing cutouts, floor gaps. That stuff travels.

field_implications.mold_risk: Even with nothing visible yet, treat it as a likely mold spot: warmth, moisture, and time add up fast down there.
field_implications.air_movement_concern: Warm, wet air rises, and the HVAC and stack effect pull it up into the house, so what's growing down there can end up upstairs unless you keep the air in check.
field_implications.containment_note: Worth setting up negative air and containment here, especially if the HVAC pulls from or pushes into the crawl.

underside_subfloor_under_shower_pans.when: Any shower or tub over a crawlspace on a water loss in or near that bathroom.
procedure: Get into the crawl and work through the underdeck to the spot right under the shower pan or tub.
Find it by the drain and supply lines coming through the subfloor.
Meter the underside of the subfloor under the fixture and out to its edges, plus the joists right there.
Compare against a dry reference spot of the same subfloor elsewhere in the crawl.
Photo and log the readings and locations so you can hit the same spots on every monitoring visit.
underside_subfloor_under_shower_pans.tool: Hammer probe recommended for subfloor over 3/4 inch: insulated pins driven into the underside of the subfloor. On 3/4 inch or thinner, a pin or pinless meter from below is usually enough; on thicker subfloor a pinless meter can miss what is going on deeper in the wood.
underside_subfloor_under_shower_pans.caution: Watch your swing. Do not smash the pins into the foundation, stem wall, brick, block, or piers: you will break or bend the pins and can crack the masonry. Set the probe on the wood, clear of any masonry, before you drive it.
underside_subfloor_under_shower_pans.why: Wet readings up top on a shower or tub are hard to chase from above. The underside tells you if the subfloor under the pan is actually wet.
underside_subfloor_under_shower_pans.voice_note: Shower over a crawl? Go underneath, find the drain, and meter the bottom of the subfloor right under the pan: hammer probe recommended if the subfloor is over 3/4 inch. Keep the pins off the stem wall and piers: you'll wreck the pins or crack the block.

inspection.voice_note: When I drop into a crawlspace, I’m looking for staining on the joists, sagging insulation, messed up HVAC, broken plumbing straps, and pipe damage, especially on the bottom of pipes from stuff like Drano.

insulation_removal.title: Insulation Removal
insulation_removal.description: Getting wet insulation off the wood and out of the space efficiently.
insulation_removal.core_rule: Get wet insulation off the wood framing as fast as possible.

twine_removal_technique.title: Twine Insulation Removal Technique
twine_removal_technique.description: Recommended approach for removing wet insulation held up by zigzag poly twine in low clearance crawlspaces.
twine_removal_technique.sweet_spot: The most efficient method for most situations is a two-pass approach: First pass, pull yourself along the joists on your back and cut the twine junctions at each staple, hitting both sides of the zigzag as you go. Second pass, come back through to bag and remove the dropped insulation.
twine_removal_technique.reasoning: Cutting is generally easier and faster on your back while looking up. Bagging is more natural when you're positioned to scoop and stuff material into bags. Combining both actions on the same pass creates a lot of awkward tool switching and extra movement.
twine_removal_technique.voice_note: If there’s wet insulation touching the joists, I want it all on the ground today. Better to drop it all and come back tomorrow than leave any of it hanging on the wood.

key_considerations: Default method: All insulation should be bagged while still inside the crawlspace. This is the safest and most controlled approach, especially on occupied homes or Category 2/3 losses.

Alternative method (edge case): In vacant homes with hard-surface flooring, insulation can be pulled to the access hatch and kicked out onto the main level for bagging. This is significantly easier on the body.
If someone is living in the home, you have one of two options as bags come out of the crawlspace: wipe the bags down in the decon chamber, or double bag them.
Do not kick insulation out directly into an occupied home without proper containment and a decon chamber.
Never kick out wet insulation or heavily contaminated insulation. These must always be bagged inside the crawlspace.
crawlspace_insulation_removal.voice_note: Default is to bag it in the crawlspace. Only kick it out if the house is vacant and we’re on hard floors. If anyone lives there, either wipe the bags in decon or double bag them as they come out.

insulation_removal.best_practice: Priority is getting wet insulation off the framing. Small drop and time allows: bag it the same day.
insulation_removal.field_reality: Big drop, no time left, or the crew is spent: drop it all today and bag it tomorrow. That's fine: the framing is what matters.

airflow_and_drying.title: Airflow & Drying
airflow_and_drying.description: Pressure management and targeted drying techniques inside the crawlspace.

air_movement_and_pressure.core_rule: Avoid pushing air from the crawlspace up into the living space.
key_guidance: When ducting dehumidifier output into a crawlspace, remember the unit is closed-loop (no net pressurization from the machine itself). Still give the air a clear path out through foundation vents rather than back up through the hatch or subfloor: placement and path matter more than "pressure."
Do not tip or lay the dehumidifier on its side to get it into a tight crawl, even off and drained. Keep it upright and duct in (Equipment Setup: Dehumidifier Handling).
Never push air into the crawlspace through a vent: this creates positive pressure and can drive contaminants into the house.
Two good solutions: Place a fan inside the crawlspace and duct it out through a vent, or build containment over the access point with an AFD running inside the contained area.
air_movement_and_pressure.voice_note: Don’t push crawlspace air up into the house. If I’m piping a dehu in here, I make sure that air gets out through the vents, not back up the hatch.

dehumidifier_closed_loop.principle: A dehumidifier is a closed loop: equal air in and out. The unit itself does not create net pressurization of the crawl.
dehumidifier_closed_loop.failure_mode: Failure is often placement, not "pressure." A suitcase LGR pointed at the source but ~27 ft away in a ~9,000 cu ft crawl (~50×60×3) is effectively non-functional.
dehumidifier_closed_loop.voice_note: The dehu is a closed loop: equal in and out. It doesn't pressurize the crawl by itself. If it's twenty-seven feet from the wet spot in a nine-thousand-cube crawl, it's basically not working.

displacement_principle.name: Displacement principle
displacement_principle.author_note: framework_gap: tenting/ducting were described without naming why they work.
displacement_principle.principle: Duct conditioned (dehu) output to the wettest material; use vents as relief. Tenting and ducting work because they move conditioned air across the wet material: that is the displacement principle.
practice: Duct dehumidifier output to the wettest material, not just into open crawl volume.
Use foundation vents as relief paths so air moves across the target and out.
Localized plastic pocket / tent over the wet zone concentrates displacement where it matters.
displacement_principle.example_memory: Suitcase LGR about 27 ft from source in an about 9,000 cu ft crawl with open vents: too far from the load to be effective in that volume.
displacement_principle.voice_note: Displacement principle: duct the dry air to the wettest material and let the vents relieve. Tenting works because it moves conditioned air across the wet stuff, not because the box "pressurizes" the crawl.

localized_tenting.description: Creating a targeted drying chamber under a specific wet area.
method: Cut a piece of plastic the height of the crawlspace and skirt it around the affected area to create a smaller chamber.
Duct dehumidifier output from outside through the hatch directly into this localized chamber.
Use clear plastic when possible to allow light in.
Seal off nearby crawlspace vents in that zone from the outside if needed.
Particularly effective for drying bound moisture in subfloor from below on slow leak jobs.
localized_tenting.voice_note: Got a slow leak that soaked the subfloor? I’m building a little tent under it in the crawlspace and pumping dry air straight to it. That's the displacement principle: dry air across the wet material.
localized_tenting.why_it_works: Displacement principle: conditioned air is forced across the wet material inside a smaller chamber instead of dumping into the whole crawl volume.

optional_negative_air_setup.description: Optional improvisation for creating airflow/negative pressure.
optional_negative_air_setup.method: Place a regular axial fan with layflat ducting strategically in the crawlspace and run the duct out through a foundation vent. This pulls fresh air in through the hatch and other vents, or the hatch only if you cover the vents.
optional_negative_air_setup.voice_note: One trick I like is dropping a fan with layflat ducting and running it out a side vent. Pulls good airflow through the whole space.

airflow_and_drying.reference_note: Crawl tenting/ducting can create LGR intake freeze from output back-pressure: see Equipment Setup: Dehumidifier Handling: Dehumidifier Ducting & Back-Pressure. Do not tip the unit to fit the crawl: see Equipment Setup: Dehumidifier Handling.

checkbox_vs_performance.title: Checkbox vs performance
checkbox_vs_performance.rule: Distinguish performance need vs file photo. If you place gear for documentation or a billing/safety checkbox only, do not treat it as drying performance. If the space needs airflow for drying, place for performance.
checkbox_vs_performance.field_memory: Crawl air movers are often staged for the file (billing/safety checkbox) with little or no real airflow effect; sometimes the crawl actually needs the unit. The photo is constant; the need is variable.
checkbox_vs_performance.voice_note: Checkbox vs real airflow: if it's only for the photo, don't count it as drying performance. If the crawl needs air, place it to move air.

vapor_barrier_and_assemblies.title: Vapor Barrier & Assemblies
vapor_barrier_and_assemblies.description: Vapor barrier rules and manufactured home specific construction.

vapor_barrier.guidance: Repair damaged sections during the job when practical. Replacing the vapor barrier after drying is often a billable upgrade on long-term wet jobs.

key_requirements: Joints must overlap by a minimum of 6 inches and be sealed or taped
Material must extend at least 6 inches up the stem wall
It must be attached and sealed to the foundation wall
Terminate at the top of the masonry: do not run it up onto the wood sill plate
code_requirements.voice_note: When we replace a vapor barrier, it's usually code, not just a recommendation: verify the local requirement.
code_requirements.legal_note: Vapor barrier installation is governed by the local building code. The overlap and stem-wall numbers here are common practice: verify the jurisdiction. If the work state is not yet known, follow Kit Framework: Runtime Contracts: Jurisdiction.

installation_order.decision: Definitive: Vapor barrier goes in BEFORE new insulation
installation_order.reasoning: Installing new insulation first results in dragging clean insulation through dirt and debris. Installing the new vapor barrier first keeps both the plastic and the new insulation clean.
installation_order.default_rule: Always install the new vapor barrier first, then install new insulation on top of clean plastic. This is now the official RestoKit default position.
installation_order.voice_note: Vapor barrier goes down first, then insulation on top of the clean plastic. Keeps everything professional and clean.

manufactured_homes.description: Water behavior, construction details, and remediation considerations specific to manufactured homes and single-wide trailers.
assembly_layering: Metal chassis frame at the bottom
Black mesh membrane (commonly called belly wrap or underbelly) stretched across the frame primarily to support insulation and exclude rodents
Wood joists sitting directly on top of the black mesh membrane
Insulation sitting in the wood joist bays
Single-layer Masonite-style or similar subfloor on top of the joists
water_behavior: The black mesh membrane can act as a bowl: water collects on it and causes visible sagging in affected bays. Sagging is a strong visual indicator of water location
Absence of sagging does not mean the area is dry: water can still migrate through insulation and wick upward into joists and subfloor
Hot water leaks significantly increase mold risk in the insulation and on the underside of the subfloor due to elevated temperature and moisture
cutting_precautions: Exercise caution when cutting the black mesh membrane: wiring is frequently run directly against or just above it
Many older trailers contain abandoned or dead wiring from previous rewires. Cutting these on accident is usually not a major issue but must still be documented
Always notify the customer and document if newer-looking or active wiring is affected
remediation_guidance: Open all bays with visible sagging first: these are the highest probability water collection points
Remove wet or suspect insulation even without visible sagging if moisture readings, odor, or hot water history are present
Cut and remove sagging sections of black mesh membrane in affected areas to allow proper inspection and drying
notes: Meter the insulation, joists, and subfloor: a visual check of the belly membrane alone is not enough.
Inspect before cutting: wiring in these homes is often installed out of code, and sagging insulation can already have broken wires.
Check the underside of joists and subfloor for moisture wicking up from the membrane.

Low clearance or an outdoor access hatch: do not tip the dehumidifier to get it in. Keep it upright and duct dry air in (Equipment Setup: Dehumidifier Handling). Airflow, tenting, and the displacement principle stay in Airflow & Drying.

ultra_ppe.when_to_use: For crawlspaces with heavy sewage contamination, large insect infestations, extreme filth, or heavy mold.
ultra_ppe.setup: White Tyvek suit → latex gloves taped at wrist → yellow suit over the top → demolition gloves taped over the latex gloves.
ultra_ppe.voice_note: If this crawlspace is straight nasty: sewage, bugs everywhere; I’m running the double suit setup.

category_3_sewage.description: Handling long-dwell dried sewage and heavily contaminated soil in crawlspaces.
category_3_sewage.note: See Crawlspaces: Special Contamination: Long Dwell Sewage Handling for burrito method, dedicated shovel, and Crawlspaces: Special Contamination: Long Dwell Sewage Handling: Hydrated Lime (default light-layer odor/pH step after bulk removal, not disinfection; applicator PPE). For odor-sensitive occupants as an added field consideration, see Crawlspaces: Special Contamination: Occupant Odor Sensitivity. For active heavy sewage flow, see Pump Truck Deployment and Heavy Sewage Extraction.

occupant_odor_sensitivity.description: Field consideration layered on top of standard sewage-in-soil handling, not a prerequisite for hydrated lime. Lime for odor/pH after bulk removal remains the default whenever sewage is mixed into crawl dirt (a field default; not a disinfection step).
occupant_odor_sensitivity.when: When occupants are odor-sensitive (example from a prior job: pregnancy). They are often reacting to crawl/sewage smell.
occupant_odor_sensitivity.guidance: Lean on odor-control measures already in the standard path, especially Hydrated Lime after bulk removal. Go easy on heavy fogging and unnecessary chemical load.
occupant_odor_sensitivity.voice_note: If someone's home is smell-sensitive (pregnancy on a prior job, for example), lean on the light lime layer for odor after bulk removal and go easy on heavy fogging. Lime is for smell, not a disinfectant. That's on top of the standard sewage-soil handling, not a reason to skip lime.

ulv_fogging.recommendation: Many experienced techs like the ULV in a crawl for reach: with the liquid off it is an air blast that knocks dust out of the framing inside containment. The clean itself is debris removal, wipe, and wire brush, billed as cleaning by SF (no HEPA vacuuming in the standard crawl logic). A biocide fog is a separate, approved decision: pre-cleaned surfaces, registered product, label allows fogging, occupants out.
advantages: Reaches into small gaps and framing spaces (air blast or, when approved, label-allowed biocide)
Knocks dust and debris off the underside of joists and subfloor
Faster than a pump sprayer when an approved biocide is applied after pre-cleaning
ulv_fogging.voice_note: In a crawl the fogger is for reach: liquid off, it blows the dust down inside containment. The clean is debris out, rags, and the wire brush: no HEPA vac in the standard crawl. Biocide fog only if it's approved and the label allows it, after the clean, and fog on the dirt does nothing.
ulv_fogging.alignment_note: Fog is not removal. A biocide on the soil does nothing; the dry is the structure (informative). Biocide gating: see ULV vs Hand-Pump Sprayer.

standard_logic_exclusions.rule: Crawlspace standard logic excludes mold sampling, confined-space checks, and HEPA vacuuming. Asbestos pipe wrap is out of standard logic: don't disturb it, flag it, and escalate.

long_dwell_sewage_handling.description: Special procedures for long-dwell dried sewage or heavily contaminated Category 3 situations (especially in crawlspaces or soil).
steps: Cut the vapor barrier into manageable sections and roll it up like a burrito, containing the sludge, bugs, and contaminated soil inside the plastic.
Keep a dedicated small shovel stored inside a garbage bag in the van. Never carry a contaminated shovel through the customer's home or clean areas.
After bulk removal, apply hydrated lime for odor per the Hydrated Lime field note below (not a disinfection step).
long_dwell_sewage_handling.voice_note: On long-dwell dried sewage I cut the vapor barrier into sections and roll it like a burrito so the nastiness stays contained. Dedicated shovel in its own bag: never bring that thing inside clean space. Then a light layer of hydrated lime on the soil for odor after bulk removal: see Hydrated Lime for PPE and method.

hydrated_lime.when: After bulk removal of contaminated material from affected crawl soil (sewage mixed into dirt). Default odor step for that condition.
hydrated_lime.purpose: Cut crawl/sewage odor and raise pH on remaining soil after bulk removal. Field default; not a disinfection step.
hydrated_lime.method: Light layer only: do not pile or blanket heavily; avoid heavy fogging or unnecessary aerosol.
hydrated_lime.ppe: Respirator, gloves, eye protection, and coveralls for the applicator (lime is caustic).
hydrated_lime.voice_note: After bulk removal on sewage-in-dirt, a light layer of hydrated lime on the crawl soil helps with odor: it isn't a disinfectant. Respirator, gloves, eye protection, coveralls. Light layer only.
hydrated_lime.alignment_note: Informative: the dry is the structure, not the soil, and a biocide on the soil does nothing. Do not bill or describe lime as killing bacteria.

test_intake_lines: A crawl, basement, chase, or attic is its own category and class. Size it up at the hatch before entry.

A crawl is usually a non-permit space. Run a 4-gas check only when there's a reason (sewage, a gas or fuel smell, a confined space) or when company liability tolerance requires it, not routinely. The dry standard is the crawl's own, not the house. A fire-exit stair is not the drying path during occupied hours.
Attic and crawl work in protection is a heat plan. Anything that looks permit-required is outside standard logic: stop and escalate.

special_situations.title: Special Situations
special_situations.description: High-complexity environments requiring elevated PPE, different sequencing, and specialized decision rules: animal urine homes, hoarder conditions, insect infestations, and (in its own module) heavy sewage / pump-truck response. Shallow tree for scale.

animal_homes.title: Animal Homes
animal_homes.description: Homes with neglected or hoarded animals, especially cats. Cat urine is the primary driver of persistent damage and recurring smells due to uric acid crystals.
core_challenges: Heavy urine saturation in carpet, pad, subfloor, drywall, and insulation
Ammonia from urine breakdown causing respiratory irritation and potential exceedance of safe exposure limits
Uric acid crystals that reactivate with humidity, causing odors to return if not fully removed or treated
Mold amplification from sustained moisture and organic waste
Pathogens including E. coli, Salmonella, and Leptospira from animal urine and feces
Parasites and potential deceased animals adding biohazard risk

cat_specific_notes.urine_behavior: Cat urine is highly concentrated and penetrates deeply into porous materials. Uric acid crystals bond to subfloors, drywall, and insulation, reactivating with any humidity and causing persistent recurring odors.
cat_specific_notes.removal_requirement: Porous materials must be removed to the full depth of penetration. Surface cleaning or sealing is insufficient: crystals remain and reactivate later.
cat_specific_notes.treatment: Enzymatic cleaners that specifically target uric acid are required. Standard disinfectants do not break down the crystals.

dog_specific_notes.urine_behavior: Dog urine is less concentrated than cat urine and generally penetrates less deeply, making it somewhat easier to manage on sealed or non-porous surfaces.
dog_specific_notes.removal_requirement: Still requires removal of saturated porous materials, but may allow more salvage on hard surfaces with proper enzymatic treatment.
dog_specific_notes.treatment: Enzymatic cleaners effective against uric acid are still recommended for best results.

practical_procedures: Photograph and document all affected areas and animal waste before any disturbance.
Remove all saturated carpet, pad, and tack strip: double-bag contaminated materials.
Assess and remove affected subfloor, drywall, and insulation to the full depth of urine penetration.
Apply enzymatic cleaner to remaining surfaces and allow proper dwell time before extraction or wiping.
Use HEPA vacuuming and air scrubbing throughout to control airborne particles and odors.

Consider ozone or hydroxyl generators for final odor work after physical removal and cleaning. Ozone only in an empty space with everyone out (people, pets, plants), per the manufacturer's instructions. Hydroxyl runs with the space empty unless that exact unit's label and manual say otherwise. It is odor control, not removal. See Hydroxyl Generators and Ozone Treatment.
Escalate to licensed biohazard remediation teams for extreme cases with high pathogen load or structural compromise.
animal_homes.voice_considerations: Cat urine is the real problem: once it soaks into the subfloor or drywall, surface cleaning won't fix it. You have to remove to the full depth and use the right enzymatic product, or the smell comes right back when humidity rises.

ammonia_release_rule_of_thumb.description: Tiered severity guide for sudden ammonia release in an 8,000-cubic-foot basement at the 50 ppm mild-irritation threshold, assuming 3.4 mg ammonia per cat per day and full accumulated payload released at once.
thresholds: mild irritation: 50 ppm, 3 cats, about 777 days (approximately 2 years and 1 month of daily deposits)
moderate irritation: 100 ppm, 3 cats, about 389 days (approximately 1 year and 1 month of daily deposits)
severe irritation: 200 ppm, 3 cats, about 194 days (approximately 6.5 months of daily deposits)
ld50 idlh: 300 ppm, 3 cats, about 130 days (approximately 4.3 months of daily deposits)
ammonia_release_rule_of_thumb.note: These are theoretical airborne concentrations from the daily gas load alone. In a real water-loss scenario the sudden mobilization of accumulated surface deposits plus heat and dehumidification can push the payload into the breathing zone much faster than normal off-gassing.
ammonia_release_rule_of_thumb.label_note: 300 ppm is the NIOSH IDLH value for ammonia. The old 'ld50' tag is not a lethal-dose figure.
ammonia_release_rule_of_thumb.status: Back-of-envelope estimate (theoretical). Use a real ammonia meter on site.

hoarder_homes.title: Hoarder Homes
hoarder_homes.description: Tiered severity based on movement difficulty through the space. Percentages are secondary reference only.

mild.movement_difficulty: Clear or lightly obstructed paths; equipment and personnel can move normally through most areas
mild.key_challenges: Contents manipulation limited to affected zones

moderate.movement_difficulty: Narrow trails only; must turn sideways or step carefully; equipment requires staging or disassembly to move through
moderate.key_challenges: Frequent contents movement; moderate collapse risk on trails; significant time lost to navigating and staging

severe.movement_difficulty: Trails too narrow to walk; must crawl, climb over piles, or remove contents to create any path; equipment cannot be moved in until systematic clearing begins
severe.timeline_impact: 5x+ normal job duration or multi-week project
severe.key_challenges: Extreme collapse risk; no usable staging area; contents must be systematically removed before any restoration work can begin

hoarder_homes.note: Movement difficulty is the primary field metric: assess in seconds without math. Usable space percentages are secondary reference only for bidding and planning.

bug_homes.title: Bug Homes
bug_homes.description: Houses infested with fleas, bed bugs, or other insects common in hoarder/animal environments. Strict containment is required to prevent spreading infestation to the truck, shop, or other jobs.

fleas.detection: Visible jumping insects, especially around baseboards, furniture legs, and pet areas. Eggs and larvae often hidden in carpet, pad, and cracks.
fleas.risk: Can jump onto technicians and equipment; eggs can survive in the truck or shop and hatch later.
fleas.treatment: HEPA vacuuming of all surfaces, followed by licensed pest control application. Standard drying does not kill flea eggs or larvae.

bed_bugs.detection: Live bugs, dark fecal spots on mattresses or baseboards, shed skins, or musty odor in severe cases.
bed_bugs.risk: Extremely mobile; can hitchhike on clothing, tools, or debris and infest new locations.
bed_bugs.treatment: Full containment before any disturbance. HEPA vacuuming, controlled bagging of infested materials, and immediate escalation to licensed pest control. Heat treatment is an effective non-chemical option where feasible.

silverfish_and_other.detection: Silverfish are teardrop-shaped with three long tail filaments and a wiggling motion; centipedes are fast with many legs. Both appear in damp paper, textiles, and organic debris common in hoarder homes.
silverfish_and_other.risk: Silverfish do not bite people or spread disease: their droppings and shed scales can trigger mild allergies or asthma in sensitive individuals if infestation is heavy. These are primarily nuisance pests compared to cockroaches.
silverfish_and_other.treatment: HEPA vacuuming and pest control as needed. Address underlying moisture to prevent recurrence.

practical_procedures: Identify infestation type and extent before starting any work.
Establish full containment and negative air before disturbing any materials.
HEPA vacuum all surfaces thoroughly, focusing on cracks, baseboards, and furniture legs.
Double-bag all removed materials and label as infested.
Escalate to pest control for treatment before or immediately after restoration work.
Document infestation and treatment for liability protection.
When retrieving equipment from a pest/bug unit: bag LGR and gear with gloves, booties, and full PPE; contain in the van; never carry unbagged infestation off-site.
bug_homes.bug_bombing_note: Pesticide treatment (including bug bombs) goes through a licensed pest-control operator and the product label, not the restoration crew. It can be sequenced before or after contents movement or demo, with full containment already in place.
bug_homes.voice_considerations: If you see fleas jumping or find bed bug signs, stop and contain first. These bugs will hitchhike back to the truck and shop if you don't lock them down before you start moving stuff. When you pull equipment from a pest unit, bag the LGR and gear with gloves and booties (full PPE), and contain it in the van so you don't spread the infestation.

equipment_bagging_and_retrieval.title: Pest-unit equipment bagging and retrieval
equipment_bagging_and_retrieval.description: When pulling LGR/dehumidifiers, air movers, or other gear from a confirmed or suspected bug/pest unit, bag the equipment before it leaves the work area. Do not drag infestation into the van, shop, or the next job.
procedure: Confirm pest/bug unit status before moving equipment (fleas, bed bugs, cockroaches, or other hitchhikers).
Don gloves, booties, and full PPE appropriate for the infestation before handling gear.
Bag each piece of equipment (LGR/dehu, air movers, cords as practical) so pests cannot hitchhike on or inside housings.
Seal bags; note any visible pests in the bag for liability documentation.
Contain bagged equipment in the van: do not place unbagged gear on clean shelves or next to clean inventory.
Decon outer PPE / change booties before entering the cab or clean shop zones.
equipment_bagging_and_retrieval.voice_note: Bug unit: bag the LGR and gear with gloves and booties on. Full PPE. Don't drag the infestation into the van. Seal it, note any cockroaches or bugs you see, and keep it contained for transport.

core_challenges: Immediate bites and discomfort for technicians
High risk of spreading infestation to equipment, vehicle, and other job sites
Hidden eggs and larvae that survive standard cleaning and drying
Need for specialized pest control beyond normal restoration scope

shared_controls.title: Shared Controls
shared_controls.description: PPE, containment, decontamination, and escalation rules that apply across animal, hoarder, and bug environments.

ppe_and_containment.ppe: Full respirator with appropriate filters, Tyvek or equivalent coveralls, gloves, and eye protection. Ammonia levels can be high: monitor and upgrade respiratory protection as needed. For bugs: full Tyvek with hood, gloves taped at wrists, boots or shoe covers. Change clothes and bag them before leaving the site.
ppe_and_containment.containment: Full containment with negative air and HEPA air scrubbers required. Isolate HVAC to prevent circulation of ammonia, odors, pathogens, or insects throughout the structure.
ppe_and_containment.decon: Decontamination chamber or protocol for exiting the work area to prevent tracking contaminants into clean zones or vehicles. Remove outer clothing or suit, bag it, and shower or change before entering the truck or shop.

when_to_escalate: Significant structural damage or high pathogen load (animal homes)
High ammonia levels requiring specialized monitoring
Presence of deceased animals or heavy parasite infestation
Any visible infestation of fleas or bed bugs: do not attempt to handle with restoration chemicals alone
Severe hoarder conditions where contents must be systematically removed before any restoration work can begin
shared_controls.interaction_note: Hoarder and animal homes often have co-occurring insect infestations. Bug control should be sequenced before or alongside contents removal and restoration work.

pump_truck_heavy_extraction.title: Pump Truck / Heavy Sewage Extraction
pump_truck_heavy_extraction.description: Moved to its own module. Heavy sewage response, the phase collapse, and pump truck upkeep are in Pump Truck Deployment and Heavy Sewage Extraction.

voice_entry_points: pump truck / heavy sewage (see Pump Truck Deployment and Heavy Sewage Extraction)
Bug-unit equipment retrieval: bag LGR with gloves and booties, contain in van

leadership_and_labor.title: Leadership and Labor
leadership_and_labor.description: The real dynamics of leadership, pay, burnout, and labor distribution in the restoration industry, how PM grows on the job, plus how to schedule jobs, size a crew, and hand a job from one shift to the next.
leadership_and_labor.core_principle: A lead title and lead pay come with the opportunity, and the responsibility, to lead the job. Experienced techs can work smart and protect themselves from burnout while still running the job and supporting the crew.
key_considerations: Many technicians feel the work, conditions, and liability aren't matched by pay, and burnout is common.
Experienced techs have earned the right to work smart and protect their bodies. Staying engaged on the job keeps the crew's trust and keeps the lead role meaningful.
Driving the van does not by itself make someone the lead. Leading is running the job, making good decisions, and directing the crew.
Techs who step up as the lead (making calls, talking with customers, and running the job) deserve a title and pay that reflect it, and the whole team benefits when they do.

Newer techs who do great work are a real asset, and veterans bring experience the crew relies on. Recognizing both, and having open conversations about roles and titles, helps everyone work well together.
The best leads find a good balance: they work smart, protect their bodies, and still carry the job and keep the crew's respect.
Authority is earned through effort and competence, not tenure. Crews follow leads they respect, and that respect is built every day on the job.
Project manager is not a you-are or you-aren't title. Everyone is responsible. A tech grows a little each day. See PM on Site.
Pump-truck specialists are a separate deployment decision. Managers who treat every tech as interchangeable create avoidable labor waste on heavy sewage losses.
leadership_and_labor.voice_considerations: Leading a job is a real responsibility, and a rewarding one. This work is hard on the body, so pace yourself and look after your energy. When you carry the lead title, running the job and supporting the crew is how you earn their trust. Work smart, stay engaged, and the crew will notice. PM isn't a title you wait for. Ask a tech: what percent of a PM are you as a tech?
leadership_and_labor.reference_note: Pump-truck specialists and when to send them are in Pump Truck Deployment and Heavy Sewage Extraction. PM as growth on site is PM on Site. Day-forward checklists stay sorted PM, then Lead, then Techs.

pm_on_site.title: PM on site
pm_on_site.description: Project manager is not a you-are or you-aren't title. Everyone on the job is responsible. More experienced people support and guide. A lead is a PM in the spirit of that work on site.
pm_on_site.core_principle: The PM is still 100% a technician. A tech starts at 0% PM and grows a little each day. You don't wait until you are a PM to learn it.
practical_guidance: Everyone is responsible. A title does not turn that on or off.
More experienced people support and guide. They don't hold the thinking until someone gets the title.
A lead is a PM in the spirit of the work on site. The calls, the customer, the next day, the file.
Day-forward lines stay sorted PM, then Lead, then Techs. That order says who owns the line. It is not a check you pass before you think like a PM.
PM lines are office work: scheduling, calls, coordination. The person on those lines is still a technician.
A tech starts at 0% PM and grows a little each day. Learn it while you are the tech.
pm_on_site.coaching_line: Ask a tech: what percent of a PM are you as a tech?
pm_on_site.voice_note: PM isn't you-are or you-aren't. Everyone's responsible. You start at zero percent and grow a little each day. The PM is still a tech. Ask a tech: what percent of a PM are you as a tech?
voice_entry_points: what percent of a PM are you
lead is a PM on site
pm_on_site.reference_note: Checklists stay sorted PM, then Lead, then Techs. This section is the mindset around those lines.

scheduling_crew_and_handoff.title: Scheduling, Crew Sizing, and Shift Handoff
scheduling_crew_and_handoff.description: Plain field guidance for running the days of a job: who owns it, who is on site when, how big the crew should be, how to reach the customer, and how one person hands a job to the next without losing what they knew. Guidance, not a rulebook; the job and the company decide.

job_ownership.description: Ideally one lead or tech opens the job and carries the initial work (scope, demo, and setup). Monitoring and minor adjustments are the part that can pass to other crews.
practical_guidance: Where it can be done, the person who opens the job stays on it through scope, demo, and setup. Monitoring and minor adjustments are the work that passes to other crews.
One person in control at the field level helps the customer. Too many new faces is confusing, and one familiar lead is reassuring.
The tech who opened the job already knows the order of work and does not need to re-read the documentation to find it.
It also saves review time. A newcomer has to catch up on the file before they can act.
Companies try to assign people to jobs for this reason. On-call schedules and rotations make it hard, so plan for it: make the handoff good and keep the owner clear.
job_ownership.voice_note: One lead opens it and carries it through setup. Monitoring can move around. When the schedule won't allow that, make the handoff count.

scheduling.description: Build the schedule around the safe order of the work, then fit people and travel to it.
practical_guidance: Plan Day 1 in the phase order: source control and signed authorization first, then extraction, then selective demo, containment, and equipment setup as the job calls for them. Schedule people and equipment to fit that order.
Decide who is on site when. Extraction, demo, and setup are the heavy early work; later visits are mostly checks and adjustments and do not need the same crew.
Before leaving Day 1, put the equipment checks and monitoring visits on the calendar with a name next to each one. Visits set on the fly are the ones that get missed.
Be realistic about travel time and who is actually available that day. If the day will not fit, say so early and move the work, rather than rushing the steps that protect the job file.
On-call schedules and rotations can change who is available. Plan for that when you set the next visit (see Job Ownership).
When the next visit is set, write down when and why in the job file, so the next person is not guessing.
After-hours calls follow Emergency Calls. If triage says it can wait, schedule it for daytime.
scheduling.voice_note: Plan the day so the safe order of work fits in it. If it doesn't fit, move the schedule, not the safety steps.

crew_sizing.description: Match the crew to the job type and the phase. The right size is the one that does the work safely without people tripping over each other.
practical_guidance: Size the crew to the job type and phase, not to habit. Extraction, demo, and setup are the heavy lifting early; monitoring visits are usually lighter and more focused.

A second person is worth it when it makes the work safer or faster: heavy or awkward lifts, a tight or contaminated crawl, one person cutting while one vacuums, building containment, or placing a lot of equipment.

Where a space is tight, hot, or contaminated, a buddy topside is part of the plan. See Crawlspaces: Safety & Access: Confined Space: Before Entry and Safety and Health: Crew Practices, and let those set the minimum, not this section.
Don't overstaff. Extra people in a small space get in each other's way and add traffic through containment and clean areas.
Don't understaff to save labor. One person alone on heavy or risky work, or rushing a task built for two, shows up later as injuries, missed steps, and callbacks.
Put the person who knows the task on the step that is hard to redo, such as containment, cutting, or readings, and pair a newer tech with them.
If someone does work alone, someone else knows where they are and when to expect them.
Heavy sewage with active flow is a specialist call. See Pump Truck Deployment and Heavy Sewage Extraction.
crew_sizing.voice_note: Right-size the crew. Enough hands to do it safely, not so many they trip over each other.

monitoring_staffing.description: Monitoring is detail work. The load for a day depends on the job and on what turns up at each stop, so the PM plans the day with room to flex.
practical_guidance: Monitoring is detail work. Good readings, a careful look at the equipment, and noticing what changed all take time at each stop.
The load depends on the job and on what turns up. Two quick stops can leave much of the day open, and one problem job can take the whole day.
Rushing leads to missed details and damage. If a stop runs long, let it.
The PM plans the day so it can flex when one stop runs long, and moves other stops if needed.
Staffing (one or two people) is the PM's call, based on the job and on whether a lead is training someone.
monitoring_staffing.voice_note: Monitoring is detail work, so give each stop the time it needs. The PM plans the day to flex when one runs long.

customer_contact.description: The lead going to the job calls the customer that morning, and reads the file first.
practical_guidance: The lead going to the job calls the customer that morning. Every job on their day gets a call, even a monitoring visit.
Give a window, not an exact time. For example: "Unless something comes up, I'll be there around this window. I'll let you know if something changes."
Read the day's job files before you call. Access notes (keys, garage door codes, lock boxes, panels) are in the job file for the customer and project; check them before the call so you arrive ready.
If the plan changes, call again as soon as you know and say what will happen when you get there.
customer_contact.voice_note: Call before you roll, give a window, and read the file first. Unless something comes up, I'll be there around this window, and I'll let you know if it changes.

shift_handoff.description: When one person hands a job to another, the job should not lose what the first person knew. One owner at a time, and a written trail. Keep it light for a monitoring visit and fuller when ownership changes.
handoff_items: Where the water is, where it came from, and what is still wet or unknown.
What has been removed, and what is still to come.
Moisture readings and where they were taken.
Equipment placed and running: what, where, and anything adjusted.
Open safety items: hazards, entry conditions, PPE, anything an incoming person should not walk into blind.
Customer promises and concerns: what they were told and what they asked for.
The next visit: when it is, and what gets done.
Keys and access: how to get in, written in the job file.
practical_guidance: Match the handoff to the visit. A monitoring visit needs a light handoff: readings, equipment status, anything unusual, and the next visit. When ownership changes, use the full list.
One clear owner per job at any time. At the handoff, say out loud and write down who has it now.
Hand off in person or by call when you can, and back it with a written log entry the same day. The log is what survives if the call is forgotten.
Keys and access notes go in the job file, so the next person can get in without calling around.
Say where the photos are, so the next person can find them without asking.
Take readings at the same fixed points the last person used, so the numbers compare. See documentation and Monitoring: Fixed Point Techniques.
The incoming person checks the equipment against what the handoff said and speaks up early if something does not match.
An open safety item is handed over by name, not buried in the notes. The incoming person knows it before starting in that area.
If something promised to the customer cannot be kept, the outgoing person says so in the handoff and the customer hears it early.
shift_handoff.voice_note: Handoff in plain words: where the water is, what's out, what the numbers say, what's running, what's unsafe, what the customer was told, how to get in, and when you're back. Write it down. One owner.

scheduling_crew_and_handoff.reference_note: Documentation, monitoring, equipment, safety, and crawl-entry rules stay where they are; this section only points to them.

pump_truck_deployment.title: Pump Truck Deployment and Heavy Sewage Extraction
pump_truck_deployment.description: Heavy sewage response with a pump truck: how managers deploy the specialist, what the specialist does when the normal phase sequence collapses, and how the truck and its tank stay clean. On request only; it stays off the job flow unless a heavy sewage call brings it up.
pump_truck_deployment.core_principle: Managers must treat pump-truck specialists as a distinct resource, not just another tech with a different truck. These units are the correct first response for high-volume sewage and should not be diluted across ordinary Category 1/2 calls when a true heavy loss is active.
pump_truck_deployment.role_description: Distinct specialist role usually carried by one or two trucks in a fleet equipped with a sewage pump and extendable rollout tubing. These units handle large-volume Category 3 sewage (especially crawlspaces and basements) where ordinary extraction is insufficient. On many of these calls the normal phase sequence collapses.
key_points: One or two trucks in a typical fleet carry the sewage pump and long rollout tubing.
Deploying a standard tech to a pouring sewage crawlspace creates unnecessary labor and risk; the specialist should go first.
After the source is controlled, the same crew or a follow-on crew transitions into the normal remediation sequence using the rest of the framework.
The specialist role benefits from the kit holding what only comes up a few times a year: rare access problems, tubing tricks, and decontamination sequences.

dispatch_check.description: Before sending the pump truck, ask whether the volume is enough to need it. The restoration pump truck sits in the middle: more than portable extractors can handle, less than a specialized pumping company's large truck.
practical_guidance: Ask: is the volume enough? If the water is something you can mop up, roll up in plastic vapor barrier (visqueen), or dry out, it doesn't need a pump truck. Real volume does.

A typical restoration pump truck, also called an extractor van or pump unit, is a removable unit that slides into a van and bolts down. It often comes with a hose on a pull-out reel, and good companies have that setup.
The truck-mounted or pump-truck waste tank is about 100 gallons. Usable capacity at shutoff is a little less than the tank size, so know your unit's tank and know when a job is bigger than it.

Compare the two scales: a cubic foot of water is about 7.48 gallons, so a 100-gallon tank is only about 13 cubic feet. A crawlspace holding a few hundred cubic feet of water (300 cubic feet is about 2,200 gallons) is thousands of gallons, many van loads.

A van tank holds far more than a household vacuum but far less than a big truck. If the job can be done in about two van loads of suction, that can be the better call over the expense of calling in another company to sub out the pump, so weigh it.

A big dedicated plumbing-type pump truck is usually for something like a sewer main pushing back out, or other very large volumes. Most restoration companies don't have very large trucks, so for those call a specialized plumbing or pumping company. Their truck is a dedicated vehicle where the whole back is a tank, with a massive hose, like a dump truck for water.
For active, high-volume sewage with the source still open, see Emergency Calls: Heavy Sewage Override and Phase Collapse.
dispatch_check.voice_note: Is the volume enough? If you can mop it, roll it up, or dry it, skip the pump truck. A couple of van loads may be worth doing yourself. Much more than that, weigh calling the big pumping company.

role_reality: Often the first unit on a visible, active sewage loss.
Primary objective is rapid volume reduction so a plumber can access and repair the source.
Full assessment, documentation, and selective demo sequences are secondary until the flow is controlled.
Manager deployment of these specialists is different from standard tech dispatch.

phase_collapse.description: When sewage is actively pouring or standing in large volume and the source is still open, the linear Phase 1 checklist is secondary to getting the pump in and the volume under control. Authorization and basic safety still gate the work; everything else yields to mitigation.
practical_sequence: Confirm signed authorization (or emergency self-authorization if company policy allows).
Deploy pump truck and rollout tubing; begin bulk extraction immediately.
Stabilize enough that the plumber can enter and fix the source.
After source control and bulk volume reduction, resume documentation, baselines/measurements, and selective access before normal Phase 2 remediation and Phase 3 drying progression.
phase_collapse.resume_note: Match Phase 1: Phase Collapse Note: after volume is controlled, full documentation, measurements, and selective access resume before normal Phase 2/3 work. Authorization and Category 3 safety still gate the job.

key_activities: Identify whether the volume and access require the pump truck versus ordinary extractors.
Protect access routes and living space from tracking while moving contaminated material.
Coordinate tightly with the plumber so extraction and repair happen in the correct order.
Document the volume removed and the condition at the moment the source is fixed: this protects the scope narrative later.
