operator_support.description: Technicians often rotate through running the extractor van. Some companies assign one person, but a rotation is common and it varies. Starting the engine and operating the pump motor can take time for anyone who doesn't run the unit regularly.
practical_guidance: Refer to the engine manual for your unit when starting or operating the pump motor. Every unit is different, and the kit does not store manuals.

If the person on the unit doesn't run it regularly, offer: "If you need a reminder on how to start or operate the pump motor, let me know and I can look up the manual for your unit and walk you through it."
To find the right manual, give the make and model of the unit.
operator_support.voice_note: Haven't run the unit lately? Say so, and I'll look up the manual for your unit and walk you through starting the pump motor.

cleanliness_and_upkeep.description: After every extraction, and especially after a large sewage loss, the truck gets cleaned so it is ready for the next call.
practical_guidance: Clean the tank after every extraction, especially a large sewage loss.
Check disposal rules (federal, state, and local) before dumping, including whether the RV dump or facility accepts it.
Dump the tank at an RV dump. Pay the dump fee if there is one.
Use the hose to wash out and flush the tank so everything is flushed.
Clean the hose out when you clean the tank.
cleanliness_and_upkeep.voice_note: Dump it, flush it, wash the hose. A clean tank means a truck that's ready for the next call.

vehicle_hygiene.description: Vehicle hygiene is a primary concern given what a pump truck handles.
practical_guidance: Treat vehicle hygiene as a primary concern. The truck handles sewage and heavily contaminated water.
Companies handle it differently. Some keep to regular cleaning, and some require a treatment product in the tank to help keep the bacterial load down. Follow the product label and company policy.
A divider between the cab and the pump is a good thing: it keeps the vehicle cleaner and easier to maintain.
vehicle_hygiene.voice_note: Keep the truck clean, follow the product label and company policy, and a divider between the cab and the pump makes the job easier.

voice_entry_points: when to send the pump truck
pump truck tank cleaning and dumping
pump truck engine start / operating the pump motor
pump_truck_deployment.voice_note: If the call comes in as sewage pouring out of the basement or crawl, send the pump truck. Don't send a regular van and hope they can improvise it (the kit's Field Adaptations section). This is not a normal Phase 1 walk-through job. If you can see and smell sewage pouring, the pump goes in first. Get the volume under control so the plumber can work. The rest of the framework still applies after the source is fixed.
pump_truck_deployment.reference_note: The Phase 1 collapse rule and the emergency call override are in the first two. Dried or long-dwell sewage in a crawl is in Crawlspaces: Special Contamination: Long Dwell Sewage Handling.

practical_judgment.title: Practical Judgment
practical_judgment.description: Guidance for making sound technical decisions under real-world constraints. The framework provides technical ideals, but field conditions often require practical judgment.
practical_judgment.core_principle: Know the technical ideal. Then make the best defensible decision possible with the time, manpower, crew willingness, and conditions you actually have.
key_considerations: Manpower reality: expecting one person to do all the dirty work while others stay clean is not always practical
Time of day and day of week: late Friday decisions may reasonably differ from Tuesday morning
Training situations: using a job to train new techs is a valid factor in decision making
Protecting the structure over the weekend vs. perfect first-day execution
Resource management: a good Phase 1 stabilization can be smarter than an incomplete aggressive approach
Know the technical ideal, then adjust intelligently rather than blindly pushing through
Localized drying and stabilization can be a valid first-day move when full removal isn't practical
Document your reasoning when you deviate from the technical ideal
Plan the next visit to complete what could not be done on Day 1

key_considerations.note: Field decisions are heavily influenced by company culture, staffing levels, workload, overtime policy, travel distance, and daily managerial pressure. The same company can swing between 'get it done today' and 'clock out at 4:30' depending on conditions. Know your company's real expectations on any given day.

All technicians within the same company must use the same monitoring and documentation methods. Inconsistent approaches between techs create confusion during handoffs and weaken the defensibility of the job file. The monitoring module techniques should be standardized company-wide.

minimize_passes.principle: Minimize the number of times you travel across the same ground.
minimize_passes.description: Every pass through an area costs time and physical energy. Plan each trip so it accomplishes as much as possible.
examples: Crawlspace: Cut twine on the way in, then bag and remove insulation on the way back instead of switching tasks mid-pass.
Van or stairs: Always carry something that needs to go back instead of making empty trips.
Jobsite movement: Stage demo debris and equipment near the path you'll already be walking. Batch moves instead of carrying one piece at a time across the same route repeatedly.
minimize_passes.voice_note: Don't make extra trips. If you're already going that direction, take something with you: debris, tools, or equipment. Saves your body and the job time.

practical_judgment.voice_note: Don't be stupid about it, but don't kill yourself or burn out your crew trying to hit some perfect standard when you're short-handed on a Friday evening.

noise_mitigation.description: Practical steps to reduce noise impact on occupants, especially those working from home or with noise sensitivity.
customer_facing_practices: Ask early in the job if anyone works from home or is particularly noise-sensitive.
Turn air movers down (or use lower speed settings) when possible on clean Category 1 jobs.
Reinstall a solid door between the work area and living areas whenever practical: this provides significantly better sound isolation than plastic alone.
Stage loud equipment (air movers, dehus) as far from occupied bedrooms or offices as the drying layout allows.
noise_mitigation.voice_note: Ask up front if anyone’s working from home or sensitive to noise. On clean jobs I’ll drop the air mover speed when I can, and I try to get a real door back up between the work zone and the living space: plastic doesn’t do much for sound.

good_enough.core_principle: Good enough is a real and necessary part of field work. Seeking perfection on every task every day is unsustainable and often counterproductive when it prevents you from completing the job on time or burns out the crew.

spectrum.acceptable_shortcuts: Using a piece of trim, cardboard, or even freehand when a four-foot level isn't worth the extra trip for a seam that will be covered or fixed by the next trade. These are pragmatic trade-offs that experienced techs make without compromising the final result.
spectrum.chronic_sloppiness: Consistently cutting crooked, skipping basic protection, or doing visibly poor work on every task. This is different from occasional judgment calls: it becomes a pattern that someone downstream has to fix and that reflects on the whole operation.
spectrum.competitive_perfection: Some techs treat the work as a personal standard and will go get the straightedge every time. That's admirable but not required of everyone. The job doesn't demand samurai-level perfection from every technician on every cut.

good_enough.daily_grind_reality: Most techs are trying to get through a full day of physical work, hit their production goals, and go home without destroying their bodies. When you're already behind and know you won't finish everything perfectly, experienced judgment says prioritize the tasks that actually matter to the final outcome and let the low-impact details slide to 'good enough.'
good_enough.decision_framework: Ask: Does this shortcut create a problem someone else has to fix at equal or greater cost? Does it affect the customer's perception or the final quality in a noticeable way? If the answer to both is no, good enough is acceptable. If either answer is yes, take the extra step or trip.
good_enough.voice_note: You can't chase perfection on every single thing every single day. There's a difference between a pragmatic 'good enough' cut that won't matter and straight-up sloppy work that someone downstream has to fix. Know which one you're looking at.

remembering_edge_cases.description: Many of the highest-cost mistakes in restoration are not failures of the standard sequence: they are the absence of a rarely-needed tool or technique that only appears once or twice a year. RestoKit's job is to hold those lessons so the next time is not another expensive re-learning.
remembering_edge_cases.guidance: When a rare edge case costs significant labor, write a short voice note into Field Adaptations or the owning module the same day. Do not wait for the next occurrence.

rush_mode_remembering.description: In a rush the pattern is one thing done well, then the rest gets forgotten. The kit flags the note at the trigger and stages it ready, so the next item is already open instead of rebuilt from memory.
rush_mode_remembering.rule: Finish the thing in front of you. The staged template is the reminder. Surface only the notes this visit earned (Visit Note Cadence). Do not read a standing plan or a scope sheet into a visit that did not change them.
rush_mode_remembering.voice_note: You did the one thing. The note for it is already staged. Take that one. Leave the rest.

test_intake_lines: A client refusal that leaves a required or expected step is a written notice to the parties who have a stake, filed before the work if they do not object in time. That notice is what a later email quotes. The memory of the talk is not.
The water standard is the floor, not the whole job. Cite the 2021 fifth edition. Older editions are superseded.
Extract Category 3 and leave the porous material is a limitation, written and signed by the owner. A condition that blocks compliance is negotiate, decline, stop, or accept with a written release.
Mold found after the start, or regulated material found after the start, is a complication. Written to the owner, and a change order if the scope moves.

No mold start without a written contract. Collateral damage, the price method, and the change-order path are in it. A refusal and an antimicrobial use are written. The customer's policy is not interpreted.
Disposal needs written permission. Condition 3 is packed separate. Mold waste is not labeled a biohazard unless the local rule says so.
A requested mold assessment or verification is independent of the remediator. One who is not independent is a written deviation.
A limitation comes from the owner, in writing. A complication after the start is a written notice and may be a change order.
A cited companion is used in its current edition. A research paper in the reference list is not a kit rule.
Large loss pricing method lives in estimating.
practical_judgment.reference_note: Limitations, deviations, authorization, consent, and records. Rush-mode note staging is Visit Note Cadence.

emergency_calls.title: Emergency Calls
emergency_calls.description: After-hours or urgent calls require fast upfront triage to separate true emergencies from slow leaks or emotional reactions. The most common mistake is showing up without asking the right questions first.
triage_questions: Is water actively running or pooling right now?
Has anyone been displaced, lost power, or can't stay in the home?
Is there immediate safety or health threat: sewage backup, electrical exposure, or structural collapse risk?
How long has the issue been present and when was it first noticed?
emergency_calls.true_emergency_criteria: Active water, displacement, or immediate safety/health threat. These justify after-hours response and potential immediate action.
non_emergency_examples: Slow leak discovered weeks or months ago with visible mold
Customer has emotional reaction to mold but no active water or displacement
Issue present for days with no ongoing source or immediate threat

benign_anxiety.rule: Reassure the customer that the issue can wait until morning. Show up if needed for minimal stabilize (plastic/equipment), then schedule full work for the next day: no after-hours premium roll for anxiety alone.
benign_anxiety.voice_note: I hear you: this can wait until morning. We'll stabilize what's needed and schedule the full work for daytime.

genuine_panic.rule: Panic does not skip triage. Run Triage Questions first (or bind to True Emergency Criteria). After-hours / immediate roll only if True Emergency Criteria still met after triage: active water, displacement, or immediate safety/health threat (including Heavy Sewage Override). If triage shows non-emergency, de-escalate and schedule per Non Emergency Examples / benign path. Do not roll premium just because the caller is panicked.
genuine_panic.triage_gate: Triage Questions → True Emergency Criteria (and Heavy Sewage Override when applicable)
genuine_panic.true_emergency_action: If criteria still met after triage: after-hours / immediate response is justified.
genuine_panic.non_emergency_action: If triage shows non-emergency: de-escalate, reassure, schedule daytime: align with Non Emergency Examples and Benign Anxiety path.
genuine_panic.voice_note: I know this feels urgent. Before we roll, I need three quick answers: is water still active, is anyone displaced, and is there an immediate safety or health threat like sewage or electrical. Those answers decide whether we come tonight or schedule for morning.

emergency_calls.on_site_protocol: If the situation does not meet true emergency criteria, do not begin demo or major work without first consulting the project manager or owner. Document the triage answers and customer statements for billing justification.
emergency_calls.mitigation_to_restoration_note: Do not move from mitigation to restoration after hours. Limited demo for Category 1 losses or other time-sensitive situations is permitted only if minimal airflow can be established to prevent mold spread.
emergency_calls.voice_considerations: Before you even get in the truck, run triage: is water still running, is anyone displaced, and is there an immediate safety or health threat. Those answers (not the caller's panic level) tell you whether it's a true emergency or something that can wait until morning.

heavy_sewage_override.description: Active, visible, high-volume sewage (especially with an open source) is a true emergency that justifies after-hours response and collapses the normal assessment sequence into pure mitigation until the plumber can work.
heavy_sewage_override.triage_addition: Is sewage actively flowing or standing in large volume that ordinary extractors cannot handle in a reasonable time? If yes, treat as pump-truck priority.

service_contract.title: Service Contract
service_contract.description: Obtain signed authorization from the material interested party before billable restoration scope or demolition. Life-safety water shutoff may proceed under company emergency self-authorization policy when active flooding or sewage creates immediate risk: still document.
key_activities: Present scope of work and obtain signature on work authorization and any required releases
Confirm the signer has authority to approve work
Document any limitations or special instructions at time of signing
Work order review: collect biocide/antimicrobial consent (yes/no) with the authorization; a 'no' can change scope
critical_decision_points: Has the correct person signed?
Are there scope limitations that need to be noted before starting?
practical_guidance: Do not begin demolition or billable restoration scope until the authorization is signed: that protects everyone.

Life-safety carve-out: water shutoff (and other immediate life-safety actions) may proceed under emergency self-authorization when company policy allows; active flooding or sewage with life-safety risk. Document what you did and why. See Pump Truck Deployment and Heavy Sewage Extraction: Phase Collapse.
Many homeowners are overwhelmed; keep the explanation short and professional: 'I need your signature before I can start any work. This protects both of us.'
If the homeowner is hesitant, calmly explain that no work can begin (and no billing can occur) without it.
Document any verbal instructions or concerns the customer gives you at signing time.
service_contract.voice_considerations: Keep this phase short and firm. Do not negotiate or start working while they 'look for the paperwork.' Life-safety shutoff first when policy allows; still no demo or billing without a signature.

life_safety_carve_out.allows: Life-safety water shutoff and emergency self-authorization when company policy allows (active flooding/sewage life-safety).
life_safety_carve_out.still_requires: Signed authorization before demolition or any billable restoration scope.
life_safety_carve_out.document: Record the emergency action, time, and reason.
life_safety_carve_out.voice_note: No demo, no billing without a signature. Water shutoff for life safety can go first when policy allows: document it.

legal_and_liability.title: Legal and Liability
legal_and_liability.description: What protects the customer, the crew, and the company on paper: what the kit is and is not, authorization, limitations, deviations, consent, records, and what a restorer must not claim. Not legal advice; company counsel and local law win.
legal_and_liability.core_principle: If it isn't written, it didn't happen. A deviation without a written reason and notice is a story, not an explanation.

disclaimer_framing.kit: RestoKit is a field aid that aligns with the principles of IICRC S500 and S520 but is written entirely in its own words. It does not reproduce IICRC text, signature language, or trademarks. The body of knowledge comes from field practice across restoration companies, including real-world operations the standards don't address. RestoKit is not the standard, not a training course, not affiliated with, approved, or endorsed by IICRC, and not a legal, medical, or coverage opinion.
disclaimer_framing.standards: The standards describe themselves as a floor, not every method; they go out of date; the publisher does not verify, enforce, certify compliance, or warrant results. A compliance claim belongs to whoever makes it.
disclaimer_framing.outside_scope: Assessing indoor contamination (IEP work), regulated materials (asbestos, lead, silica, mercury, PCBs, pesticides, fuels, solvents, radiological), and bird/bat-dropping pathogens are outside the water and mold standards.

work_authorization_and_contract.authorization: Written work authorization signed by the owner or the owner's agent before services. Expected. Life-safety shutoff under company emergency policy is the only carve-out, and it is documented (see Service Contract).
work_authorization_and_contract.contract_contents: Recommended contents: parties and contacts, work description, collateral-damage responsibility, known limitations, permits, duties, start and estimated completion, price or price method, change pricing and change-order path, payment terms, default/termination, insurer or surety involvement, subcontractors, warranty, completion criteria including drying goals, and how conflicts are resolved. Dated, signed, each page initialed, a copy to each party.
work_authorization_and_contract.mold: No mold remediation start without a written contract. Expected.
work_authorization_and_contract.source_correction: Finding and fixing the leak is the owner's job unless the restorer is hired for it. Say so in the authorization.
work_authorization_and_contract.bid_is_not_authorization: A bid or estimate is not a signature. No demo and no billable scope from a bid alone (see estimating).

change_orders.rule: A material change in scope, time, or price is a written change order (what changed, time, price, payment), accepted in writing by an authorized party and the restorer.

limitations_complexities_complications_c.limitation: A restriction another party puts on the scope or outcome (e.g., 'extract the Category 3 but leave the porous materials', 'no containment', 'return contaminated contents as-is'). Only the owner or agent can impose it. Written and signed before non-emergency work, with the consequences.
limitations_complexities_complications_c.complexity: Makes the job harder but still doable (access, after-hours, weather, permit space, occupancy, imposed timeline). Approved in writing.
limitations_complexities_complications_c.complication: Arises after the start and forces a change (mold found, regulated material found, delays). Written notice to the owner as soon as practical; change order if scope moves. Do not just work through it.
limitations_complexities_complications_c.conflict: Disagreement about how the work is done. If compliance is blocked: negotiate, decline, stop, or accept with written release/disclaimer. Resolution documented; attorney review of a waiver is recommended.
limitations_complexities_complications_c.illegal_or_dangerous: An illegal or unreasonably dangerous condition is resolved, the project refused, or the work stopped. Required. Reason and events written.
limitations_complexities_complications_c.shared_walls: A shared wall (multi-unit) brings the lease, the code, tenant notice, and insurance into the plan.

deviation_procedure.rule: Before leaving a required or expected step: write what forced it and what you did instead, notify the parties with a stake (owner, carrier, property manager, IEP as applicable), and file that notice before proceeding if they don't object in time.
examples: Spray, fog, or coat without physical removal on a mold scope.
Leaving Condition 3 in place (needs a management plan).
A non-independent assessor doing verification.
Customer refuses containment or removal.
Small mold removal with source capture only (see Limited Containment Demo).

informed_consent_antimicrobials.rule: Consent is collected once, on Day 1, with the work authorization and work order review (phase1 Verify Paperwork): brief the customer, label (active ingredients) and SDS available, written consent. At application: trained applicator, label PPE, occupants out. Record type, method, time, quantity, dilution, location. No claim beyond the label.
informed_consent_antimicrobials.tier_note: required: label, registration, training; expected: consent records

who_decides_what.restorer: Preliminary determination of category; drying plan and goals; post-remediation evaluation (own check).
who_decides_what.iep: Assessment of Condition 1/2/3 and sampling strategy; post-remediation verification. Independent of the remediator when assessment or verification is requested; a non-independent assessor discloses that in writing (a written deviation).
who_decides_what.when_an_iep_is_expected: High-risk occupants, care or public settings, possible aerosolized contaminants, a reported health issue, or a need to confirm contamination.
who_decides_what.specialists: Licensed trades (electrical, plumbing, HVAC/NADCA), asbestos/lead abatement, structural engineer for load-bearing removal, conservators, firearms, instruments, data recovery.
who_decides_what.health_questions: Go to a physician or public health. Evacuation information can be given; it is not medical advice. Occupant symptom reports are written in the file, not diagnosed.

qualifications_and_licensing.rule: The license matches the work (country, state, municipality). Intrusive work may need a contractor license; mechanical-system cleaning may need a specialty license. Where the law requires a certification, the job does not start without it. Training alone is not the qualification. Work outside expertise is hired out or the customer is told to retain the specialist.
qualifications_and_licensing.insurance: Workers' compensation where the law requires it; commercial general liability, commercial auto, and contractors pollution liability are named for mold work. Subcontractors carry their own coverage, including pollution liability with the remediator named as additional insured.
qualifications_and_licensing.out_of_state: Work outside the home state follows that state's license, permits, and coverage. Required. If the work state is not yet known, follow Kit Framework: Runtime Contracts: Jurisdiction.

minimum_file: Monitoring log: affected and unaffected readings, equipment inlet/outlet, goals, location of each reading, instrument, who
Equipment and chemical logs with quantity and time; biocide consent and right-to-know/SDS
Contents inventory signed and dated; disposal permissions
Who entered the contained area; incidents
Estimates and invoices; time records where billing needs them
Prior water, mold, asbestos, or lead history the client reported
Client odor or health observations, recorded as reported (no medical opinion)
Permits, notices, waivers, and lien documents
records_and_retention.retention: Keep records for the jurisdiction's retention period (required where that law exists). Recommended minimum: the longest limitations period. The clock often starts at discovery, not the work date. If the work state is not yet known, follow Kit Framework: Runtime Contracts: Jurisdiction.
records_and_retention.after_emergency: Complete the file and close the communication gaps once the emergency is over.
records_and_retention.honesty: Readings are recorded as measured. Never invent, smooth, or backfill readings.

legal_and_liability.insurance_boundary: The restorer does not interpret the customer's policy. See Insurance Dynamics: Policy Rule.
must_not_claim: That RestoKit, the company, or the job is 'IICRC certified' or 'IICRC approved' because it used this kit. (Individual IICRC certifications, if held, are stated as such.)
That following the standard proves the job met the law or is finished.
That a biocide, fog, ozone, or coating removed mold or sanitized beyond what the label says.
That the house is 'mold-free', 'safe', 'cleared', or 'passed' without the independent verification that says so. The restorer's own check is an evaluation.
Medical advice, or that symptoms are or are not caused by the loss.
That asbestos or lead is absent without lab results.
legal_and_liability.waivers: A client refusal that blocks compliance is documented with written advice of the consequences and an attempted waiver. A waiver may not clear liability if the job was taken knowing it could not be finished.
legal_and_liability.voice_note: Signed before we start. Limits in writing from the owner. Anything we skip gets a written reason and a notice. We don't interpret the policy, we don't give medical advice, and we never call our own check a clearance.

glossary.title: Glossary

terms.definition: Part of the structure hit by primary or secondary damage.

The machine itself: an air filtration device (fan + filter, usually pre-filter and HEPA) that pulls particles out of the air. This is the unit type word on Equipment - Master lines (write AFD, not HEPA). When recirculating it is often called an air scrubber. A negative air machine is an AFD set up to create negative air pressure: placement/use, written as "AFD on negative air" (not a separate type word). HEPA is only a filter type that many machines can have; a model name like HEPA 700 stays the model as labeled.
A fan made or used for professional drying.
Air movement, measured as volume (CFM) or velocity (fpm).
An IEP's read of history and inspection data on contamination, with sampling only if needed. Not the restorer's evaluation.
Moisture held in the material's cell or crystal structure. Some belongs there (wood, concrete): don't dry it as if it were free water.
How dirty the water is: 1 clean (sanitary), 2 contaminated enough to make people sick, 3 badly contaminated. Set by where the water came from and what it ran through; time and heat can move it up.
Evaporation load when drying starts: under ~5%, ~5-40%, over ~40% wet porous surface; 4 = bound water in low-evaporation materials or assemblies.
Containing, removing, and properly disposing of unwanted substances.
Mold ecology: 1 normal, 2 residue from a known Condition 3 source in the same building, 3 actual growth (active or dormant, visible or hidden).
An engineering control that isolates an area, normally 6-mil poly, often with a pressure difference.
A seal over an opening (vent, door, duct) inside the work area.
Unwanted substances not normal indoors that can harm health or damage the building, systems, or contents.
Contaminants moving from a dirty area to a clean one.
Primary is direct wetting; secondary followed from it (humidity, growth, residue); pre-existing was not caused by this loss.
Short type word for a dehumidifier in Equipment - Master and related notes. Example: "LGR 6000Li, dehu, 10/27 (photo 3:42 PM PT)".
Removing moisture from air. Refrigerant units condense; desiccant units use sorption.
Temperature where air reaches saturation; cooler surfaces condense water.
Leaving a required or expected step, with a written reason and notice to the parties with a stake. Carelessness is not a deviation.
Sanitizer reduces the count (~99.9%); disinfectant inactivates target pathogens (~99.999%), not necessarily spores; sterilizer is meant to kill spores.
A fair estimate of the material's moisture before the loss, read from unaffected material or similar buildings in the area.
The target the restorer sets and writes for the end of drying: a moisture reading that meets or is below the dry standard, on a named material.
A controlled space where drying is pushed. A job can have several, each with its own category and class.
Part of the work plan: target ranges and methods for humidity, temperature, and airflow.
Equipment or barriers that prevent or sharply reduce exposure (containment, negative air, de-energizing).
Moisture content where a material neither gains nor loses moisture at a given RH and temperature.
The restorer's gathering and weighing of information (pre-restoration evaluation, post-remediation evaluation).
Water vapor the wet materials will add to the drying environment.
Fog under 50 microns (poor wetter); mist 50-100; spray usually over 200 (doesn't capture airborne particles).
Liquid on surfaces and in pores; all of it is removed in drying. Wood fiber saturation is about 25-30% MC.

A filter type: high-efficiency particulate air, at least 99.97% at 0.3 micron. Many things can have HEPA filters (AFDs, vacuums, and others). HEPA is not the unit type and is not slang for the machine. On equipment lines write AFD as the type; a label like HEPA 700 is a model name only when that is what the unit is labeled.
Removing vapor from the air at least as fast as the materials release it.
Grains of water vapor per pound of dry air. Specific humidity is per pound of moist air.
A person qualified to assess microbial ecology, sample, interpret, and verify return to Condition 1.
Gathering what is needed to call category, condition, class, or status.
Settled mist or product residue; it is cleaned and is not the return to Condition 1.
Owner-imposed restriction / harder-but-doable factor / after-start change / disagreement on method.
Field clock: short is 48 hours or less, long is over 48 hours in warm conditions.
Plaster, wood, concrete, masonry / multilayer wallboard, multilayer subfloors, gym floors.
Anyone substantially and directly affected by the project: who gets the deviation notice.
Reducing further damage by controlling the spread of moisture and contamination.
Content = % of oven-dry weight on a meter calibrated for that material; otherwise it is a relative level.
Record of how far water went, including adjacent dry areas.
Indicates moisture is present; gives no number.

An AFD set up to create negative air pressure (more air exhausted than supplied). Placement/use of an AFD, not a separate equipment type word. On Equipment - Master lines write "AFD on negative air" (with model if known, e.g. "HEPA 700, AFD on negative air, …").
More air exhausted than supplied, so the space is lower pressure than its surroundings.
The restorer's own check after remediation (visual, odor, moisture; for mold also towel wipe and dry).
A check by an independent party (IEP) that the area is back to Condition 1: normal for that kind of space, with no real leftover risk.
The restorer's category call so a scope can be written (for mold: also suspected Condition 3, assumed Condition 2, need for an IEP).
The restorer's recommended corrective actions from the inspection; feeds the work, drying, and safety plans.
Limiting further damage to an item that can't be fully restored.
The physics of air-water mixtures; temperature and humidity are the field pair.
How full the air is with vapor compared with saturation at that temperature.
Removing microbial contamination / the firm responsible for it.
Controlled removal of excess moisture from air and materials to a set goal.
The firm responsible for restoring the structure, systems, or contents.
Itemized services / the document saying how the scope will be carried out.
Someone with the skill for a specific decision (IEP, HVAC, conservator, electrical, fire suppression, firearms, instruments).
What reasonably prudent members of the trade commonly do.
Reads temperature and RH at minimum; some give GPP and dew point.
Fast structural or cosmetic failure, can't be adequately cleaned, cost is prohibitive, or the goal can't be reached.
Vapor moving through a material, driven by vapor-pressure difference and permeability.
Free water available for growth at the surface; surface RH 80% is about aW 0.80.
The part of air pressure from water vapor; the driver of drying.
Where the water came from. Field shorthand.

Risk bands for wood moisture: 12–14% is the standard working range; 16% and up is the red zone and the cutoff for dry-rot and mold risk. Not a dry standard: that comes from unaffected wood in the same structure.
More than 1 percent asbestos by lab analysis.

Under OSHA, thermal system insulation and surfacing material in buildings built by 1980, plus asphalt and vinyl flooring installed by then, until an accredited inspector or industrial hygienist clears it.
One material, uniform in color and texture and installed at the same time. One positive sample makes the whole area asbestos-containing.
The standard bulk-sample asbestos test.
A finer test for floor tile, mastic, low results, and air clearance.
The signed record that follows each sample from collection to the lab.

glossary.voice_note: Ask for any term and get one plain sentence.

initial_assessment.title: Initial Assessment
initial_assessment.description: First on-site evaluation. Identify hazards, determine category and class, verify the source, set realistic Day 1 scope, and decide required engineering controls.
key_activities: Safety 360 and staging
Customer interview and loss history
Non-intrusive walkthrough (visual + smell)
Visual sweep for standing water: identify extraction priority areas
Category/class determination and hazard identification
Source isolation verification
Early stabilization of immediate dangers
Engineering controls decision
Initial moisture readings on exposed surfaces (after bulk water removal)
critical_decision_points: What is the water category? (Err high if unsure)
Are engineering controls required before intrusive work?
Is the Day 1 scope realistic?
practical_guidance: Visual check for standing water first. If you see pooling, don't waste time metering: extract it immediately after source control and signed auth. The meter comes out after bulk water is gone to find hidden wicking and how far it traveled.
Day 1 is almost never full demo + complete drying. Focus on signed paperwork, source control, bulk extraction, basic containment, and drying setup.
Visible water is often not the origin: hunt for hidden COL behind walls, under floors, or from internal sources.
Internal plumbing failures (toilet supply lines, fridge ice makers, washing machine hoses) are more common than most people assume.

On Category 2 or 3, protect yourself first (PPE, limit movement through the space) and get bulk contamination out. Do not spray a biocide before the survey as a default: a biocide needs pre-cleaning, a registered product used per its label, and a trained applicator (see ULV vs Hand-Pump Sprayer). Wiping a walking path clean is fine.
If a ceiling is sagging, stabilize it with a zip pole as soon as the water is shut off: ideally before or right after source control.
Initial moisture readings are only on whatever surface is currently exposed. You cannot reliably read the subfloor until surface materials are removed or lifted.

Day 0 intake uses Inspection (Note Templates) plus the every-visit notes. Map or demo work stages or updates Mitigation Scope - <Room> and room Source of Loss / Pre-existing Damage as needed (Visit Note Cadence). Log materials layer by layer as they are opened, the same day.
initial_assessment.voice_considerations: Walk the tech through this phase step-by-step. Strongly emphasize 'Do not touch anything until authorization is signed' and the Category 3 / visible mold control gate.
test_intake_lines: A material scope change is a written change order with time and price.
Pre-existing damage is written down before it is mixed into this loss.
No services before a written authorization signed by the owner or agent. Source correction stays the owner's unless the authorization says otherwise.
Asbestos and lead that might be disturbed are identified before demo, and the people on site are told.
No pack-out without an inventory the client has signed, and no disposal without documented permission. A wet piano, instrument, firearm, or appliance is a specialist line.

PPE is required. Equipment stays until the goals are verified in the materials. Contaminants are remediated before drying. Repairs after dry are a re-evaluated scope, done by qualified licensed persons.

moisture_mapping_tape_line.rule: Put the blue tape a little bigger than the main wet area: at least 6 inches to a foot past where you first pick up the edge. Readings fade and get splotchy toward the outside. Get all of that fuzz of signal inside the tape.
moisture_mapping_tape_line.never: Never tape in the middle of the fuzz. If you do, there's moisture on the other side of your tape.
moisture_mapping_tape_line.voice_line: Tape past the fuzz. Six inches to a foot beyond the last hit, so nothing wet is outside the line.

source_control.title: Source Control
source_control.description: Stop the water at its origin and verify it has truly stopped before proceeding.
key_activities: Locate and shut off water at angle stop or main
Verify the water has actually stopped (visual confirmation)
Document source and stop time
critical_decision_points: Is the water truly stopped?
Do I need a plumber or utility involvement?
practical_guidance: Never assume the valve fully stopped the flow. For toilet supply line failures, open the tank and hold the flapper open to confirm no more water is entering.
Visual confirmation at the source is required before moving to extraction.
If you cannot stop the water, escalate immediately: do not proceed with extraction while it is still actively leaking.
source_control.voice_considerations: 'After shutting the water off, I need to verify it's actually stopped. For a toilet supply line, that usually means opening the tank and holding the flapper.'
test_intake_lines: Source repair is the owner's scope unless it is hired. Regulated hazards stop the water procedure and go to the specialist.

common_locations: Near the water meter (often outside or in basement/crawlspace)
Inside the house near where the main line enters (utility room, garage, basement)
Under kitchen or bathroom sinks (localized shutoffs)
field_tips: Always try to locate the main shutoff early, even if the leak appears localized.
On older houses, shutoffs can be seized, missing handles, or in awkward locations. Don’t assume they’ll work smoothly.
After shutting off the water, always verify it has actually stopped (visual confirmation).

common_issues: Supply line failures (toilet supply lines, fridge ice maker lines, washing machine hoses) are very common failure points.
Drain line issues: clogs, collapsed lines, or failed joints can cause slow leaks or backups.
Appliance-related failures (washing machines, dishwashers, water heaters, ice makers).
Fixture failures (toilet tank components, faucet cartridges, shower valves).
when_to_involve_a_licensed_plumber: The source of the leak is not obvious or accessible.
There is significant damage to plumbing lines (not just a supply hose).
The job involves modifying or rerouting plumbing.
There are signs of major issues (low pressure, multiple leaks, sewage involvement).
The homeowner or adjuster wants a professional plumbing assessment.

old_plumbing_considerations.galvanized_steel: Common in older homes. Prone to corrosion and restricted flow. Can hide leaks inside walls or under floors.
old_plumbing_considerations.polybutylene_pb: Used in some homes from the late 1970s to mid-1990s. Known for failures at fittings. Flag it if seen.
old_plumbing_considerations.copper: Generally reliable but can develop pinhole leaks in certain water conditions.
old_plumbing_considerations.pex: Common in newer construction. Generally reliable but can be damaged by improper installation or physical impact.
old_plumbing_considerations.polybutylene_and_aged_cpvc: Polybutylene (PB) and aged CPVC become extremely brittle with age. Shut off the main water supply before working around these pipes in any situation, even minor movement or vibration can cause sudden failure.

field_tips: Internal plumbing failures are more common than external sources on many residential jobs.
Put pressure caps on opened water supply lines even if the valve is secure. It looks professional and avoids liability.
Be careful not to create new leaks while moving or working around fixtures and appliances.
On higher contamination jobs, be extra careful about how water is being moved to avoid backflow into clean water supplies.
plumbing.polybutylene_voice_note: If you see polybutylene or old brittle CPVC, shut the main off first. That stuff can snap just from you bumping it. No exceptions.

extraction.title: Extraction
extraction.description: Mechanical removal of standing and extractable liquid water to reduce drying load and secondary damage risk.
key_activities: Pre-extraction controls verification (especially Category 2/3)
Electrical safety (GFCI)
Bulk water removal
Carpet/pad extraction with proper technique
Saturated material decisions
Aerosol and cross-contamination control
Waste handling
On Category 3 sewage jobs, line the cargo area before loading contaminated equipment and debris
critical_decision_points: Are controls verified before disturbing contaminated water?
Which materials must be removed now vs dried in place?
practical_guidance: Don't waste time metering standing water. If you see it pooling, extract it. The meter comes out after the bulk water is gone to find where it traveled and how deep.
Work extraction from the outer edges of the visible wet area inward toward the heaviest saturation. Starting in the center pushes moisture further into unaffected areas.
When using a carpet extraction wand near baseboards, set the wand down at the wall and pull outward: never push toward the baseboard. The lip will drive water under the baseboard if you push.

Extract first, then build containment: on the vast majority of losses, including Category 3. The water is spreading and has to be stopped; full plastic first gets in the way (doors, contents) and negative air first is rarely achievable. Containment first only as the exception (Equipment Setup: Containment First Exceptions).
Put a lipped mat or tray under dehumidifiers in case they leak: it's cheap insurance against secondary damage claims.
GFCI protection is good for your equipment, your liability, and the customers home. Scales up in importance and demand as job size increases.
extraction.voice_considerations: Emphasize technique details: outer-to-inner extraction and the carpet wand baseboard rule. These small habits dramatically improve results.

sewage_liner.title: Category 3 Cargo Liner
sewage_liner.when: Required on Category 3 sewage jobs when you will haul contaminated equipment or debris from the extraction. The job condition is sewage: you are transporting the extractor, its hoses, and contaminated debris bags. Do not treat this as a default for ordinary demolition. Demo debris is solid. The risk here is liquid from a torn bag or a dripping hose.
sewage_liner.how: Before you load the van or truck, line the cargo area with one large sheet of plastic. Run it up one side wall, across the floor, and up the other side wall, like a bowl, with a raised lip at the back door.
sewage_liner.load: Dirty equipment, the extractor and its hoses, and debris bags go in the lined area, so a torn bag or a dripping hose stays on the plastic instead of soaking into the vehicle.
sewage_liner.after: When the run is done, fold the plastic in on itself and dispose of it, or clean it as Category 3 contaminated material. Lining the cargo area first saves decontaminating the vehicle.
sewage_liner.voice_note: Category 3 sewage, and you're hauling the extractor, hoses, or dirty bags? Plastic down first: up one wall, across the floor, up the other wall, with a lip at the back door, like a bowl. Dirty gear goes in the bowl. Fold it in and throw it away, or clean it as Category 3, so the van doesn't get soaked.

ambient_humidity_assessment.title: Ambient Humidity Assessment (Pre-Equipment Screen Only)
ambient_humidity_assessment.description: Capture room temperature and RH in the main living area or a representative unaffected space before any containment or equipment is placed, so the impact of the equipment shows. This is a pre-equipment screen only: once drying equipment is running, use GPP and temperature (Base Science: Psychrometry) as the primary control metrics, not RH alone.
key_activities: Take temperature and RH reading in an unaffected main area before equipment is placed
Document location, timestamp, and the starting readings so later readings show the impact
If the space already feels damp or musty, or there is visible moisture, note it and plan dehumidification from the start
ambient_humidity_assessment.voice_line: Quick ambient reading in the main area before we set anything up (temp and RH), so we can show the impact once the equipment is running. That's a pre-equipment screen only: once gear is running we drive off GPP, not RH alone.

integration.notes: Pre-equipment screen used with source control / early assessment. After equipment placement, prefer Base Science: Psychrometry (GPP-first). Not a substitute for hold or drying GPP control.

ambient_humidity_assessment.scope_note: Pre-equipment screen only. Capture room RH before equipment is placed so the impact shows. After equipment is placed, switch to GPP-first psychrometry: do not use starting RH as the primary drying performance metric.

contents_handling.title: Contents Handling
contents_handling.description: Assessment, protection, cleaning, pack-out, pack-in/around (on-property storage), or disposal of personal property affected by the loss. This is one of the most visible parts of the job: do it well and you build serious trust.
key_activities: Photograph everything before you touch it: wide shots plus close-ups of condition. This is non-negotiable on anything valuable or disputed.
Quick triage: obvious trash gets bagged, photographed, and set aside; disposal only after documented permission. Everything else typically gets packed unless it's clearly ruined.
Clean before packing on water jobs. On fire, soot, or heavy mold losses, decide between on-site cleaning or pack-out to a proper cleaning facility.
Proper packing, labeling, and chain of custody.

Consider 'pack-it': systematically moving items to a clean area of the house instead of a full pack-out when practical. On whole-house contamination losses where the entire property is affected (heavy fire that traveled through HVAC, widespread mold from crawlspace hot water breaks, major Category 3, etc.), there may be no clean area available. In these cases, fully clean and seal off one room early to create a dedicated clean storage zone. Move salvageable contents there once, then you can aggressively gut the rest of the property without repeatedly moving belongings through contaminated areas.
This clean zone strategy is situational. It is most useful when the contents are worth saving and the occupants plan to keep them.
Contents protection is liability armor as much as physical protection. Err on the side of caution: it’s usually the correct business decision.
Organized contents work beats disorganized work every time. Take the time to do it right the first time.
Be both nice and efficient. Customers want their things treated with care, but they also want their house back quickly. The best techs do both: they’re respectful without being slow or precious.
Use clean staging areas with poly or ram board. Never set dirty or sooty items directly on clean surfaces.
Don't handle drugs, money, or weapons.

contents_return.description: Process for returning customer personal property from storage back into the home after reconstruction is complete. Focuses on protecting finished surfaces, smart body mechanics, proper equipment use, staging boxed contents, thorough redocumentation, and rebuilding positive customer rapport.
key_activities: Confirm all reconstruction, painting, and final cleaning is complete before returning any contents
Wear booties by default on every entry until floor protection is fully installed
Install fresh floor protection before moving any items inside
Use corner guards on high-quality finishes and new construction when appropriate
Move large furniture and major items into their respective rooms first
Remove drawers and shelves from heavy furniture and shelving units before moving the main body
Use furniture dollies, chest straps, and two-man elbow straps for heavy items
Use furniture sliders when tipping up tall bookshelves or cabinets
Stage all boxed contents inside each room for customer unpacking
Redocument every major item for damage before and after placement
Actively engage with the customer during placement to rebuild rapport
Customer-directed placement of large items
Final customer walkthrough and sign-off
Is the home 100% finished with all final cleaning completed before we start the return?
Does the quality of the home and finishes justify installing corner guards?
Are we using the right moving equipment for heavy items?
Never bring contents back until the home has passed final cleaning.
Always wear booties until floor protection is down.
Install floor protection on all high-traffic paths. Use corner guards only when the home has high-quality finishes or new construction where even minor bumps could cause visible damage.
In older or heavily used homes, floor protection is usually sufficient.
Remove drawers and shelves from heavy furniture and shelving units before moving the main body: move them separately.
Use furniture dollies, chest straps, and two-man elbow straps for heavy items.
When tipping tall bookshelves or cabinets, use furniture sliders under the base.
Tip tall items backward carefully so drawers or shelves don’t fall out.
Stage all boxed items inside each room so the customer can unpack them at their convenience.
Take clear photos of every major item before and after placing it, comparing to the original pre-existing damage photos.
Use this phase to rebuild positive rapport with the customer: they will usually be present directing placement. Be friendly, crack appropriate jokes, and take extra care of their belongings.
contents_return.voice_considerations: This is one of the most customer-facing phases. Stay calm, professional, and personable. This is your chance to leave a strong final impression.

contents_handling.voice_considerations: Talk like a pro who genuinely cares about people’s stuff but still knows how to move a job forward. Sound respectful, organized, and confident.
reference_lines: Three calls: restore, dispose, or preserve. The parties with a stake take part.
Inventory before removal, signed by the client: description, quantity, condition, location, number. No disposal without documented permission.
Category 1 contents are dried, then cleaned. Category 2 or 3 contents are cleaned, then dried. Wet contents are dried before packing and do not go back into an unrestored room.

Category 2/3 mattresses, box springs, pillows, and stuffed pieces are generally unrestorable. Swollen compressed-wood case goods are discarded. Category 3 porous items that cannot be fully cleaned are disposed.
Air washing a Category 2/3 porous item can drive contamination in. High-pressure washing is an outdoor method. Vacuum dry soil before a wet clean.
Electronics leave the humid room the same day; a wet TV, computer, or appliance is a specialist evaluation. Firearms, instruments, art, and data are specialty lines. A wet piano is a specialist move.

Mold contents: Condition 3 is packed separately; package exteriors are cleaned before they leave the chamber; a contents vacuum is at least three passes in a cross pattern; a textile at Condition 3 is checked for hyphae before a clean is promised; an unrestored return is labeled.
practices: Sort on site first: trash, pack-out, clean-on-site.
Work from least damaged to most damaged so clean items are not re-contaminated.
Contents work is where you build or destroy trust: customers remember how you handled their things.

ozone_treatment.title: Ozone Treatment
ozone_treatment.rule: Ozone requires clearing the house. Nobody goes in while it runs.
ozone_treatment.fire_contents: Fire-job contents: wiped and cleaned items go on shelves in a shipping container with an ozone generator to pull the remaining smell, especially porous items like furniture and clothing. Nobody goes in while it runs.

engineering_controls.title: Engineering Controls
engineering_controls.description: Establishing containment, negative pressure, air filtration, and other controls to manage contamination and airflow.
key_activities: Determine required control level
Install floor protection and critical barriers early
Build full containment when needed

Set up and verify negative pressure / HEPA scrubbing. Mold scope: minimum -5 Pa (-0.02 in. WC) established before the first disturbance, verified by manometer, plastic direction, or indicator smoke; 4 ACH. Water-only jobs: about -5 Pa or more negative is the kit target; quarter bounce is a quick field check, not the verification.
Ongoing verification during the job
If mold is more than a few square feet, consider a decon chamber or external door to working area access.
critical_decision_points: What level of containment is actually required?
Is negative pressure holding under load?
practical_guidance: Use a framing laser for fast, straight tape lines when hanging poly: it dramatically improves speed and quality.
When pulling plastic tight wall to wall into double-sided tape, place the edge about a fingertip width beyond before sticking, which gives just enough flex not to overstress the tape.
Place the negative air machine on the wall furthest from the door. Install makeup air on the same wall as the door but as far from the machine as possible.
Keep containment 18 inches to 2 feet beyond affected materials when possible.

On very small bathrooms with a water-only scope you often don't need negative pressure: equipment can go in the tub or on a vanity. On any mold scope the room still gets containment and the minimum negative before disturbance (see Containment: Mold Pressure). If there is a window, use it for negative: small spaces push dust into the house easily.
Re-verify containment integrity and negative pressure at the start of every monitoring visit, especially on Category 2/3 or mold jobs.
engineering_controls.voice_considerations: Practical sequence most techs actually use: quick floor protection + extraction first, then proper containment. Full walls before extraction is often inefficient on residential jobs.

negative_pressure_targets.continuous: About −5 Pa or greater (more negative). Hold continuous while work is open.
negative_pressure_targets.air_changes: When sizing or verifying, target 4+ ACH. Size the machine; add a second unit if the chamber is large.
negative_pressure_targets.field_check: Quarter bounce on 6-mil (or equivalent billow). Flat or flapping = lost pressure. A manometer reading is the record on a mold scope.
negative_pressure_targets.voice_note: Neg air target: about minus five pascals continuous, or more negative. Size for four-plus air changes an hour. Quick field check: bounce a quarter on the six-mil; if it's flat or flapping, you lost pressure.
negative_pressure_targets.mold_scope: Mold scope is not this note: see Containment: Mold Pressure (-5 Pa minimum before work, verified by manometer, plastic direction, or smoke).

gas_appliance_backdraft.risk: A negative-pressure chamber that includes or sits next to a gas appliance can starve the flue and pull combustion products (CO) back down the vent.
checks: Identify gas appliances in or adjacent to the chamber before pulling hard negative.
Check flue draft while negative air is running.
Plan makeup air from the clean side so the flue is not starved.
HEPA over a heater intake is temporary only, not a substitute for draft/makeup planning.
gas_appliance_backdraft.voice_note: Gas appliance in or next to a negative chamber: check flue draft and plan makeup air before you pull hard. Negative air can starve the flue and pull CO back down the pipe.

floor_and_surface_protection.title: Floor and Surface Protection
floor_and_surface_protection.description: Protection laid before work so walk paths, finished floors, and what stays in the home are not damaged or soiled. Each kind is its own billable line.
floor_and_surface_protection.carpet_runner: Self-adhesive runner: carpet masking and protection. Essential on carpeted walk paths.
floor_and_surface_protection.floor_paper: Floor paper (Ram Board brand paper): the normal floor protection. Billed SF.
floor_and_surface_protection.protection_board: Heavy cardboard protection board: for glass doors, moving appliances over hardwood, and heavy concrete or tile work over nice hardwoods. A different product from floor paper. Billed SF.
floor_and_surface_protection.painters_plastic: Painter's plastic: billed SF for whatever it covers (contents, windows, any purpose).
floor_and_surface_protection.corner_protection: Corner protection: billable in high-end or new-construction homes with real demo, using protection board or floor paper. Take photos and write a clear reason for the insurer. Temporary corner guards for an extraction hose are not billed separately: they are part of the extraction fee and company procedure.

containment.title: Containment
containment.description: Plastic and isolation for every job. Minimal containment (doorway isolation, floor protection) is the baseline, even on clean Category 1; full containment with negative pressure and an airlock comes in before demo or when contamination risk exists. Covers containment types, when to use each, the build sequence, mold pressure, HVAC intake, gas appliances, and blowouts.
containment.default_top: The home's ceiling is the top. Do not build a poly top. Scoping default, so a poly ceiling is not scoped: Scoping: Order of Work: Engineering Controls Before Demo: Containment Top.

zipper_doors.single_zipper: Place the zipper so the bottom sits right where the plastic meets the floor. Cut two 45-degree angles about 18 inches wide at the bottom (starting roughly 4 inches outside each side of the zipper) to create a flap with no trip hazard. Run the zipper up 2–4 feet, then add another set of 45-degree angles near the top, leaving 1–2 feet at the ceiling. This creates a wide C-shaped opening that’s easy to scoot equipment through.
zipper_doors.double_zipper: Install two zippers 3–4 feet apart running straight up and down. Cut straight across the bottom between them. This creates a full-width door that can be rolled up, which is much better when moving furniture, dealing with accessibility, or frequently moving equipment in and out.
zipper_doors.placement_note: Place doorways in locations that are convenient for both workflow and the customer, if they need to move through the area.

types: Full containment with negative pressure and airlock

even_category_1.note: Even on Category 1 jobs, some level of containment should be used. Minimal containment (doorway isolation, floor protection) should be standard on nearly every job. Full containment becomes necessary once significant demolition or material removal begins.
even_category_1.core_mindset_extension: Always take the opportunity to build plastic. It’s a billable item that’s cheap for the customer, saves equipment runtime, and shows you’re being proactive and professional on the job. Reducing air volume is one of the highest-ROI moves you can make, even on clean water losses.

blowout.definition: A break or failure in the containment seal that allows air to blow out from the contained area into the surrounding space, typically under negative pressure.
common_causes: Tape not adhering well to painted or textured surfaces
Insufficient support poles allowing plastic to sag or pull away
Foot traffic or equipment movement stressing seams
Temperature changes causing plastic to expand/contract
Poor initial sealing technique or missed spots during build
Overly aggressive negative pressure without enough makeup air or poles
blowout.identification: Visual inspection during daily monitoring visits. Look for gaps at floor-wall junctions, loose or flapping plastic, air movement at seams, or customer reports of dust/odor migration. May be noticed by customer or discovered by tech on re-verification.
repair_techniques: Add an additional ZipWall pole or support to pull plastic tight
Apply a second line of blue tape along the affected seam
Use staples with a small cardboard backer on painted or poor-adhesion surfaces
Re-tape or reinforce the double-sided tape base if lifting
Patch small holes or tears with tape or additional plastic
Reduce negative pressure slightly if over-pulled and causing repeated failures: never below the -5 Pa minimum on a mold scope; fix the barrier and supports instead
blowout.prevention: Anticipate problem areas while building. On painted or glossy surfaces where tape adhesion is questionable, pre-install staples with cardboard backers at key points. Use extra poles on larger spans or where plastic will be under load. Double-tape critical seams on Category 2/3 jobs. Test seal integrity before leaving the site on initial setup and at start of each monitoring visit.
blowout.field_notes: On water-only cleaning jobs, blowouts are common and usually not catastrophic since final detailed cleaning happens at the end. Fix it promptly when found, document the occurrence and repair in the daily log, and note any pattern if blowouts recur in the same location. Chronic or repeated blowouts in the same spot may indicate a need to upgrade the initial containment design. On a mold scope it is different: a breach or loss of pressure stops the work until the barrier and pressure are back, and the breach is reported and recorded (Containment: Mold Pressure).

gas_appliance_backdraft_check.when: Gas appliances sit inside or adjacent to a negative-pressure chamber.
gas_appliance_backdraft_check.voice_note: Before you pull hard negative around a gas water heater or furnace: check flue draft and plan makeup air. Don't starve the flue.

containment.core_mindset: Always take the opportunity to build plastic. It’s a billable item that’s cheap for the customer, saves equipment runtime, and shows you’re being proactive and professional on the job. Reducing air volume is one of the highest-ROI moves you can make.

when_to_use.always: On every job, regardless of category, even clean Category 1. Minimal containment is the baseline; full containment when demo or contamination risk exists.
when_to_use.demo: Before any demolition or dust-creating work
when_to_use.isolation: To isolate the affected area instead of conditioning the whole house
when_to_use.air_volume: Anytime you can reduce air volume to make equipment more effective

recommended_sequence: Perform bulk extraction first, before contents and plastic, in every category (contents first only if they block the water path; containment first only as the exception: see Equipment Setup: Containment First Exceptions; sewage pump-out may need containment first; Cat 3 crawl: hose breaks the hatch containment, so use heavier path protection)
Floor protection only where the water path or work path needs it, not a blanket first step
Build plastic to isolate the affected area
Set up full containment and negative pressure if required for contamination control
Marking layout first: After deciding where you want containment, use double-sided tape to mark out exactly where the plastic is going. This way everything is ready once you cut your plastic.

Tape application technique: Hold the roll in one hand and pull out a long strip with the other. Stick just the end on the edge where you want to straddle, then pull and lay the whole strip down at once. Smooth it over, then pull out the next long section. Scoot across the floor on your knees: it’s fast once you get the rhythm. This technique works for both blue tape and double-sided tape.
Double-sided tape ripping technique: While ripping double-sided tape, give it a quick jerking back-and-forth motion. This makes the outer release liner much easier to peel off later.
Cutting plastic: Cut the plastic off the roll first before hanging. Consider using scissors instead of a knife when working near expensive finished surfaces.
Plastic orientation tip: The clean factory-cut edge of the 10-foot side can be placed right along the edge of the double-sided tape as you hang it.
Extra material: Give yourself an extra foot or more where the plastic meets the wall. Having a little extra is much cheaper and better than coming up short and having to patch it.

Practical hanging method: Use 10-foot wide plastic, oriented vertically. The home's ceiling is the top: do not hang a poly ceiling. Pull out the length you need, get on a ladder, attach the plastic to the ceiling with double-sided tape first, then work your way down the sides and bottom.

Side attachment technique: When attaching plastic to the sides, work back and forth; go a few feet down the left side, then switch to the right side, then back to the left, alternating sides as you work your way down. This keeps the plastic tight and even.
On particularly dirty Category 2 and definitely on Category 3 jobs, apply a second layer of blue tape along the seam where the plastic meets the double-sided tape on the wall.
Use ZipWall poles to support the plastic, especially useful on popcorn ceilings or when the plastic is heavy. Start your first corner with a ZipWall pole if needed.
Running negative pressure? You’ll need more poles. The smaller the room, the more poles per foot you need to keep the plastic tight and prevent it from sucking in.
When pulling plastic wall-to-wall into double-sided tape, leave about a fingertip width of extra material before sticking it: this gives just enough flex so you don’t overstress the tape.

Negative air return filter installation: Use the same size filter as your negative air machine. Tape it securely from the outside of the containment with airflow pointing inward. Then go inside and cut the plastic on the right, left, and bottom edges to create an inward-pulling flap.

Negative air transition: Once contaminants have been removed and cleaning is complete, switch the negative air machine to static/recirculation mode inside the room. This helps retain the warm, dry air inside the space. On a mold scope, negative stays on until the restorer evaluation passes (or independent verification, when it is in the job).
containment.voice_note: Always take the chance to build plastic: billable, cheap for the customer, cuts air volume, and makes the gear work harder. Minimal containment is baseline even on Category 1; full containment before demo or when contamination risk is up.
containment.voice_considerations: Arrival protect, then isolate the wet zone, then build plastic tight, then HVAC and negative pressure if needed: technique tips after the hang plan is set.

recommended_sequence_voice_chunks.label: Arrival / protect
recommended_sequence_voice_chunks.voice_cue: Extract first, before contents and plastic. Floor protection only where the water or work path needs it. Containment first only when the job truly calls for it.
steps: Perform bulk extraction first, before contents and plastic, in every category (contents first only if they block the water path; containment first only as the exception: see Equipment Setup: Containment First Exceptions; sewage pump-out may need containment first; Cat 3 crawl: hose breaks the hatch containment, so use heavier path protection)
Floor protection only where the water path or work path needs it, not a blanket first step

recommended_sequence_voice_chunks.label: Isolate
recommended_sequence_voice_chunks.voice_cue: Build plastic to isolate the wet zone; full containment and negative pressure if contamination risk; isolate HVAC registers and returns.
steps: Build plastic to isolate the affected area
Set up full containment and negative pressure if required for contamination control
Isolate HVAC registers and returns

recommended_sequence_voice_chunks.label: Build
recommended_sequence_voice_chunks.voice_cue: Mark layout with double-sided tape first, then hang: cut off the roll, ceiling first, work sides alternating, leave a little extra at the wall.
steps: Marking layout first: After deciding where you want containment, use double-sided tape to mark out exactly where the plastic is going. This way everything is ready once you cut your plastic.

Tape application technique: Hold the roll in one hand and pull out a long strip with the other. Stick just the end on the edge where you want to straddle, then pull and lay the whole strip down at once. Smooth it over, then pull out the next long section. Scoot across the floor on your knees: it’s fast once you get the rhythm. This technique works for both blue tape and double-sided tape.
Cutting plastic: Cut the plastic off the roll first before hanging. Consider using scissors instead of a knife when working near expensive finished surfaces.
Plastic orientation tip: The clean factory-cut edge of the 10-foot side can be placed right along the edge of the double-sided tape as you hang it.
Extra material: Give yourself an extra foot or more where the plastic meets the wall. Having a little extra is much cheaper and better than coming up short and having to patch it.

Practical hanging method: Use 10-foot wide plastic, oriented vertically. The home's ceiling is the top: do not hang a poly ceiling. Pull out the length you need, get on a ladder, attach the plastic to the ceiling with double-sided tape first, then work your way down the sides and bottom.

Side attachment technique: When attaching plastic to the sides, work back and forth; go a few feet down the left side, then switch to the right side, then back to the left, alternating sides as you work your way down. This keeps the plastic tight and even.

recommended_sequence_voice_chunks.label: HVAC / negative pressure
recommended_sequence_voice_chunks.voice_cue: ZipWall poles for support: more poles under negative pressure. Install the return filter correctly, then transition to recirculation after cleaning: on mold, not until the evaluation passes.
steps: Use ZipWall poles to support the plastic, especially useful on popcorn ceilings or when the plastic is heavy. Start your first corner with a ZipWall pole if needed.
Running negative pressure? You’ll need more poles. The smaller the room, the more poles per foot you need to keep the plastic tight and prevent it from sucking in.

Negative air return filter installation: Use the same size filter as your negative air machine. Tape it securely from the outside of the containment with airflow pointing inward. Then go inside and cut the plastic on the right, left, and bottom edges to create an inward-pulling flap.

Negative air transition: Once contaminants have been removed and cleaning is complete, switch the negative air machine to static/recirculation mode inside the room. This helps retain the warm, dry air inside the space. On a mold scope, negative stays on until the restorer evaluation passes (or independent verification, when it is in the job).

recommended_sequence_voice_chunks.label: Technique tips
recommended_sequence_voice_chunks.voice_cue: Jerk the double-sided tape for easier liner peel; second blue-tape seam on dirty Cat 2/3; fingertip of flex when pulling wall-to-wall.
steps: Double-sided tape ripping technique: While ripping double-sided tape, give it a quick jerking back-and-forth motion. This makes the outer release liner much easier to peel off later.
On particularly dirty Category 2 and definitely on Category 3 jobs, apply a second layer of blue tape along the seam where the plastic meets the double-sided tape on the wall.
When pulling plastic wall-to-wall into double-sided tape, leave about a fingertip width of extra material before sticking it: this gives just enough flex so you don’t overstress the tape.

containment.mold_pressure: On a mold scope, nothing is disturbed until containment is up. Minimum negative is minus 5 pascals, minus 0.02 inches of water column, established before the work. Four air changes per hour, drawn from the entry across the work area to the farthest point, exhausted outside when possible. Polyethylene, when used, is 6 mil and fire-retardant. A breach or a loss of pressure stops the work until the pressure is back, and the breach is reported. Do not collapse this into the live about-minus-five, four-plus, quarter-bounce note.
test_intake_lines: If the building is still contaminated, the mechanical system is isolated from the indoor air. Equipment that ran inside a critical containment is cleaned or wrapped before it leaves.
No food, drink, or smoking in the work area. Contaminated clothing and used gloves stay with the contaminated debris. Coveralls on before the line.
Flaps open inward and are sized to hold the pressure. Containment stays until demolition, cleanup, and the evaluation or verification are done.
air_filtration_setup: Place the negative air unit inside containment, preferably near the farthest point from the entry; draw from the entry across the work area.
Exhaust filtered air outside when possible, away from intakes, windows, and doors.
Balance total CFM so negative pressure holds with all drying equipment running.
Leak test the air scrubber so all incoming air passes the HEPA filter; change pre-filters with the unit running; change the HEPA filter off the job; seal the intake before shutdown.
An air filtration device is not a substitute for containment and source removal.
containment.mold_pressure_layout: Mold containment uses critical barriers on openings and can be split into the work area, a dirty chamber, and a clean chamber. Flaps open inward and are sized to hold the pressure. The exit goes direct outside when possible. Decon chamber at least 3x3 ft, ideally 4x4 ft (field rule of thumb).

hvac_systems.title: HVAC Systems on Water and Mold Jobs
hvac_systems.description: Thin module. The building's mechanical system can spread humidity and contamination even if water never touched the unit.
key_rules: Category 1 water in ducts and components: drain or vacuum, then dry the system. Expected.

Category 2/3 that entered the system, especially internal insulation or fiberglass duct board: a qualified contractor evaluates and cleans to NADCA ACR; lined duct, duct board, or flex that is wet and contaminated is replaced.
A contaminated system is not run during the restoration. The building system is not the dryer.
If the building is still contaminated, isolate the HVAC from the indoor air (seal supplies and returns; HVAC intake ban in containment).
Exhaust fans, fireplaces, energy recovery, elevators, and central vacuums change the pressure your drying system is fighting.
Downflow or horizontal duct under the floor can hold moisture unseen: check it.
Coil cleanliness is a static pressure-drop test (manometer before/after), not a look through the panel. Clean both sides. A filtration upgrade keeps the designed airflow and pressure drop.
An antimicrobial in the system is registered for that use, or it is not used. No fog into a cavity or duct you cannot see. An opaque coating waits for independent verification when one is in the job.
A design moisture problem (condensation, undersized drainage) is outside the water-damage scope: note it and refer it.
A plenum or chase is part of the building, not duct-cleaning scope: it is cleaned with the structure.
Barriers on supplies and returns stay in place until the evaluation (or verification, when in scope) passes.
Applicable law and the manufacturer's instructions are confirmed before any HVAC servicing; that work is a qualified HVAC contractor's. Required.
hvac_systems.voice_note: Contaminated HVAC stays off and gets isolated. Wet lined duct or duct board on a Cat 2 or 3 gets replaced by a qualified contractor. The building system isn't the dryer.

hvac_intake_ban.rule: Never use a trash bag or plastic bag on a live HVAC return/intake as a containment lid.
hvac_intake_ban.why: Hard draw can suck the bag into the system, injure the tech removing it, and collapse containment.
hvac_intake_ban.do_instead: Shut the HVAC system down. HEPA-cover supplies and returns the proper way before work.
hvac_intake_ban.voice_note: Hard ban: never bag a live HVAC return or intake as a containment lid. Shut the system down and HEPA-cover supplies and returns the right way.

electrical_safety.title: Electrical Safety
electrical_safety.description: Thin field electrical controls for water-loss work: kill power where wet meets live circuits, protect people, then power tools safely.
key_rules: Standing water plus energized circuits = stop. De-energize at the breaker before you work wet areas or open wet walls near wiring.

Treat breakers as the primary shutoff. Confirm the circuit is dead before you trust it: identify, isolate, verify. Formal lockout/tagout is done by an authorized, trained person under the employer's program (29 CFR 1910.147).
Use GFCI protection on temporary power and wet-area tools. GFCI does not fix undersized or coiled cords: see Equipment Setup: Power: Extension Cord Safety.
Do not reset a tripped breaker into a flooded panel or wet junction. A wet electrical system stays off until a qualified electrician clears it; a submerged breaker is replaced (required).
