Large equipment loads run off a power box (also called a spider box) only when the pre-setup power survey shows the house circuits cannot carry them, or when circuits in the work zone are off, wet, or not trusted. Temporary power uses ground-fault outlets. Do not daisy-chain household circuits. See Pre-Setup Power Survey and Spider Box.
practical_guidance: On arrival safety walk: look for submerged outlets, warm/hot cords, tripped GFCI, and panels in the wet zone.
If you cannot safely de-energize, hold work in that zone and escalate: extraction and demo wait on electrical control.
electrical_safety.voice_considerations: Peer tone, short. Lead with stop-work: water and live power don't mix; kill it at the breaker, verify dead, GFCI on temp power.
electrical_safety.voice_note: Water and live power: stop. Kill it at the breaker, verify the circuit is dead, then work. GFCI on temp power. Basic LOTO mindset: identify, isolate, verify.

when_to_involve_a_licensed_electrician: There is standing water near electrical panels, outlets, or switches.
Electrical components have been burned or heavily smoked.
You need to verify power is off to an area.
There is damaged or exposed wiring.
The job requires moving, modifying, or repairing electrical components.
Aluminum wiring is present and work is needed in those areas.

old_electrical_systems.aluminum_wiring: Used in many homes built between ~1965–1975. Requires special connectors and handling. Can be a fire hazard if not addressed properly. Note it and be cautious about disturbing connections.
old_electrical_systems.knob_and_tube: Found in very old homes. Fragile and often not up to modern code. Water exposure makes it even more hazardous.

wet_nm_cable: NM-B cable (what most people call Romex) wicks. The paper wrap and filler inside the jacket pull water along the run by capillary action, past where the jacket looks wet: worst when cut ends or box ends sat in water.
Once wet, the copper conductors and the bare ground can corrode, and the failure can show up months later, not on day one. After the jacket dries you often can't see it.
Cable manufacturers and industry guidance treat dry-location cable as a replace after water exposure (rain, flood, storm water, pipe leak), not a dry-and-reuse.
There's no insurance rule written for wicked wire specifically. With the adjuster, the case is corrosion and safety, backed by the manufacturer recommendation.
Document it: wet or stained paper wrap at a cut end or box, green or darkened copper, how far along the run the wet went, and the manufacturer recommendation in the file.
The electrician decides what gets cut and replaced. Techs document and flag; they don't cut or pull wire to make the call.
common_hazards: Standing water near outlets, switches, light fixtures, or appliances is extremely dangerous.
Water can travel through walls and reach electrical components you can’t see.
Burned or damaged electrical panels, outlets, or wiring are common on fire jobs and older water losses.
Hidden corrosion on connections can develop over time after water exposure.
field_tips: Never assume power is off. Verify it.
Use a non-contact voltage tester when appropriate.
Keep extension cords and equipment out of standing water.
Treat any electrical component that has been exposed to water or fire as potentially compromised until verified safe.
Slow down around electrical systems. Rushing electrical decisions is how people get hurt.
electrical_extras.lockout_tagout: Lockout/tagout is done by a qualified authorized person (29 CFR 1910.147). On residential jobs, clearly communicating that power is off to an area still prevents accidents.

drying_and_monitoring.title: Drying and Monitoring
drying_and_monitoring.description: Active drying using equipment combined with ongoing data collection to verify progress toward drying goals.
key_activities: Psychrometric baseline and goal setting
Equipment placement and test run
Daily monitoring walks (same locations, consistent data)
Equipment performance checks and adjustments
Controls verification on every visit
Progress analysis and adjustments

meta.description: Knowledge base for local tenting as a targeted drying technique. Used to concentrate drying power on specific problem areas that are difficult to dry with open-room methods.

tenting.description: Local tenting involves creating temporary enclosures using poly sheeting to isolate and dry specific wet areas more effectively. It allows you to pipe dry air directly to the problem area while controlling temperature and humidity within the tent.
when_to_use: Bound moisture in subfloors (especially under vaulted or high ceilings where open-room drying is inefficient)

Behind or under cabinets and toe kicks. Solid-wood boxes can tent and dry in place on Category 1 only. Particle-board, MDF, or compressed-wood bottoms that sat wet come out first (Demolition: Decision Logic: Material Decision Matrix: Cabinets).
Underside of finished floors you want to save
Small, confined wet areas where full-room drying would be wasteful or ineffective
Targeted drying of wall cavities or specific structural assemblies
when_not_to_use: Large open areas (better served by standard equipment placement)
Low-evaporation assemblies like tile unless water intrusion is minimal
Situations where creating and maintaining the tent would cause more damage than it solves

basic_requirements: Use 6-mil or thicker fire-retardant poly sheeting
Seal the tent as well as practical to contain dry air
Pipe a dehumidifier directly into the tent (positive pressure into the enclosure)
Include an air vent or exhaust path unless the tent opens into a crawlspace
Use a humidistat inside the tent to control conditions
Keep temperatures reasonable: avoid excessive heat inside the tent
best_practices: Make the tent as small as possible while still covering the wet area effectively
Monitor temperature and humidity inside the tent regularly
Ensure good airflow across the wet surfaces inside the tent (small air movers or directed ducting can help)
Check for condensation on the inside of the poly: adjust airflow or temperature if it becomes excessive
Document the tent setup with photos for the job file

field_tips: Local tenting works especially well when you have bound moisture in subfloors under vaulted ceilings: it concentrates the drying effort instead of trying to condition the entire large air volume.

Under cabinets and toe kicks: Use existing gaps or carefully lift the toe kick to see the bottom panel and the floor under it. Tent the cavity when the box can dry in place (solid wood, Category 1 only). Particle-board, MDF, or compressed-wood bottoms that sat wet get replaced, not tented: see Demolition: Decision Logic: Material Decision Matrix: Cabinets.
Under bathtubs: Tenting can be very effective if you can get dry air underneath without major demolition.
Always use a humidistat inside the tent. Without one, you risk over-drying or creating condensation issues.
If the tent is venting into a crawlspace, you usually don’t need an additional vent. If venting into the living space, include a controlled exhaust path.
Local tenting is often more effective than aggressive high-velocity air movers alone on materials with bound moisture.
Combine with low-velocity airflow inside the tent when dealing with wood or other sensitive materials.
limitations_and_risks: Creates additional work to build and later remove the tent
Can trap moisture if not properly vented or monitored
Not effective on low-permeability materials like tile unless very small water volume
Risk of condensation on the poly if temperature differential is too great
Requires monitoring: you can’t just set it and forget it
related_techniques: Wall cavity drying (flood cuts + directed air or negative pressure)
Targeted equipment placement without full tenting (sometimes sufficient)

critical_decision_points: Are we on track with drying goals?
Is moisture rising or new issues appearing?
practical_guidance: Document the drying process daily (equipment performance, moisture readings at consistent locations, adjustments made). Final verification must show materials have met the established dry standard with supporting data and photos. 'It felt dry' is not defensible.

Walk every drying job the exact same way every day. Start at the dehumidifier, record inlet vs outlet grains, check every air mover, take moisture readings in the same locations as Day 1, and make at least one intentional adjustment.
Check dehumidifier performance every morning: a healthy unit should typically pull 15–25 grains on an active job.

Pay special attention to commonly missed wet areas: under and behind cabinets, subfloor underneath base plates, California corners, inside vanity kickboards, and under shower pans. A particle-board, MDF, or compressed-wood cabinet bottom that sat wet is a replace, not another day of air (Demolition: Decision Logic: Material Decision Matrix: Cabinets). Solid-wood boxes can dry in place on Category 1 only. Shower or tub over a crawl: meter the underside of the subfloor from below, hammer probe recommended for subfloor over 3/4 inch (see Crawlspaces: Inspection: Underside Subfloor Under Shower Pans), keeping the pins off the masonry.
When drying bound moisture in wood, lower velocity airflow is often more effective than high-CFM blasting. It allows better heat transfer and creates a more gradual moisture gradient.
Small rooms can overheat quickly. Always use a humidistat in small spaces and monitor temperature daily. Never leave a small contained space without temperature control.
If the job isn’t drying well after two days, look first at airflow across wet surfaces, then at hidden moisture sources, then at equipment sizing.

Category 2/3 and mold: air movers stay off until remediation and selective demo are done (remediate before restorative drying). Category 1: the air-mover counts in Equipment Setup: Sizing and Calculations: Air Mover Sizing assume air on wet surfaces in place; the kit's habit of waiting for exposed framing (except layflat injection or improvised negative cavity drying) is field practice, if you dry Category 1 in place, set air per those counts and document it.
Do not take surface moisture readings immediately after spraying: meter reads chemistry. Wait for flash-off; hammer-probe framing if you need a structural number (see Moisture Readings After Spray).

Revolution LGR (and similar) can freeze at intake when output is ducted into tenting with excessive back pressure: peel rear filter for ice; real driver is restricted output airflow (see Dehumidifier Ducting & Back-Pressure).

On a monitoring walk, stage 04 Monitoring for materials already in play (Visit Note Cadence). Do not prompt for a new material unless the user elects it. A gear move for a wet-spot shift stages 06 Equipment with what, why, and how.
drying_and_monitoring.voice_considerations: This is one of the highest-value phases for daily support. Structure monitoring as a repeatable checklist the tech can follow verbally.
drying_and_monitoring.monitoring_module_note: Detailed fixed-point techniques, screw method, crawlspace wire extension, and chasing the wettest spot are now in the dedicated 'monitoring' module. Reference it for implementation details during daily visits.

green.meaning: Standard working range. Still compare to unaffected wood in the same structure: a reading in this range is not automatically at dry standard if the unaffected wood is drier.

red.meaning: Red zone: the real cutoff for dry-rot and mold risk.

traffic_light.description: Risk bands for field action on wood moisture, not a replacement dry standard. 12–14% is the standard working range. 16% and up is the red zone and the real cutoff for dry-rot and mold risk. The dry standard comes from unaffected wood in the same structure (see Base Science: Dry Standards). A reading in the 12–14% working range may still be above the unaffected wood in this structure: keep drying to that standard.

dry_standards.voice_note: The goal is a moisture reading that meets or is below the dry standard, written against a named material: unaffected wood in this house sets it. Two to four points on wood is a field check, not the goal. Twelve to fourteen is the standard working range. Sixteen and up is the red zone for dry-rot and mold risk. A reading in the working range is not done if the unaffected wood is drier.

moisture_after_spray.title: Moisture Readings After Spray
moisture_after_spray.rule: Do not take surface moisture readings immediately after spraying: the meter reads the chemistry, not the framing.
moisture_after_spray.wait_for_flash_off: Wait for flash-off before surface readings. If you need a structural number sooner, hammer-probe the framing.

probe_insulation.guidance: Insulated hammer probes have insulation up the shaft to the body, so surface film does not short them. Bare screws or uninsulated pins have no shaft insulation: surface film can bridge the heads and give a falsely high reading unrelated to cavity moisture. Safer to wait for flash-off regardless of probe type.
probe_insulation.voice_note: After spray, wait for flash-off before you meter. Bare pins can bridge surface film and read false high: insulated hammer probes are better, but waiting is safer either way.

moisture_after_spray.voice_note: Don't take surface moisture right after spraying: you're reading the chemistry. Wait for flash-off, or hammer-probe framing if you need a structural number.

test_intake_lines: The goal is a moisture reading that meets or is below the dry standard, written against a named material. Within 10 percent is a common company shortcut used with a fixed 12–14% standard, not a rule. First monitoring visit is the day after the dry starts, then daily.
On a mold scope, containment and the air machines stay on until the independent party says verification passed, when verification is in the scope.

A log that closes a job has affected and unaffected readings, equipment inlet and outlet, the goal, and the location of each reading. Emergency work fills the missing records once the emergency is over.
The map is a diagram of where the water went. A thermal image is confirmed with a meter. Same meter, same locations, daily until the goal.
Equipment stays until the goal is verified in the materials. A goal change is a written notice. Contents go back after the final clean, not before.

thermal_imaging.title: Thermal Imaging
thermal_imaging.description: IR images help find affected areas and back up the moisture map. Always confirm with a meter.
thermal_imaging.billing: Billing is optional and up to the company; many companies do not bill it. The kit sets no unit: per image or per job is the company's choice.

general_cleaning.title: General Cleaning
general_cleaning.description: General cleaning on restoration jobs. Keep it simple: your goal is to return the area to pre-loss condition or better.
general_cleaning.core_approach: Work **top to bottom** and **outside in**. Start with ceilings and high areas, then work your way down the walls, and finish with the floors.
practical_tips: Follow the wall around the room in one direction so you don’t miss anything.
Clean one logical section at a time before moving on.
Always read the label on the chemical you’re using. It tells you required PPE, proper dilution, dwell time, and what surfaces it’s safe for.
Dilute chemicals correctly: failing to do so is a very common mistake.
Carry a trash bag with you for small debris when it makes sense.
general_cleaning.voice_note: Top to bottom, outside in. Read the label on your chemicals.

spot_pretreatment.title: Spot Pretreatment During Demo
spot_pretreatment.guidance: When demo opens something up and exposes a heavily soiled or contaminated spot (mold growing or blooming, cat urine or fur, sewage soiling), treat that spot right away for odor and contamination. Do not wait for the full cleaning pass. Read the label for PPE, dilution, and dwell time. Pretreatment does not replace removal or the full cleaning: the spot still gets physically removed or cleaned.
spot_pretreatment.voice_note: Opened up a nasty spot during demo? Treat it now for smell and contamination. It still gets cleaned later.

ulv_vs_hand_pump_sprayer.title: ULV vs Hand-Pump Sprayer
ulv_vs_hand_pump_sprayer.description: Equipment selection guidance for applying disinfectant to exposed framing, walls, and complex surfaces after demolition.
key_rules: First decide whether a biocide line is warranted at all. A Category 1 loss that stayed Category 1 generally does not get one. Not every loss warrants a biocide.

When a biocide is warranted and the label allows fogging, ULV is the faster tool for open framing and complex surfaces after pre-cleaning. ULV is significantly faster and more cost-effective than pump sprayers on medium to large jobs.
Physical cleaning comes first. Fog or spray is a supplement, never the removal.

rules_of_thumb.small_complex: Small or complex spaces with lots of plumbing, wiring, or irregular framing: Prefer ULV
rules_of_thumb.medium: 1,000 – 3,000 sq ft of surface area: ULV is usually preferred
rules_of_thumb.large: Over 3,000 sq ft of surface area: Strongly prefer ULV
rules_of_thumb.open_framing: Open joists or two-story walls: Default to ULV
rules_of_thumb.note: These pick the applicator after the biocide decision. They are not a reason to apply.

when_not_to_use_ulv.label_restriction: When the product label does not specifically allow ULV or fogging use
when_not_to_use_ulv.heavy_soil: When heavy visible contamination or sludge is present: physical cleaning required first
when_not_to_use_ulv.chemical_type: Product choice follows the label. Use only a product whose label allows fogging/ULV for that use. Do not assume a product class (AHP, botanical, quat, bleach) is fog-approved: read the label. An unregistered fog is not used.
when_not_to_use_ulv.sensitive_environments: Occupied buildings, healthcare facilities, or homes with infants, elderly, or chemically sensitive occupants
when_not_to_use_ulv.unseen_cavity: No fogging into a cavity or mechanical system you cannot see and clean afterward unless the label covers that use.
when_not_to_use_ulv.occupants: Occupants and pets out of the treatment area; follow the label re-entry time.

ulv_vs_hand_pump_sprayer.financial_note: On large framing jobs, choosing ULV over pump spraying can save 50%+ in labor hours and reduce equipment rental days.
test_intake_lines: A Category 1 loss that stayed Category 1 does not get a biocide line.
Pre-clean before any biocide. Only a registered product, label directions, and the client's written approval.
Pre-clean before any biocide. Organic matter deactivates many of them.
Only a federal or state registered product, label directions, and the label protection. Unregistered product is not a line.
A biocide line needs the client's written approval and the right-to-know record.
No biocide without training, the safety data sheet, the label, and occupants out. The file records type, method, time, quantity, dilution, and location.

consent_and_records.before: Consent was collected on Day 1 with the work authorization (phase1 Verify Paperwork): confirm it's in the file. Label and SDS on site; applicator trained for that product; label PPE worn; occupants out.
consent_and_records.record: Product, method, time, quantity, dilution, and location go in the file.
consent_and_records.claims: No claim beyond the label. A biocide is not a substitute for removal.

safety_requirements: Full label PPE (respirator under the written program, gloves, eye protection, suit as required).
Post 'Do Not Enter' signage with the product's re-entry time.
Turn off and isolate the HVAC system serving the area.
Never fog near open flames, sparks, or energized equipment that the label warns against.
Calculate the volume and the diluted amount; mix exactly per label; start farthest from the exit and work toward it; allow full labeled dwell time.

trash_management_and_logistics.title: Trash Management and Logistics
trash_management_and_logistics.description: Efficient trash and debris management is a frequently overlooked but critical part of restoration. It affects job site cleanliness, safety, crew efficiency, and how professional the job looks to the customer.

core_approaches.clean_as_you_go: Remove trash after completing each task or area. Preferred when customers or occupants are still active in the home. Keeps the site safer, cleaner, and more professional.
core_approaches.lightweight_waste: For small lightweight trash like tape wrappers, plastic, and paper, some techs prefer to drop waste directly into a trash bag as they work rather than letting it accumulate on the floor.
core_approaches.batch_then_clean: Demo and bag material for most of the day, then do a full cleanup at the end of the day. More efficient for pure production but creates a much messier site during work hours.

daily_handling.staging: Stage trash during the day, ideally right behind the work vehicle or in an approved area (driveway/sidewalk with permission).
daily_handling.hauling: Load up and haul trash back to the shop at the end of the day after tools are secured. Try to leave with a full vehicle load whenever possible.

vehicle_loading.dump_truck: Excellent for heavy debris. Stone, gypsum Crete, or self-leveler should only be filled halfway. Drywall, wood, and general construction debris can generally be filled normally. Always factor in weight when mixing materials.
vehicle_loading.cargo_van: Default for most residential jobs. Much easier to overload without realizing it.

contaminated_material.description: All contaminated debris must be properly sealed before leaving the work area.
methods: Wipe down the exterior of the bags with a sanitizing rag
contaminated_material.location: This process should be done inside the decon chamber before the bags exit containment.

equipment_decisions.van: Default method for nearly all residential jobs.
equipment_decisions.dumpster: Consider only on large multi-room or whole-house guts that will generate significantly more than one full vehicle load per day.
equipment_decisions.chute: Primarily for commercial jobs more than two stories high with heavy debris volume.

key_principles: Maintain clear walkways at all times.
Match your trash removal rhythm to the occupancy of the home.
The truck or van is often the real bottleneck, not how fast you can bag material.

final_verification.title: Final Verification
final_verification.description: Final checks to confirm materials have reached acceptable moisture levels and no hidden issues remain before customer sign-off.
key_activities: Pre-verification controls gate
Final moisture verification at established points
Structural and contents inspection
Controlled teardown only after verification passes
Customer walkthrough and education
Documentation package assembly
critical_decision_points: Have all materials met drying goals with data?
Are there remaining borderline readings or hidden concerns?
practical_guidance: Never begin teardown of containment and equipment until final moisture verification has passed. Tearing down early is one of the fastest ways to create callbacks.
Check previously elevated or suspect areas one more time, including wall cavities, subfloors, and insulation zones.
Walk the customer through every room that was affected. Show before/after photos and explain what was done in plain language.
Document any remaining repair needs clearly and provide written recommendations.
final_verification.voice_considerations: Be deliberate. This phase is about defensibility as much as technical completion. 'We don’t tear down until the data says we’re done.'
final_verification.mold_verification: When verification is in the scope, containment and the air machines stay on until the independent party says it passed. Teardown waits on that file entry. It is not a gate on every mold job. A third party is recommended when the clean is uncertain, occupant health is a concern, or the owner wants sampling. The restorer evaluates. An independent party verifies.

restorer_evaluation.mold: Remediator's own check before containment comes down: visible growth and the associated dirt, dust, and debris gone; no malodor; towel-wipe clean; remaining materials dry. If there is no independent verification, the air scrubbers stay on until this check is done and written.
restorer_evaluation.water: Drying equipment stays until the goal is verified in the materials (not when the air feels dry). Same meter, same locations. Materials that cannot reach the goal are an unrestorable call, documented.
restorer_evaluation.contents: Contents check is visual, odor, towel wipe, and dry. A fail is a reprocess or an unrestorable call. Contents go back after the final clean.
restorer_evaluation.words: Post-remediation evaluation = the restorer. Post-remediation verification = an independent party (IEP). Do not call your own evaluation 'verification' or 'clearance'.
restorer_evaluation.repeat_until_pass: Repeat clean steps (HEPA vacuum, wipe) until the area passes the restorer's check before an independent inspection is scheduled.

job_closeout.title: Job Closeout
job_closeout.description: Controlled teardown, site restoration, customer walkthrough, warranty discussion, final signatures, and securing the property after verification has passed. This is the final sequence that protects the work already done and sets up long-term trust.
key_activities: Controlled teardown of equipment, containment, and floor protection only after final verification passes
Site restoration and final cleaning during equipment removal
Customer walkthrough with before-and-after photos and plain-language explanation
Warranty explanation and duration
Final customer signatures and contact information handoff
Securing the property and vehicle loading
Capture of any lessons learned for the team
critical_decision_points: Has final moisture verification actually passed with supporting data?
Does the customer clearly understand what was done, what to watch for, and that we are a phone call away?
Are all billable items, scope changes, and time accurately captured before we leave?
practical_guidance: Never begin teardown until the final verification numbers and photos confirm dry standard. Tearing down early is one of the fastest ways to create callbacks.
Work carefully during equipment removal to protect finished surfaces: use floor protection and corner guards where needed.
During the customer walkthrough, show before-and-after photos side-by-side and explain in normal language what was removed versus dried, and why.
Clearly explain the warranty coverage and duration. Give them a direct number for any post-job concerns.
Walk the customer through every affected area so there are no surprises later.
Document any remaining repair recommendations in writing and give the customer a copy.
Before leaving, do one final visual check of the whole contained area for any missed debris or equipment.
warnings: Teardown before verification passes is a high-risk move that often leads to callbacks or disputes.
Weak or rushed customer walkthroughs are a common source of later confusion about what was done and what the customer is responsible for.
Failing to capture accurate final billables and scope changes while still on site creates billing problems later.
job_closeout.voice_considerations: Keep this phase calm and professional. The job isn't done until the customer understands what happened and the site is left clean and secure. 'Verification passed: now we pull equipment carefully and walk the customer through everything.'

documentation.title: Documentation
documentation.description: The defensive documentation discipline that runs through the entire job. Image storage is extremely cheap compared to the cost of not having them. Good documentation protects everyone (you, the company, the customer, and the file) when questions come up later about scope, pre-existing damage, or what was actually done.
documentation.core_principle: Document before you touch, document as you reveal hidden conditions, and maintain consistent fixed-point records so the story of the job is clear and defensible from Day 1 to closeout.
key_habits: Photo sweep the entire affected area and overall loss before any physical work begins.
Photograph every hidden area the moment it is exposed during selective demolition.
Use consistent fixed-point locations for daily moisture readings and photos so trends are visually obvious.
Document pre-existing damage thoroughly before starting work and note homeowner statements about it.
Photograph equipment placement, containment setup, and any scope expansions the same day they occur.
decision_criteria: When in doubt, take the photo. The cost of storage is near zero; the cost of weak documentation on a disputed scope or callback is not.
Any time scope expands or a judgment call is made (Category upgrade, remove vs dry, equipment change), document the condition that drove the decision.
Daily monitoring should always include the same photo angles as previous visits so progress (or lack of progress) is obvious.
practical_guidance: Take both wide/overview shots and close detail shots. One without the other is often useless later.
Consistent naming or at least date/time in the filename makes the package dramatically easier to navigate weeks or months later.
Fixed-point photos of the same locations used for moisture meter readings create visual evidence that supports the numbers.
Pre-existing damage photos protect both the tech and the company if the customer later claims something was caused by the loss.

Follow the call unless the job is an edge case or the note is wrong. Leaving it means a written reason, what was done instead, and notice to the parties who have a stake. That note is what a later email quotes. The email cites the file and the call. It does not certify the job.
A layer just opened is written the same day, layer by layer. That stages Scope, and room SOL when it is the source. It does not rewrite Day forward unless the plan changed (Visit Note Cadence).
warnings: No before photos or weak baseline documentation makes scope changes and added demo very difficult to defend.
Inconsistent photo locations day-to-day weaken trend data and make it harder to justify dry time or equipment decisions.
Skipping documentation on 'small' or 'straightforward' jobs is exactly when problems surface later.
documentation.voice_considerations: Treat documentation as a non-negotiable reflex, not an administrative task. Short prompts like 'Photo this before we move anything' or 'Document the spot we just opened' keep it habitual.
documentation.file_to_email: Follow the call unless the job is an edge case or the note is wrong. Leaving it means a written reason, what was done instead, and notice to the parties who have a stake. That note is what a later email quotes. The email cites the file and the call. It does not certify the job.

category_decision.title: Category Decision
category_decision.description: How to verify, adjust, or upgrade the preliminary water category on site. Category drives PPE, engineering controls, containment, and removal decisions. Always err high when uncertain.
key_activities: Confirm or adjust preliminary category from the loss history and visible conditions
Hunt for the Cause of Loss (COL): visible water is rarely the full story
Identify signs that justify upgrading (odor, discoloration, organic debris, dwell time >48 hours in warm conditions = long dwell, visible mold)
Document the final category and justification
critical_decision_points: What is the actual category based on evidence on site?
Do I have enough information to decide, or do I need to treat it as higher risk until proven otherwise?
practical_guidance: Visible water is often not the origin. Hunt for hidden COL behind walls, under floors, or from internal sources (toilet supply lines, fridge ice makers, washing machine hoses are very common).

Storm water, wind-driven rain, and roof or window leaks are not Category 3 by how they got in. Call the category from what the water carried and touched, how long it sat, and the temperature. Staining alone is not contamination and not rot: meter and probe it (Base Science: Water Category: Nuances: Weather Related Water).

If water has been present more than 48 hours in warm conditions (long dwell), or shows any signs of contamination, treat it as Category 2 or 3 until proven otherwise. Short dwell = ≤48 hours; long dwell = >48 hours: same clock as Base Science: Water Category: Decision Rules: Long Dwell Rule.
On Category 2 or 3, upgrade PPE and limit traffic before extensive metering. Biocide only after pre-cleaning, with a registered product and label directions, not as a reflex before the survey.
Category can migrate upward over time. Re-verify on every visit and adjust controls/PPE accordingly.
When in doubt, protect the customer and yourself: higher category is almost always the safer and more defensible choice.
category_decision.voice_considerations: Category is the gate for everything that follows. Past forty-eight hours warm is long dwell: elevate. If you're unsure, treat it higher and document why. You can always downgrade later with evidence; you can't easily go back up.
test_intake_lines: Toilet overflow with urine and no feces is Category 2. Sewage and any beyond-trap backflow are Category 3 regardless of color. Category 2 or 3 is remediated before restorative drying. Class 4 is bound water, not a bigger wet area.

Category 2 defaults to removing carpet and pad. The customer may elect to keep and clean the carpet in certain instances by signing a release of procedure. Category 3 takes both, plus the gypsum, the insulation, and the wallpaper. Wet cellulose comes out on any category.
Sewage carpet comes out. Cleaning it in place aerosolizes endotoxins.
Category follows where the water came from and what it contacts. Time and temperature can move it. A regulated substance does not by itself change the category.
Sewage or changed-category porous materials come out before any treatment. In-place clean is not the control.
Category 2 or 3 does not enter the dry until remediation is done. Category 1 demolition is only to speed the dry. A trauma scene and regulated material take the remediation branch.
Wet lined duct, duct board, or flex that is also contaminated is a replacement. A design moisture problem is not in the water-damage scope.

Three exits from a mold inspection: Condition 1 and no work, Condition 2 or 3 and a plan, or not enough information and an independent assessor. Condition 2 in that plan is a written assumption. An intrusive opening is captured at the source.
Condition 1 is normal ecology. Condition 2 is residue from known growth in that same building. Condition 3 is actual growth, hidden included. Assuming a condition is written, with the rationale.
Higher-risk occupants: elderly, infants, convalescents, immunocompromised.

hazard_sampling.title: Hazard Sampling
hazard_sampling.description: Bulk sampling of suspect asbestos (and lead or other regulated material) before any disturbance. The phases say when (Phase 0: Hazard Sampling, Phase 1: Confirm Sampling Results or Hold). This module says who, how many, and how. The stop rule lives in Demolition: Controls & Limits: Asbestos Demo Limits.

rules: To clear a material as not asbestos, the samples must be taken by an accredited inspector or an industrial hygienist (CIH) and run by an accredited lab. Only that clears presumed material.
A tech sampling for an internal go/no-go is screening. It does not clear the material and does not replace a required survey. Results pending or presumed: leave it alone.

Survey, notice, and inspector rules vary by state. Follow Kit Framework: Runtime Contracts: Jurisdiction. Until the work state is known, stay with these state-neutral rules and say the local survey requirement must be checked.
who_samples.tier_note: State survey rules vary. Oregon and Washington examples are in Examples by State. Use them only when the remembered state matches. Check the current rule in that state (Demolition: Controls & Limits: Asbestos Demo Limits: Jurisdiction Caveat).

oregon_small_repair_note.text: Oregon OAR 340-248-0250(1)(f): removing less than 3 square feet or 3 linear feet of asbestos-containing material is exempt from DEQ licensing and certification, notification, and the survey requirement, only if removing asbestos is not the primary objective, it is part of a needed repair, and removal follows the OSHA asbestos methods of compliance (OAR 437-003-1926.1101(g)). Projects can't be split up to fit under it. The rule names no emergency condition; it covers any needed repair. It is most known from plumbing repairs, and some restoration companies apply it to small inspection cuts. That use is company policy, not settled law and not a kit permission. It exempts the survey only: suspect material is still sampled or presumed, the OSHA presumption and work-practice controls still apply, and it is not the retired three-foot work permission. Check the current rule. Apply this note only when the remembered state is Oregon.
oregon_small_repair_note.not_a_default: Oregon example only. Apply only when the remembered state is Oregon. It is not a kit permission for other states.

Oregon.survey: A contractor renovating or demolishing a home built before 2004, or a commercial building of any age, needs an accredited-inspector survey first. The owner-occupant exemption is for owners doing their own work, not for a restoration company.
Oregon.small_repair: See Oregon Small Repair Note. Oregon example only, not a default.

Washington.survey: Before the work, the owner or agent needs a good-faith inspection by an AHERA-accredited inspector, or must assume asbestos and treat it that way. Regional clean air agencies such as SWCAA and PSCAA add their own survey, posting, and notice rules.
Washington.citations: RCW 49.26.013 and the local agency rule.

rules: Building age is a prompt, not a clearance. Suspect material of any age gets sampled or presumed. Older homes raise the bar. State survey examples are in Hazard Sampling: Who Samples: Examples by State. Use them only when the remembered state matches (Kit Framework: Runtime Contracts: Jurisdiction).
Default: baseboards and trim in older or suspect homes wait for results. Outlet covers and switch plates on clean Category 1 only if the drywall stays intact. Document it (Limited Targeted Access).
On Category 2 or 3, visible mold, or long dwell, sample before major demo.

Results delayed? Treat it as positive and don't disturb it. Containment, negative air, and PPE protect the space while you wait; they don't permit the cut. Work that doesn't touch the material can continue, or the job goes on Hold.
Asbestos-containing (more than 1 percent) or presumed asbestos goes to licensed abatement (Asbestos Demo Limits).
A homogeneous area is one material that is uniform in color and texture. Inspectors also split it by when it was installed: a later patch, repair, or different application is its own area.
Water staining alone does not make a new area.
One positive sample makes the whole homogeneous area asbestos-containing. Don't average across samples.
Layers are separate materials: wallboard, joint compound, skim coat or texture, paint. Describe the layers on the chain of custody.

wall_system_note.text: EPA allows tape and joint compound used only at joints to be reported with the wallboard as one wall-system composite. Skim coat and texture are never composited. Some states don't allow it: the inspector decides.

minimum_counts.tier_note: These are the school (AHERA) protocol counts. Surveys outside schools commonly follow them, and some agencies require them. They are a floor for an inspector, not a ceiling.

rows.surfacing_material: Sprayed or troweled (popcorn, texture, plaster, fireproofing): at least 3 under 1,000 sq ft, 5 up to 5,000 sq ft, 7 above 5,000 sq ft.
rows.thermal_system_insulation: Pipe, duct, and boiler insulation: at least 3 per area. At least 1 from a patched section under 6 linear or square feet. Fittings sampled enough to tell.
rows.joint_compound: At least 3 per area, taken at joints and corners. Add-on texture or skim coat: at least 3 more, taken between the joints.
rows.miscellaneous_and_nonfriable: Floor tile, sheet vinyl, mastic, caulk, roofing: enough to decide. Two is a common minimum and 3 is common practice. Resilient flooring and its mastic installed by 1980 are presumed asbestos until cleared.

steps: Photograph each sample spot and mark it on the diagram before you cut.
Mist the spot with amended water (water plus a drop of dish soap) before you penetrate it.
Take a small sample through every layer. About a teaspoon for friable material; about a 1-inch square for non-friable.
Each sample goes in its own sealed, labeled bag. Use one ID per sample, matching the diagram, the photo, and the chain of custody.
Seal the sample spot and HEPA-vacuum or wet-wipe the debris. Never sweep dry.
Keep others out of the room. Respirator, wet methods, and HEPA controls for sampling: Demolition: Controls & Limits: Asbestos Demo Limits: Required Controls.

practical_note.text: Tape an open garbage bag, with about a foot of tape along its top edge, just under the cut. It catches the dust, so there's little to vacuum or wipe. Still carry a wet rag, because it won't catch everything. The same tape seals the hole, or use a second piece. It works for ceiling samples too.

notes: Accredited lab (NVLAP or equivalent proficiency). PLM is the default; TEM is for floor tile, mastic, and low or borderline results.
Asbestos-containing means more than 1 percent. A trace result under 1 percent is not ACM but can still matter for worker exposure: read the report with the inspector.
Price and turnaround vary by lab; rush costs more.
Labs charge per sample, and adjusters may ask about extra samples. Write down why each sample was taken: what material, which homogeneous area, and which rule set the count.
Common field pattern: a small cut in one wall gets one sample per material it goes through. A whole room gets at least 3 per material. Bigger areas follow Minimum Counts.
A count that is too low clears nothing. If the count is short or in doubt, the material stays presumed.

hazard_sampling.lead: Pre-1978 paint falls under the EPA renovation rule. Test with an EPA-recognized test kit or a certified inspector or risk assessor, or presume lead. See Safety and Health: Stops.
hazard_sampling.voice_considerations: Suspect material? Wet it, take a small sample through every layer, bag and label it, seal the spot. One positive makes the whole area positive. Our samples don't clear anything; an accredited inspector's survey does.

limited_targeted_access.title: Limited Targeted Access
limited_targeted_access.description: Low-risk, non-destructive or minimally invasive access allowed on clean Category 1 losses before full demolition or before asbestos results return in older or suspect homes.
key_activities: Remove outlet covers and switch plates (clean Cat 1 only)
Limited inspection behind plates if needed for moisture or source tracing
Avoid removing baseboards, trim, or cutting drywall until asbestos results are back negative
Document exactly what was accessed and why
critical_decision_points: Is this a clean Category 1 loss with no suspect materials or older-home concerns?
Will limited access help locate the source or hidden moisture without creating liability?
practical_guidance: On truly clean Category 1 (no odor, no discoloration, short dwell, no visible mold), you can safely pull outlet covers and switch plates to check for hidden moisture or wiring issues.
Baseboard removal in older homes or with suspect material waits for asbestos results: disturbing caulk or paint can release fibers, and presumed asbestos is not disturbed (required).
If you need to see behind a wall on a clean Cat 1, consider a small inspection hole with proper dust control rather than full removal.
Anything beyond outlet covers/switch plates generally moves you into selective demolition territory: follow the Demo Order and safety gates.
Always document what you accessed and that it was low-risk Category 1 with no visible contamination.
limited_targeted_access.voice_considerations: Clean Category 1 only: outlet covers and switch plates are OK to pull. Older-home baseboards stay put until asbestos results are back: sample-wait is the default.

equipment_setup.title: Equipment Setup
equipment_setup.description: Practical setup of drying equipment (dehumidifiers, air movers, AFDs) including placement logic, GFCI protection, containment/negative pressure sequencing, and initial psychrometric goal setting.
key_activities: Run the pre-setup power survey before loading or placing equipment: project the load, map nearby circuits, and use a power box only when the survey shows a shortfall
Position dehumidifiers for good airflow and condensate drainage (use drip trays)
Place air movers to create directed airflow across wet surfaces rather than just circulating room air
On Category 2/3: set up AFD early; after bulk extraction, isolate heavily contaminated areas under negative pressure (containment first only as the exception)
Reduce air volume with containment early to make equipment more effective
Record initial equipment placement and baseline psychrometrics (temp, RH, GPP in affected + unaffected areas)
critical_decision_points: Does the pre-setup power survey show a power box is needed?
Is GFCI protection needed?
Do I have the right equipment mix and placement for the current Category and air volume?
Should I build containment and go negative before or after bulk extraction?

industry_rules_of_thumb.description: Collected field shortcuts for equipment sizing, not kit ratios. Some are outdated or oversimplified. Size by the unit type and rated CFM, the manufacturer guidance, and the readings.

square_footage_rules: Square-footage shortcuts exist in the field and vary by company. This kit does not invent pint ratios. Size by the unit type, the manufacturer guidance, and the readings.
cubic_footage_rules: Cubic-footage shortcuts exist in the field and vary by company. This kit does not invent pint ratios. Size by the unit type, the manufacturer guidance, and the readings.
Cold conditions (under 65°F) usually need more capacity than a mild-weather start.
other_common_rules: Older pint-per-square-foot shortcuts exist in the field. This kit does not use them as kit ratios.
Small closed rooms (bathrooms, closets): always give them their own dedicated unit.
dehumidifiers.notes: Cubic footage is generally more useful than square footage once you have ceiling height. This kit still does not invent pint ratios; the meter moves the count.

linear_foot_rules: Linear-foot shortcuts exist in the field and vary by company. Air mover sizing varies by type and rated CFM. Size by the unit type and rated CFM, the manufacturer guidance, and the readings. No invented counts.
square_footage_rules: Square-footage air-mover shortcuts exist in the field and vary by company. Size by the unit type and rated CFM, the manufacturer guidance, and the readings. No invented counts.
cfm_based_rules: This kit does not invent a CFM-per-square-foot ratio. Size by the unit type and rated CFM, the manufacturer guidance, and the readings.
Higher velocity for open surfaces, lower velocity for cavities and bound moisture.
other_common_rules: Create a 'wall of air' or circular airflow pattern
Add extra units for ceilings, hallways, and rooms with many corners
air_movers.notes: Field shortcuts vary by company. Use unit type, rated CFM, manufacturer guidance, and the readings.

combined_equipment_rules: Dehumidifiers are usually calculated early (for bids). Air movers are adjusted more after demo opens the structure.
Good containment can reduce total equipment needed by lowering air volume.
When in doubt on Day 1, slightly oversize dehumidifiers: easier to turn units off than to add them later.
known_limitations: Most rules of thumb assume average temperatures (70–80°F). Cold jobs need more capacity.
Modern construction (LVP, vapor barriers, thinset + liners) often requires more aggressive airflow than older rules account for.
Bound moisture in wood and thick materials dries slower than free moisture: rules based on surface water underestimate drying time.
Small rooms frequently overheat when standard calculations are followed blindly.
industry_rules_of_thumb.alignment_note: These are collected field shortcuts, not kit ratios. Size equipment by the unit type and rated CFM, the manufacturer guidance, and the readings. Equipment Setup: Sizing and Calculations: Class Sizing Factors and Air Mover Sizing follow that same rule and do not invent pint or CFM ratios. The meter moves the count.

sizing_and_calculations.description: How to figure equipment needs in real jobs. Dehumidifier sizing is usually done early for estimates and bids. Air movers get adjusted more once the structure opens up during demo. Size by the unit type and rated CFM, the manufacturer guidance, and the readings, with no invented ratios.

dehumidifier_sizing.core_approach: Work in cubic feet when possible. Size dehumidifiers by the unit type, the manufacturer guidance, and the readings. This kit does not invent pint-per-cubic-foot ratios. The meter moves the count.

class_guidance.class_1: Class 1 jobs are usually lighter on moisture load. Size by the unit type, the manufacturer guidance, and the readings.
class_guidance.class_2: Size by the unit type, the manufacturer guidance, and the readings. No fixed pint-per-cubic-foot ratio.
class_guidance.class_3: Higher initial moisture load. Size by the unit type, the manufacturer guidance, and the readings. No fixed pint-per-cubic-foot ratio.
class_guidance.class_4: Specialty dry. Size by the unit type, the manufacturer guidance, and the readings.

practical_adjustments: Temperature matters. Below 65°F, add capacity. Cold air holds less moisture, so the vapor pressure gradient is weaker.
Containment helps a lot. Good containment reduces the air volume and can let you run fewer machines effectively.
Small closed rooms (bathrooms, closets, laundry rooms) usually need their own dedicated dehumidifier regardless of size. They overheat and short-cycle easily.
Round up on Day 1. It’s easier to turn a unit off later than to play catch-up if you undersized.
dehumidifier_sizing.bidding_vs_on_site: For estimates and bids, calculate based on affected cubic footage and Class. Once demo starts and walls/floors open up, you usually already have enough dehumidification. The real changes happen with air movers.

air_mover_sizing.core_approach: Focus on moving air across wet surfaces instead of just circulating room air. After demo, you will almost always need more air movers than you planned on Day 1.
starting_points: Air mover sizing varies by type and rated CFM. Size by the unit type and rated CFM, the manufacturer guidance, and the readings. No invented counts or ratios.
Add or reposition as needed for wet ceilings, long hallways, and rooms with lots of corners.
For bound moisture in wood or thick materials, lower velocity directed airflow is often more effective than high-CFM blasting.
air_mover_sizing.field_reality: This is where most adjustments happen. Once selective demolition exposes framing and increases surface area, reposition and add air movers aggressively. Dead zones kill drying progress faster than almost anything else.

when_to_run_what.dehumidifiers: Start them as soon as extraction is done and it’s safe to do so. They help control humidity migration even while demo is still happening.
when_to_run_what.air_movers: Category 2/3 or contaminated: wait until contaminated porous material is out or framing is exposed, or use targeted cavity drying. Clean Category 1 with materials staying in place: air movers go on at setup, sized by the unit type and rated CFM, the manufacturer guidance, and the readings (Air Mover Sizing).

variance_factors: Containment reduces the effective air volume: use it to your advantage when sizing.
Modern flooring (LVP, sheet vinyl) often traps moisture underneath. This can require more aggressive airflow and sometimes localized tenting.
Bound moisture in wood or thick materials dries slower. Plan on longer drying times and more consistent airflow rather than just adding more machines.
Cold jobs need more capacity than the numbers suggest. Heat helps drive moisture out.
common_mistakes: Using the same equipment count from Day 1 after demo opens everything up.
Oversizing dehumidifiers in small rooms and creating overheating problems.
Under-equipping air movers after selective demolition: this is the most common shortfall on jobs that dry slow.
Ignoring temperature. Cold spaces dry slower even with the right number of machines.
Running air movers across contaminated (Category 2/3) finishes before demo: it spreads contamination. On clean Category 1 drying in place, air movers belong on the wet surfaces from setup.
sizing_and_calculations.voice_considerations: Figure your dehus for the bid based on the initial assessment. Once we start cutting, the real work is usually repositioning and adding air movers. Dead air is what kills these jobs. Keep the air moving across wet surfaces and adjust as the structure opens up.

class_sizing_factors.status: Informative. This kit does not invent fixed pint or CFM ratios. Size by the unit type and rated CFM, the manufacturer guidance, and the readings. The meter moves the count.

simple_method_cu_ft_per_pint.conventional_refrigerant: Size by the unit type, the manufacturer guidance, and the readings. No fixed cu-ft-per-pint ratio.
simple_method_cu_ft_per_pint.low_grain_refrigerant: Size by the unit type, the manufacturer guidance, and the readings. No fixed cu-ft-per-pint ratio.
simple_method_cu_ft_per_pint.desiccant_air_changes_per_hour: Size by the unit type, the manufacturer guidance, and the readings. No invented air-change ratios.

class_sizing_factors.worked_example: Start from the unit type, the rated capacity, and the manufacturer guidance, then let the readings move the count.
class_sizing_factors.detailed_lgr: Do not invent pint or air-change ratios. Size by the unit type, the manufacturer guidance, and the readings.
class_sizing_factors.air_movers: Air mover sizing varies by type and rated CFM. Size by the unit type and rated CFM, the manufacturer guidance, and the readings. No invented counts or ratios. Aim airflow along the wall across wet surfaces.

practical_guidance: GFCI cords and plugs are your friend. If your working space doesn't have them consider bringing your own plugs or cords with them.

Most techs extract first, then build full containment: on Category 1, 2, and most Category 3 losses. Full plastic before extraction is usually slower and messier, and negative air first is rarely achievable.
Reduce air volume early: containment is one of the highest-ROI moves you can make. It makes every dehu and air mover more effective.
Position air movers to scrub wet surfaces directly. High velocity across materials beats just moving air around the room.
On small bathrooms you can often place equipment in the tub or on a vanity to save floor space, but take advantage of a window for makeup air if running negative pressure.
Put a lipped mat or tray under every dehumidifier: cheap insurance against secondary damage claims.
Document exact equipment placement with photos and a simple diagram on Day 1.

When gear is placed, pulled, counted, or only repositioned, stage 06 Equipment through Visit Note Cadence. Adjusted-today is what, why, and how, so a later reading can be lined up with the move. A same-count move still gets the note.
equipment_setup.containment_first_exceptions: Containment and negative before extraction is the exception, not the default. Exceptions where containment goes first: sewage actively spreading into clean, occupied areas; a known mold disturbance; suspect or known asbestos/lead in the path; or occupants who cannot leave (infants, immunocompromised). Otherwise: extract to stop the spread, then isolate heavily contaminated areas under negative pressure (heavy contamination is isolated under negative).
equipment_setup.voice_considerations: Equipment in: dehus and air movers positioned to actually hit the wet surfaces. Extract first to stop the spread; on Category 2/3 contain and go negative after the water is under control, or first only when the job truly calls for it. Reduce the air volume early; it makes everything work better.
equipment_setup.noise_reduction: When setting up air movers, inform the customer that fans have been turned down to lower speed settings. This significantly reduces noise while remaining effective at circulating air. Lower velocity airflow can actually be more effective than high-speed blasting when drying bound moisture in wood. Lower speeds also reduce power consumption.
test_intake_lines: Air mover sizing varies by type and rated CFM. Size by the unit type and rated CFM, the manufacturer guidance, and the readings. No invented counts or ratios. The meter moves the count.
Size dehumidifiers by the unit type, the manufacturer guidance, and the readings. Equipment Setup: Sizing and Calculations: Class Sizing Factors does not invent pint ratios. The meter decides.
Do not invent pint or air-change ratios. Size by the unit type, the manufacturer guidance, and the readings.
No direct-fired heat without ventilation. Indirect-fired exhaust goes outside. Carbon monoxide is monitored.

A contaminated mechanical system stays off. Category 2 or 3 in fiberglass duct board or internal insulation is a qualified contractor, not a water-tech clean. Coil cleanliness is a pressure-drop test, not a look through the panel.
On a mold job the building system is not the dryer. An antimicrobial in the system is registered for system use, or it is not used.
The person applying a biocide is trained for that product. Training is part of the scope.
Inspection and the legal safety rule are required. The maker's instructions are expected. A tool out of inspection is not a billable production unit.
Lockout is a qualified authorized person.
A monitored fire or suppression system is shut down before work around it. 480-volt three-phase is not a residential circuit. A generator is in the plan when power is short or off limits.

taping_and_routing.description: Secure cords and condensate lines to prevent trip hazards, equipment damage, and pump failure.
rules: Tape down flat every cord and hose that crosses a walkway, every few feet.
Blue painter's tape only on finished floors: no duct or gaffer tape.
Keep condensate lines as straight as possible, no dips or loops; secure with blue tape when running up to a sink, shower, or tub.
Lipped mat or tray under dehumidifiers. Leave 12-18 in. clearance at intake and exhaust.
taping_and_routing.voice_note: Tape every cord and hose that crosses a walkway: blue tape only on finished floors. Keep drain lines straight, no loops.

dehumidifier_handling.title: Dehumidifier Handling
dehumidifier_handling.rule: Do not tip or lay a dehumidifier (LGR or suitcase) on its side to fit it into a tight crawl. Powered off and drained does not change this.
dehumidifier_handling.why: Compressors and the oil and refrigerant circuits are not built for sideways handling. Draining the unit does not make tipping safe.
dehumidifier_handling.if_tipped: If a unit was tipped, stand it upright before you power it on. Follow the manufacturer guidance for how long it should rest.

low_clearance_crawl.when: Low-clearance or outdoor-access crawls, including manufactured homes, where the unit will not go in upright.
low_clearance_crawl.do: Keep the dehumidifier upright outside, or in a conditioned pocket by the hatch, and duct dry air in.
low_clearance_crawl.do_not: Do not push crawl air up into the living space.
low_clearance_crawl.reference_note: Localized tent under the wet subfloor, relief through foundation vents, and the displacement principle are already in crawlspaces. Ducted output can freeze an LGR from back-pressure: see Dehumidifier Ducting & Back-Pressure.

dehumidifier_handling.voice_note: Don't tip a dehu on its side to get it in a crawl: off and drained doesn't make it safe. If it was tipped, stand it up and follow the manufacturer before you run it. Tight crawl: leave it upright outside and duct the dry air in.

dehumidifier_ducting.title: Dehumidifier Ducting & Back-Pressure

lgr_freeze_from_back_pressure.guidance: Revolution LGR (and likely others) can freeze at the intake when output is ducted into tenting/tanking with too much back pressure: the unit starves for airflow.
lgr_freeze_from_back_pressure.tell: Peel the rear filter and see ice.
lgr_freeze_from_back_pressure.misblame: Often blamed on cold crawl temperatures; the real driver is restricted output airflow.
lgr_freeze_from_back_pressure.voice_note: LGR freezing at the intake with output ducted into tenting? Peel the rear filter: if you see ice, it's back pressure starving airflow, not just a cold crawl.

dehumidifier_ducting.voice_note: If the Revolution freezes with the output ducted into a tent, check back pressure: peel the rear filter for ice. Restricted output airflow starves the unit.

equipment_field_basics.air_mover_types: Axial: high CFM, lower static pressure; open floors and surfaces. Centrifugal (snail): lower CFM, higher static pressure; cavities, under cabinets, wall-drying systems.
equipment_field_basics.dehumidifier_types: LGR: most common, reaches lower grains and handles cooler air better than conventional. Conventional refrigerant: weaker in cool air or at low humidity. Desiccant: very cool spaces or very low grains.
equipment_field_basics.dehumidifier_placement: Central to the affected area or pulling from the wettest/most contaminated zone; 12-18 inches clearance at intake and exhaust; exhaust pushes dry air toward wet areas or air-mover intakes; condensate line sloped to a safe drain. Very high temperatures cut LGR capacity. Do not tip or lay the unit on its side to fit a tight crawl (Equipment Setup: Dehumidifier Handling).
equipment_field_basics.air_mover_mistakes: Air blowing in circles without hitting wet surfaces; no airflow under LVP, carpet edges, or into cabinets; fans too far from the wall; short-circuiting (one mover's intake pulling another's exhaust); not repositioning as drying progresses.
equipment_field_basics.afd_basics: Air scrubbers recirculate filtered air; negative air machines exhaust out of the contained area. AFD is not a substitute for containment and source removal; never exhaust into clean areas; change filters on dirty jobs.
equipment_field_basics.material_meter_notes: Hardwood: watch cupping, crowning, gapping; low-velocity or directed airflow; shoe molding off for airflow. LVP/laminate act as vapor barriers: the plank can read dry while the subfloor is soaked; get under it or remove it. Concrete slab reads higher than wood and drywall and releases slowly; plan for it. Plaster dries slowly and cracks if dried too fast: low velocity, no rapid temperature swings.

power_survey.title: Pre-Setup Power Survey
power_survey.purpose: Decide before setup whether a power box is needed. The survey prevents two common mistakes: tripping breakers because the house circuits cannot carry the load, and defaulting to a power box on jobs that do not need one. A power box (also called a spider box) usually means cords through doors, and garage doors left open.
order_of_steps: 1. Project the equipment from the job conditions. Water class and the wet area give the dehumidifiers and air movers. Occupancy and mold add air scrubbers. Add a heater if one is needed.
2. Total the projected amps from each unit's nameplate, the label that lists its electrical rating. Use the nameplate, not a typical-draw guess.

3. Survey only the circuits near the work area, not the whole house. This is a short survey, usually 10 to 15 minutes. Photograph the panel and note breaker sizes and ground-fault breakers. Labels are often wrong, so treat them as a hint. Map outlets to breakers with a circuit tracer (a breaker finder), or by flipping breakers with the homeowner's OK. Note existing loads already on those circuits: a fridge, sump pump, furnace, space heaters, or a home office.

4. Write a simple circuit map: circuit, breaker size, outlets, existing load, amps free. A phone photo of the panel plus a quick sketch of the room is enough. The survey goes in the job file as the justification for using a power box, or for not using one.
5. Keep continuous load to about 12 amps on a 15 amp circuit and 16 amps on a 20 amp circuit. Kitchen, bathroom, and garage circuits are often 20 amp, so they are often good places to plug in.

6. A power box is used only when the projected load exceeds the free circuit capacity. The shortfall sets how many you need, usually one. Assign equipment to circuits from the map before anything goes on the truck.
power_survey.typical_draws: A typical large dehumidifier draws roughly 6 to 8 amps and an axial air mover roughly 1 to 3 amps, but always use the nameplate.
customer_side: Tell the homeowner up front about power use and reimbursement, and give them the usage record described in this section so they can claim reimbursement from their insurer. Do not promise coverage, and do not quote a power company's rate.
Plan cord routing and containment, or a door, so equipment can run without propping doors open.
power_survey.usage_record: Record the total nameplate amps of the equipment placed, then give the homeowner a simple usage record so they can claim electricity reimbursement from their insurer. The record lists each unit, its nameplate amps and voltage (usually 120 volts), and the dates it was placed and removed, or the days it ran. Estimate energy as amps times volts times hours, divided by 1000, in kilowatt-hours. If a unit ran around the clock, hours are the days run times 24. The homeowner or insurer applies their own power company's rate; we do not quote rates. For coverage and baseline bills, use Electricity Bill Increases. If the company bills a homeowner electricity reimbursement line, this record supports it. Do not promise coverage.
power_survey.voice_note: Power survey before setup, before the truck is loaded. Project the equipment from the job conditions, add up the nameplate amps, and map only the circuits near the work area. Use a power box only when the load is more than the free capacity. Tell the homeowner about power use, give them a usage record of nameplate amps, voltage, days run, and estimated kilowatt-hours, and route cords so doors are not left open. Do not quote rates.

extension_cord_safety.title: Extension Cord Safety
extension_cord_safety.description: Longer extension cords increase electrical resistance, which generates heat. This risk grows with higher-draw equipment like portable heaters and in confined spaces like crawlspaces where heat has nowhere to go.
key_rules: Match cord gauge to both length and load. Longer runs or higher amperage require heavier gauge wire.
Rule of thumb: Under 50 ft and under 15 amps → 14-gauge is usually fine. Over 50 ft or anything pulling heater-level amps → step up to 12-gauge. Over 100 ft or heavy continuous loads → 10-gauge.
Space heaters are high-draw devices. Plug them directly into a wall outlet whenever possible. If an extension cord is required, use a minimum 12-gauge cord and keep the run as short as practical.
Never use a coiled extension cord under load. Coils trap heat and significantly increase fire risk even on properly rated cords. Fully uncoil before use.
Inspect cords periodically during operation. If any section feels warm or hot, stop and correct the setup (wrong gauge, too long, coiled, or damaged cord).
GFCI protection is required but does not prevent overheating from undersized or coiled cords.
practical_guidance: In crawlspaces, prioritize short, heavy-gauge cords. If running power a long distance for a heater, consider staging the heater closer to a power source and ducting the heat instead.
Voltage drop on long or undersized cords reduces equipment performance (heaters won’t put out full heat).
Treat extension cords as temporary only. They are not a substitute for proper permanent power.
extension_cord_safety.voice_considerations: Keep it short and direct. Most techs already use GFCI: the gap is usually thinking about cord gauge vs. length/amps and the coiled cord hazard in tight spaces like crawlspaces.

temporary_power_distribution.name: Spider box (temporary power distribution)
temporary_power_distribution.what_it_is: A portable distribution box that takes one high-amp feed and splits it into several GFCI-protected 20-amp circuits, so the drying setup runs off its own power instead of the home's general circuits.
when_to_use: When the pre-setup power survey shows the projected load is more than the home's free circuits can carry. The shortfall sets how many boxes you need.
Household circuits are off, wet, or not trusted in the work zone.
rules: The feed comes from a matching high-amp receptacle (for example a range or dryer outlet), a generator, or a connection set up by a qualified electrician. Techs don't wire into the panel.
Match the plug, cord and amperage to the source. No adapters that defeat the rating, and no cheater plugs.
Keep the box off the floor and out of standing water, and route the feed cord where it won't be pinched by doors or containment.
Spread the load across the box's circuits and keep each one inside its rating. Cord rules still apply (Equipment Setup: Power: Extension Cord Safety).
Run the pre-setup power survey before equipment arrives. If the survey shows a power box is needed, plan the feed and the box before setup starts.
temporary_power_distribution.voice_note: Don't default to a power box, and don't just hope the house breakers will hold. Run the power survey first: project the equipment, add up the nameplate amps, map the nearby circuits, and use a power box only when the load is more than the free capacity. If you need one, feed it from a proper high-amp source or have an electrician set it up, keep it dry and off the floor, and spread the load.
temporary_power_distribution.default: Do not default to a power box. Run the pre-setup power survey first. Use a power box only when the survey shows the house circuits cannot carry the projected load, or when household circuits in the work zone are off, wet, or not trusted.

wood_floor_drying.title: Wood Floor Drying Mats
wood_floor_drying.setup: Lay the mats perpendicular to the length of the boards (the flooring direction). Connect them in a circuit so every panel draws from the main unit's suction. Tape the edges down to seal.
wood_floor_drying.when_to_use: An uncommon, situational, fairly advanced tool. Whether the floor can be saved is often a close call, and the mats often cannot dry it even then. A couple of days trying to pull the moisture out can become a sunk cost if the floor has to be demoed anyway, so weigh that before setting them up.

heaters.title: Heaters
heaters.space_heater: Small space heater: low power, for small areas, crawlspaces, and borderline temperatures. Billed QTY x DAYS.
heaters.commercial_heater: Commercial heater (electric thermal energy system, the big heater): large, high power draw, in many sizes and power ranges. Billed like an XL dehumidifier or higher; the rate is the company's. Billed QTY x DAYS. Plug it in and make sure it is right for the air volume and conditions; look up that unit's spec sheet in the field. The homeowner documents electricity use with their insurer for reimbursement.

hydroxyl_generators.title: Hydroxyl Generators
hydroxyl_generators.what_it_is: A hydroxyl generator uses UV lamps (the maker calls them optics) to make hydroxyl radicals from water vapor in the air. Makers sell larger units for odor work after fire and smoke, flood, sewage, mold, and similar losses; some need an air mover to run.
hydroxyl_generators.not_ozone: It is not an ozone generator. EPA says ozone generators sold as air cleaners should not be used in occupied spaces. Some devices sold as hydroxyl or active oxygen units do put out ozone; California's air board (CARB) keeps a list of known ozone generators, and CARB counts hydroxyl generators as electronic air cleaners that must test at or below 0.050 ppm ozone to be certified.
hydroxyl_generators.occupied_spaces: Makers differ. Some say their units can run in occupied areas, with a minimum room size and a set distance from anyone sleeping or staying put; others have a separate unoccupied mode and say it can exceed exposure limits and needs PPE and monitoring if workers are present. University of Colorado researchers (CIRES) do not recommend ozone or hydroxyl generators for fire odor and advise staying out while one runs, then airing out. Default: run it with the space unoccupied unless the label and manual for that exact unit say otherwise.
hydroxyl_generators.safety_label: Read the maker's safety label and manual before every setup, and follow them over anything here.
hydroxyl_generators.limits: Hydroxyl radicals react fast and are used up quickly in indoor air, so researchers doubt they reach odor held in walls and other surfaces. Clean the source; do not count on the unit in place of cleaning.
hydroxyl_generators.optics: The UV optics contain a small amount of mercury. Replace a cracked optic, and follow the maker's cleanup steps if one breaks.
hydroxyl_generators.sources: EPA: Ozone Generators that are Sold as Air Cleaners, and Residential Air Cleaners: A Technical Summary. CARB: air cleaner certification list and Potentially Hazardous Ozone Generators list. CIRES (University of Colorado): After the fire FAQ. Maker manuals: Pyure Odorox MySpace and Boss XL3; BoiE commercial hydroxyl generators.

equipment_decon.title: Equipment Decontamination
equipment_decon.rule: Billable as long as the equipment was delivered clean to the job on arrival.
equipment_decon.when: Decon the equipment after the job.
equipment_decon.hose: Count hose by length: add 1 per 50 ft, as the sheet line says.

van_organization.title: Van Organization
van_organization.description: How to set up and maintain your work vehicle for efficiency, safety, professionalism, and reduced physical strain. A well-organized van directly impacts job speed, callbacks, customer perception, and your own quality of life on the road.
van_organization.core_principle: Your van is a mobile workshop, not a rolling junk drawer or trash fire. Customers will occasionally see inside it. What they see should look like a professional operation, not chaos. In vans without a physical barrier, maintain a clean front to dirty rear flow with a clear transition zone. Good organization saves time, reduces mistakes, and makes you look like someone who takes the work seriously.

vehicle_type_recommendations.core_recommendation: Use a proper cargo van. Full-size cargo vans are the standard for restoration work because they support organized zoning, racking, and efficient access.
unsuitable_vehicle_types: Trucks with toppers or camper shells over the bed: Not recommended. Storage is usually inadequate, leading to constant unpacking and kneeling in the bed. Inefficient and unprofessional.

Vans with no divider between cab and cargo: Strongly discouraged for regular Category 2/3 or mold work. Without a physical barrier you constantly move contaminated air forward into your breathing space.
Open-grate dividers: Acceptable only if consistently plastic'd off on jobs with contamination risk (demo dust, chemicals, mold spores). Treat plastic'ing the grate as a required step on dirty jobs.

cab_separation_and_contamination_control.core_rule: Treat the driver and passenger area as a clean zone. Prevent airborne contamination from migrating forward whenever possible.

divider_guidance.solid_metal_divider: Best option. Maintains hard separation. Still plastic off gaps or vents on heavy demo or Category 3 work.
divider_guidance.open_metal_grate: Common. On any job with contamination risk, cover the grate with plastic from the cargo side and seal edges with tape. Quick and effective protection against micro-dosing the cab.
divider_guidance.no_divider: Poor long-term choice for restoration work. If you must use one temporarily, be extremely disciplined about what crosses into the front half of the cargo area.

practical_guidance: On Category 2/3 jobs or jobs with visible mold or heavy demo, plastic off open grates before starting work. Keep a small dedicated roll of plastic and tape for this purpose.

clean_dirty_flow.principle: In non-barrier vans, load and store dirty/contaminated items from the back forward. Keep clean items staged from the front backward. Maintain a clear transition zone in the middle rather than letting everything mix.
clean_dirty_flow.ppe_and_clean_items: Keep your main PPE bag on a top shelf or in the forward-most clean zone. Floor-level storage in a non-barrier van almost guarantees contamination over time.

functional_zones.description: Recommended layout for a standard cargo van without a solid barrier.
functional_zones.clean_front_zone: Driver/passenger area and forward cargo. Documentation, tablet, clean PPE bag, personal items, and clean consumables you want protected.
functional_zones.transition_zone: Middle of the cargo area. High-frequency items that can tolerate some exposure (certain tools, tape, general consumables). Keep this zone narrow and disciplined.
functional_zones.dirty_rear_zone: Back half to rear doors. Extraction equipment, wet/contaminated tools, used PPE, waste staging, and demo debris.
functional_zones.high_protected_storage: Top shelves or overhead racks. PPE bag, clean respirators, moisture meters, electronics, and anything you want kept off the floor and away from dirty gear.
functional_zones.immediate_access_zone: Rear or side door area. Phase 1 go-kit or tote. Clearly separated so you are not digging through contaminated items to reach it.

racking_and_shelving.core_principle: Good racking turns the van into a functional workshop. Choose systems that handle real weight, vibration, and daily use.

options.professional_modular_systems: Ranger Design steel shelving, Sortimo-style modular systems, or restoration-specific modular kits. These are durable and designed for contractor use.
options.custom_2x4_and_plywood: Excellent low-cost alternative when you know how to make good cuts. Often cheaper than commercial systems and can be superior because it is custom-fitted to your exact van and workflow. Particularly strong choice for economy vans.
general_rules: Heavy items live low and secured.
Leave clear walkways: do not block access.
Secure everything that can shift while driving.

theft_and_security.core_principle: Visible tools attract thieves. Make your van a harder target and limit what can be quickly grabbed.
key_practices: Install window grills/mesh and consider dark window tint.
Use lockable tool safes or bolted security boxes for high-value items (moisture meters, thermal cameras, power tools, electronics). Secure boxes to the van.
Add an alarm and visible steering wheel or pedal lock for deterrence.
On higher-risk jobs or overnight parking, bring high-value portable items into the cab when practical.
Use multiple GPS trackers (3–5 units) distributed across the van itself, tool bags, meter case, and carry bag for redundancy and better recovery chances.
