water_category.description: Practical field determination of water contamination category. Category drives containment, PPE, removal aggression, and overall risk management. This section organizes common causes of loss by category along with decision rules and nuances that techs actually encounter.

category_1.definition: Clean water from a sanitary source. Touching it, swallowing it, or breathing its mist is not a real health risk. Running through a clean building doesn't change that; running through a dirty one can change it right away.
common_col_examples: Toilet supply line failure (angle stop or supply line above floor)
Refrigerator ice maker supply line failure
Dishwasher supply line failure
Washing machine supply line failure (not the drain hose)
Kitchen or bathroom faucet supply line failure
Tub or shower supply line failure
Water heater supply line or expansion tank failure
Whole house humidifier supply line failure
Clean rainwater entering through a window or skylight with no debris pickup
Ice machine or beverage dispenser supply line failure
Toilet tank overflow from a clean, well-maintained tank with no additives or visible buildup
Melting ice or snow entering without picking up contamination
category_1.field_notes: True Category 1 toilet tank water requires the tank to be clean, relatively new or well-maintained, with no additives, no scum, no discoloration, and no odor. Most older tanks do not meet this standard.
category_1.time_effect: Time and temperature can move it up; odor is often the first sign. Field clock: treat it with Category 2 caution after 48+ hours warm, especially with organic materials (the 48-hour clock is a field rule of thumb).
category_1.default_actions: Standard drying protocols. Normal PPE. Containment usually not required unless the loss is very large.

category_2.definition: Water carrying enough contamination to make people uncomfortable or sick if they touch it or swallow it.
common_col_examples: Washing machine drain hose failure or disconnection
Dishwasher drain line leak or failure
Toilet bowl overflow on the room side of the trap with some urine and no feces
Toilet tank overflow from a tank with additives, moderate scum, discoloration, or buildup
Fire sprinkler activation (wet systems confirmed relatively new and well-maintained with no additives)
Sump pump failure or discharge line backup with minor organic content
Hydrostatic pressure seepage through foundation or slab (moves to Category 3 if it carries sewage, sludge, or strong odor)
Roof leak that has traveled through insulation, drywall, or accumulated dust
Clean supply line water that has sat more than 48 hours in warm conditions
Air conditioning condensate or chilled water drain backup
Water softener drain line failure
Steam cleaner or carpet cleaning equipment discharge
Refrigerator defrost drain or pan overflow
Bathroom sink or tub drain overflow with soap scum and hair
Punctured water bed or aquarium (no chemical additives)
category_2.field_notes: Fire sprinkler water is often Category 2 when the system is relatively new and well-maintained. Always attempt to verify system condition with the building engineer or property manager. Hydrostatic seepage and condensate water are also commonly Category 2.
category_2.time_effect: Clean water frequently migrates into Category 2 after 48 hours. Warm, stagnant conditions accelerate bacterial growth.
category_2.default_actions: Aggressive extraction. Remove carpet and pad. The customer may elect to keep and clean the carpet in certain instances by signing a release of procedure. Elevated caution on porous materials. Standard containment is usually sufficient.

category_3.definition: Badly contaminated water. It can carry disease germs, toxins, or other harmful agents and can make people seriously sick through contact or swallowing. It may also carry trace regulated materials such as pesticides.
common_col_examples: Water originating from under a toilet (failed wax ring, cracked flange, or drain line issue)
Sewage backup from main line or ejector pump failure
Any waste-line backflow from beyond a trap, regardless of visible content or color
Toilet overflow that includes bowl contents or solids
Toilet tank overflow from a heavily scummy, old, or severely contaminated tank
Fire sprinkler activation (most systems: due to age, stagnant water, corrosion, additives, or unknown condition)
Dry or pre-action fire sprinkler systems
Flood water carrying mud, silt, sewage, or debris
Rising water from rivers or streams, and any seawater flooding
Wind-driven rain or storm water that the inspection shows is badly contaminated (it picked up sewage, soil, silt, or debris on the way in). The way it got in does not make it Category 3 by itself
Any water with visible sludge, fecal matter, or strong sewage odor
Septic system backup or drain field failure
Long-dwell water (any source) that has developed strong musty or sewage odor
Water that has traveled through heavily contaminated crawlspace soil or debris
Burst drain line or main sewer line inside the structure
Water from a severely clogged or overflowing floor drain with organic buildup
category_3.field_notes: Fire sprinkler water should default to Category 3 unless you can confirm with the building engineer or property manager that the system is relatively new, well-maintained, and free of additives. Older systems, black iron pipe, and dry/pre-action systems are frequently Category 3. When in doubt, treat sprinkler water as Category 3. Fire-suppression water is not Category 1 by default; ethylene glycol or a non-potable connection moves it up. The Category 3 default is a deliberately cautious field rule.
category_3.time_effect: Already at highest contamination level. Extended dwell significantly increases hidden mold and bacterial growth risk behind finishes.
category_3.default_actions: Remediate before restorative drying. Controls and worker protection before entry; respirator per the safety program. Contaminated porous materials come out (removal is the control, not in-place cleaning). Containment with negative pressure where gross contamination is isolated. Document everything.

time_and_migration.description: Category can increase over time even if the water started clean.
rules: Category 1 water sitting more than 48 hours in warm conditions should be treated with Category 2 caution at minimum (short dwell ≤48h; long dwell >48h: same clock as Base Science: Water Category: Decision Rules: Long Dwell Rule and Category Decision).
Any water with visible organic material, sludge, or strong musty/sewage odor should be treated as Category 3.
Time + warmth + porous organic materials (drywall paper, carpet pad, insulation) is the fastest path to category migration.
time_and_migration.voice_note: Clean supply line water that sat for three days is no longer clean. Time moves the category up.

decision_rules.default_rule: When uncertain about category, default to the higher category. Over-calling is almost always safer than under-calling on residential and commercial jobs. Going higher while you gather information is protection; the written category still follows what the inspection finds.
decision_rules.toilet_rule: Any water that originated from under the toilet (wax ring, flange, or drain line) is Category 3 until proven otherwise. Toilet tank water should be evaluated based on tank condition, additives, smell, color, and buildup.
decision_rules.fire_sprinkler_rule: Fire sprinkler water should be treated as Category 3 unless confirmed otherwise by the building engineer or property manager. Older systems, unknown condition, or dry/pre-action systems default to Category 3.
decision_rules.weather_rule: Wind-driven rain and other storm water are not Category 3 by default. Set the category from the inspection (source, path, dwell time, temperature, and contamination found) and write down why. Badly contaminated storm water is Category 3 (Base Science: Water Category: Nuances: Weather Related Water).
decision_rules.long_dwell_rule: Any water present more than 48 hours in warm conditions should be handled with elevated category protocols, even if it started as clean supply line water. Field clock: short dwell ≤48 hours; long dwell >48 hours. Use the longer band when warmth, organics, or odor accelerate migration. This aligns with the principles of IICRC S500 and S520.
decision_rules.odor_rule: Strong musty or sewage odor overrides visual appearance. Treat as Category 3.
decision_rules.regulated_material_rule: A regulated or hazardous material (asbestos, lead, fuels, solvents, PCBs, pesticides, etc.) does not by itself change the category. It changes who does the work: qualified persons abate it before drying. See Safety and Health.
decision_rules.voice_note: When in doubt on category, I go higher. It's cheaper than a mold claim or getting sick on a job. If it came from under the toilet, I'm treating it as Category 3. Wax ring failures are black water until proven otherwise. Strong odor beats clean looks every time. If it smells like sewage, it's Category 3.
decision_rules.alignment_note: Category follows where the water came from and what it contacts; time and temperature can move it. The 48-hour clock, the default-higher rule, and the sprinkler default are field rules layered on top.

nuances.description: Common sources where Category assignment has nuance or is frequently debated among experienced techs. These are gray areas where judgment and context matter.

fire_sprinkler_water.debate: Some sources list typical wet-pipe sprinkler water as Category 2. Others note it often contains rust, biofilm, and additives from stagnant pipes. Dry and pre-action systems are more consistently treated as Category 3.
fire_sprinkler_water.conservative_practice: Most techs default to Category 3 unless they can confirm system condition with the building engineer or property manager.
fire_sprinkler_water.resto_kit_recommendation: Default to Category 3 unless verified otherwise. Ask for system details when possible.
fire_sprinkler_water.voice_note: Fire sprinkler water is usually Category 2 or 3 because of age and stagnant pipes. If you can't verify with the building engineer, assume Category 3.

toilet_tank_water.debate: Clean toilet tank water with no additives or buildup is technically Category 1. Debate centers on how much age, additives, scum, or discoloration pushes it into Category 2.
toilet_tank_water.conservative_practice: Many techs treat older tanks or tanks with visible buildup/additives as Category 2 rather than Category 1.
toilet_tank_water.resto_kit_recommendation: Clean, well-maintained tanks with no additives = Category 1. Tanks with additives, scum, or age = Category 2. Heavily contaminated tanks = Category 3.
toilet_tank_water.voice_note: Toilet tank water isn't automatically clean. Check the tank for additives, scum, discoloration, and odor. Old or nasty tanks can push it to Category 2 or 3.

long_dwell_clean_water.debate: Everyone agrees Category 1 water can migrate upward with time and warmth. The main debate is the exact timeline and how aggressively to reclassify it.
long_dwell_clean_water.conservative_practice: Most experienced techs begin treating it as Category 2 after approximately 48 hours in warm conditions, especially if it contacted organic materials.
long_dwell_clean_water.resto_kit_recommendation: After 48 hours in warm conditions (long dwell), treat with Category 2 caution. Strong odor or visible growth = Category 3. Short dwell is ≤48 hours; long dwell is >48 hours: one coherent field clock across science, Category Decision, and the material matrix.
long_dwell_clean_water.voice_note: Clean supply line water that sat past forty-eight hours in a warm house is no longer clean: that's long dwell. Short dwell is forty-eight hours or less; long dwell is over forty-eight. Time moves the category up.

fire_plus_water_soot.debate: Whether water running through soot and smoke should automatically be treated as Category 3 due to carcinogens and toxins, or if it requires specific evidence of pathogenic agents.
fire_plus_water_soot.conservative_practice: Many techs treat significant fire + water losses as Category 3, especially with heavy soot involvement.
fire_plus_water_soot.resto_kit_recommendation: Treat as Category 3 on any meaningful fire + water event unless proven otherwise.
fire_plus_water_soot.voice_note: On fire jobs with water, I'm usually treating it as Category 3 because of what the water picked up running through the soot.

hydrostatic_seepage_and_groundwater.debate: Often listed as Category 2, but some argue it can behave like Category 3 depending on what it picks up traveling through soil or under a slab.
hydrostatic_seepage_and_groundwater.conservative_practice: Most techs treat it as Category 2 unless there is visible contamination, sludge, or strong odor.
hydrostatic_seepage_and_groundwater.resto_kit_recommendation: Default to Category 2. Move to Category 3 if visible sludge, strong odor, or known sewage involvement exists.
hydrostatic_seepage_and_groundwater.voice_note: Groundwater seepage is usually Category 2 unless it smells or looks nasty. Then it becomes Category 3 fast.
hydrostatic_seepage_and_groundwater.alignment_note: Seepage from hydrostatic pressure is listed as a Category 2 example. Rising river water is Category 3.

weather_related_water.debate: Wind-driven rain, roof and window leaks, and other storm water are often called Category 3 on sight because of how the water got in. How it got in does not set the category. What the water carried and touched does.
weather_related_water.conservative_practice: Protect yourself and the occupants while you gather information, then write the category from what the inspection shows: the source, the path the water took, how long it sat, the temperature, and any sign of contamination such as sewage, soil, silt, debris, strong odor, or growth.
weather_related_water.resto_kit_recommendation: Weather-related water is not Category 3 by default. Clean rain that came in through a roof, window, or wall and touched only clean materials is often Category 1 or 2. It is Category 3 when the inspection finds it is badly contaminated, for example rising flood water, water that crossed soil or debris, or water with sewage odor. Write down what you found and why you called it. Do not under-call it either: contaminated storm water is Category 3. The long-dwell clock still applies.
weather_related_water.discoloration: Staining from rain that ran over wood, framing, or sheathing (tannin or rust marks) is not proof of contamination by itself, and it is not proof of rot. Weigh it with odor, debris, soil contact, dwell time, temperature, and the meter. A whole-house rain loss can show wide staining with sound wood underneath. Probe and meter before you call removal.
weather_related_water.removal_and_cuts: Removal and cut height follow the category you wrote and the wet readings, the same as any loss. There is no automatic flood cut for storm water. Cut above the highest wet reading (Demolition: Decision Logic: Material Decision Matrix: Drywall: Cut Height Note).
weather_related_water.voice_note: Storm water isn't Category 3 just because it came in sideways. What did it carry and what did it touch? Clean rain on clean materials is usually Category 1 or 2. Mud, debris, sewage smell, or growth, and it's Category 3. Staining alone isn't contamination and it isn't rot: meter it and probe it. Write down why.
weather_related_water.alignment_note: Category follows the inspection: the source, the path, time, temperature, and contamination found. This aligns with the principles of IICRC S500 and S520.

water_class.description: Class is the expected evaporation load when drying starts: how much wet, porous surface is left in the drying environment and how deep the water went. It is not the contamination level (that is Category).
water_class.class_1: Smallest water load. Wet porous materials (carpet, drywall, batt or blown insulation, CMU, textiles) cover under about 5% of the room's total floor + wall + ceiling area. Dense, slow-drying materials have soaked up little.
water_class.class_2: Bigger water load. Wet porous materials cover roughly 5-40% of the total floor + wall + ceiling area. Dense, slow-drying materials have soaked up little.
water_class.class_3: Biggest water load. Wet porous materials cover more than about 40% of the total floor + wall + ceiling area. Dense, slow-drying materials have soaked up little.
water_class.class_4: Water held deep in dense, slow-drying materials (plaster, wood, concrete, masonry) or layered assemblies (double drywall, multilayer subfloor, gym floor). Takes special methods, more time, or a bigger vapor-pressure push. Class 4 means deep, not big.
water_class.per_chamber: Each drying environment has its own class (and category). A crawl, basement, chase, or attic is its own call.
water_class.why_it_matters: Class is recorded on the file. Size equipment by the unit type and rated CFM, the manufacturer guidance, and the readings (see Equipment Setup: Sizing and Calculations: Class Sizing Factors). The kit leans on materials and readings more than on the class number.
water_class.voice_note: Class is the drying load, not the contamination. Under five percent wet porous surface is Class 1, five to forty is Class 2, over forty is Class 3, and bound water in wood, plaster, concrete, or masonry is Class 4.
water_class.class_4_drying_approach: Class 4 is bound moisture in dense materials. Lower-velocity directed airflow, moderate controlled heat where safe, extended timelines, and sometimes desiccants. Open or remove low-evaporation layers first. Monitor surface and deeper readings. Blasting high CFM usually does not help much: low and slow with good heat and dehumidification.

psychrometry.description: The study of moist air and how temperature and moisture interact during drying.

core_concepts.gpp_vs_rh: Grains Per Pound (GPP) measures actual moisture in the air. Relative Humidity (RH) is misleading because it changes with temperature. Always prioritize GPP and temperature readings over RH alone when establishing baseline conditions.
core_concepts.dry_standard: The target moisture level is established from unaffected materials of the same type in the same building under current conditions (or, when none exist, from similar structures in the region), not from a universal chart.
core_concepts.vapor_pressure: The driving force for moisture movement. Moisture moves from high vapor pressure (wet materials) to low vapor pressure (drier air).
core_concepts.temperature_effect: Warmer air holds more moisture. Raising temperature increases evaporation potential, but only if dehumidification or ventilation removes the moisture from the air.
core_concepts.hold_gpp_first: During insurance or other holds with minimal equipment, use GPP delta between inlet/loss air and house air to confirm vapor management. Late-stage house air is not day-one wet air. Do not chase tighter depression or add aggressive drying while on hold.

field_implications.summary: On Phase 1, take baseline readings in both affected and unaffected areas. Record temperature, RH, and GPP. This gives the real reference point for the job. Capture room RH (Ambient Humidity Assessment) before equipment is placed so the impact shows; once equipment is running, prioritize GPP and temperature over RH alone. On Phase 0 hold with minimal gear: watch delta GPP for vapor management; a modest delta can be enough on late-stage house air. Do not chase tighter depression or expand drying while the hold is active.

psychrometry.voice_note: GPP first, not RH. Baseline temp, RH, and GPP in affected and clean reference spots. On hold, a small GPP delta can manage vapor: don't chase tighter depression until the hold lifts.
reference_lines: Humidity ratio (grains per pound of dry air), relative humidity, and specific humidity are three different numbers. Class is the evaporation load, not the contamination.
Drying has three parts: manage the air, move moisture through the material, and evaporate it off the surface. Missing one stalls the dry. Do not add air movers without a place for the vapor to go.

Constant-rate stage (surface still wet): about 600 feet per minute at the wet surface. Falling-rate stage: about 150 feet per minute plus a larger vapor-pressure difference, especially on plaster, wood, concrete, and masonry. Over-drying a dense surface while the core is wet slows migration.
Open the building to outside air only when the outdoor humidity ratio is significantly lower; otherwise run closed. The building's HVAC is not the drying system.
Moisture moves four ways: liquid flow, air transport, vapor diffusion, and capillary action. Name the path before setting the dry.

moisture_physics.description: How water moves through and is held by building materials. This determines how easily moisture can be removed and how far it travels.

core_concepts.wicking: Water travels horizontally and vertically through porous materials, often far beyond the visible wet area, especially along baseplates and under vapor barriers.
core_concepts.hidden_moisture: Surface readings can be misleading. Water commonly hides under LVP, sheet vinyl, behind baseboards, and in wall cavities.
core_concepts.free_vs_bound: Free water (in pores or on surfaces) can be extracted or evaporated relatively easily. Bound moisture (held within wood cells or thick materials) requires more time, airflow, and energy to release.
core_concepts.porosity_and_permeability: High-porosity materials (drywall paper, carpet pad, fiberglass insulation) absorb and hold water differently than low-permeability materials (vinyl flooring, concrete, closed-cell foam).
core_concepts.capillary_action: Water is pulled through tiny pores and gaps by surface tension. This allows it to move against gravity and travel long distances through materials like concrete, wood, and drywall paper.

field_implications.drying_difficulty: Materials with high porosity and permeability are generally easier to extract from but harder to fully dry once saturated.
field_implications.removal_decisions: Some materials (particle board, heavily saturated fiberglass) are often more practical to remove than to attempt drying. Wet cellulose comes out on any category.
field_implications.hidden_moisture_risk: Water can travel long distances through wicking. Always check beyond the visibly wet area, especially under flooring and behind baseboards.

water_movement_pathways.description: How water physically moves through buildings once it enters. Understanding these pathways is critical for accurate assessment, proper scope, and avoiding missed hidden damage. Water rarely stays where it first appears.

core_mechanisms.description: Water moves through buildings in four primary ways. Most jobs involve more than one mechanism at the same time.

bulk_water.description: Liquid water moving under gravity or hydrostatic pressure. This is usually the highest volume when active leaking is occurring.
bulk_water.field_note: This is what you see pooling or running. Once it hits a floor or slab, it starts looking for the path of least resistance horizontally and downward.

capillary_wicking.description: Water drawn through tiny pores and gaps in materials by surface tension. Can move horizontally and vertically, often against gravity.
capillary_wicking.field_note: This is why water shows up in baseplates, drywall paper, and insulation far from the original source. Concrete, wood, and drywall paper are all excellent wicking materials.

air_transported.description: Water vapor carried by moving air. Air movement can transport far more moisture than vapor diffusion alone.
air_transported.field_note: This is often underestimated on jobs. Air leaking through walls, ceilings, or HVAC can move moisture into hidden cavities even when there's no liquid water present.

vapor_diffusion.description: Water vapor moving through materials from areas of higher vapor pressure to lower vapor pressure.
vapor_diffusion.field_note: Slower than the other mechanisms but constant. Vapor barriers stop this movement, which is why they can also trap liquid water that gets underneath them.

layering_and_drainage.description: Modern construction uses layers to manage water. When those layers are compromised or missing, water enters and travels inside the assembly instead of draining out.

drainage_planes.description: Water resistive barriers (WRBs) installed behind cladding. Designed to catch water that gets past the siding and drain it downward and outward through flashings and weeps.
drainage_planes.field_reality: Many older homes have no drainage plane or a failed one. Once water gets behind the cladding, it has nowhere to go but into the wall cavity.

vapor_barriers_as_traps.description: Materials like LVP, sheet vinyl, and some thinset + liner systems that stop vapor movement. They protect from below but trap any liquid water that gets underneath.
vapor_barriers_as_traps.field_note: These turn floors into hidden distribution systems. Water can travel long distances under them before you see any sign on the surface.

capillary_breaks.description: Materials or gaps (membranes, coatings, stone layers, air gaps) installed to stop wicking from foundations into wood framing.
capillary_breaks.field_reality: Often missing or incomplete in older homes. This is why you frequently see moisture wicking up into sill plates and bottom plates even with no obvious leak above.

horizontal_pathways.description: Water loves to travel sideways once it hits a relatively flat surface or gap.

baseplate_highway.description: The joint between the bottom plate and the slab or subfloor is one of the most common horizontal pathways in wood frame construction.
baseplate_highway.field_observation: Water frequently slides right under the baseplate and into the next room, or travels along the baseplate for significant distances. Always check both sides of any affected wall and the rooms beyond.
baseplate_highway.voice_note: If you have wet walls on one side of a room, check the other side and the room next door. It probably went under the plate.

slab_distribution.description: On concrete slabs, water can spread laterally under flooring or through micro-gaps at the floor-wall interface.
slab_distribution.field_observation: Think of it like a thin gap (roughly 1/16 inch) around the perimeter where water just spreads out. It doesn't need much slope to move.
slab_distribution.voice_note: On slabs, assume water has spread farther than it looks. That thin gap at the wall is basically a highway.

under_vapor_barrier_flooring.description: LVP, engineered hardwood, and tile over underlayment or thinset + liner systems allow water to travel horizontally underneath while the surface stays relatively dry.
under_vapor_barrier_flooring.field_note: This is why meters can read mostly dry on top while significant moisture exists below. You have to lift edges or remove sections to verify.

vertical_pathways.description: Water moves up by wicking and down by gravity whenever it finds an opening.

wicking_up_from_foundation.description: Capillary action pulls water upward from foundations, slabs, or crawlspace soil into sill plates, bottom plates, and wall cavities.
wicking_up_from_foundation.field_note: This is very common in older homes without proper capillary breaks. Moisture can appear several feet up the wall with no visible leak above.

dropping_into_lower_levels.description: When water reaches a gap, penetration, or joint in a floor system, gravity pulls it downward into the space below.
dropping_into_lower_levels.field_observation: On a wood subfloor over a crawlspace, water often finds gaps and drops straight down. If it comes through in a single concentrated point, it can sometimes miss soaking large areas of insulation and instead run down joists or into one localized area.
dropping_into_lower_levels.voice_note: When water drops into a crawlspace from above, don't assume the insulation is fully soaked just because there's water down there. Check where it actually landed.

wall_cavities.description: Once water enters a wall (from above, the side, or wicking up), it travels down the cavity and can exit at baseplates, electrical boxes, or other penetrations.
wall_cavities.field_note: This is why you often find wet insulation and baseplates even when the leak was higher up or in an adjacent room.

high_probability_collection_points.description: These are the locations where water most commonly ends up and causes hidden damage.
items: Along and under baseplates / bottom plates
Under vapor-barrier flooring (LVP, sheet vinyl, tile)
Lower sections of wall cavities (especially exterior walls)
Sill plates and rim joists in crawlspaces
Interstitial spaces behind cabinets, vanities, and built-ins

field_implications.description: This knowledge directly affects how you assess and scope jobs.

always_check_adjacent_spaces.rule: Always check the rooms on both sides of any affected wall, plus the space below if applicable.
always_check_adjacent_spaces.why: Water travels under baseplates and along slabs much farther than most people expect.

initial_scope_is_almost_always_low.rule: Visible damage is rarely the full extent. Plan on the scope growing as you chase water into hidden pathways.
initial_scope_is_almost_always_low.voice_note: Initial visual scope is almost always low. The water has usually been busy while you weren't looking.

concentrated_vs_widespread_entry.note: Water entering through a single point (especially dropping into a crawlspace) can create very different damage patterns than widespread saturation. Don't assume uniform wetting.

meter_limitations.note: Surface readings can be misleading when water has traveled under vapor barriers or along baseplates. Physical investigation is often required.

water_movement_pathways.voice_note: Water doesn't stay where it starts. It finds the easiest path, usually under the baseplate or along the slab.

evaporation_principles.description: How water turns into vapor and moves from materials into the air. This is the core mechanism of drying.

core_concepts.vapor_pressure_gradient: Moisture moves from areas of higher vapor pressure (wet materials) to lower vapor pressure (drier air). This is the primary driving force behind all drying.
core_concepts.boundary_layer: A thin layer of humid air forms directly on wet surfaces and slows evaporation. Air movement breaks this layer and allows drying to occur.
core_concepts.air_movement_role: Air movers disrupt the boundary layer and deliver drier air to wet surfaces. Dehumidifiers remove moisture from the air to maintain the gradient. Both are required for effective drying.

field_implications.summary: Position air movers to create directed airflow across wet surfaces rather than just circulating air in the room. Dehumidifiers must remove the moisture from the air so the gradient can be maintained.

dry_standards.description: The target moisture levels for affected materials. The dry standard is a fair estimate of what the material read before the loss: taken from the same kind of unaffected material in the same building, or from similar buildings in the area.
dry_standards.core_principle: A dry standard comes from similar unaffected materials, or from similar structures and the region. The goal is a moisture reading that meets or is below that standard, written against a named material. Within 10 percent is a common company shortcut used with a fixed 12–14% standard, not a rule.
dry_standards.wood: Field check only, not the goal statement: wood within 2 to 4 moisture-content points of unaffected wood of the same type in the same building. The goal statement is the page rule.
dry_standards.non_wood_materials: Relative to the dry standard of unaffected material of the same type in the same room or building under current conditions (or similar structures in the region when there is no unaffected material). Always establish and document baseline readings on Day 1.
dry_standards.insulation_rule: Wet cellulose comes out on any category. Wet fiberglass is almost always removed rather than dried in place, especially on Category 2/3 or long-dwell jobs (unfaced fiberglass wet only at the bottom can stay). Spray and closed-cell foam removal is mainly inspection: probe for wicking height and remove a margin above it (Demolition: Decision Logic: Material Decision Matrix: Closed Cell Spray Foam: Inspection Rule).
dry_standards.voice_note: The goal is a moisture reading that meets or is below the dry standard, on a named material. Unaffected material, or a similar structure in the region, sets that standard. Within 10 percent is a common company shortcut used with a fixed 12–14% standard, not a rule. Two to four points on wood is a field check, not the goal.
dry_standards.wood_field_check: Field check, not the goal: wood within 2–4 moisture-content points of unaffected wood of the same type in the same building under current conditions (document the unaffected baseline) is a quick check. The goal is the one in Base Science: Dry Standards: Wood: a moisture reading that meets or is below the dry standard, written against a named material. The standard working range is 12–14% MC. Sixteen percent and up is the red zone and the cutoff for dry-rot and mold risk. The dry standard comes from unaffected wood in the same structure. Do not call wood 'dry' from a universal number alone.

terms.dry_standard: A fair estimate of the material's moisture before the loss: read from unaffected material, or from similar buildings in the area.
terms.drying_goal: The target the restorer sets and writes for the end of drying: a moisture reading that meets or is below the dry standard, on a named material.
terms.moisture_content_vs_level: Moisture content is a percent of oven-dry weight and is only used when the meter is calibrated for that material and temperature. Otherwise it is a moisture level (relative). A moisture sensor gives no number.

contamination_science.description: How water becomes more contaminated over time and how this affects risk, drying decisions, and removal strategies.

core_concepts.time_as_risk: Time is one of the strongest multipliers of contamination risk. Bacterial growth accelerates significantly after 48 hours in warm, moist conditions.
core_concepts.category_migration: A water loss can effectively move up in category over time. Always verify and adjust the preliminary category on site.
core_concepts.mold_growth_conditions: Mold needs sustained moisture, warmth (roughly 68–86°F), time (significant risk often after 48 hours), and organic material (paper, dust, wood) to grow.

field_implications.summary: On Phase 1, if water has been present more than 48 hours or shows signs of contamination (odor, discoloration, organic debris), treat it as higher risk and upgrade PPE and engineering controls accordingly.

mold_science.description: The biological requirements, growth dynamics, timeline risks, and hidden behavior of mold in water-damaged buildings. This section explains the underlying science of why mold becomes a problem after water intrusion, how it spreads in assemblies, and why certain materials and conditions create higher risk. It provides the foundation for understanding removal decisions, containment needs, and the importance of time as a risk factor.

what_is_mold.description: Mold is a type of fungus that grows in multicellular filaments called hyphae. It reproduces by producing spores that become airborne and can travel throughout a building. Unlike bacteria, mold can grow on surfaces and penetrate porous materials. Common genera in water-damaged buildings include Aspergillus, Penicillium, Cladosporium, and Stachybotrys (often called 'black mold').

growth_requirements.description: Mold requires four primary conditions to grow and amplify: (1) Moisture: liquid water or high relative humidity creating water activity (aW) high enough for the organism; dry-tolerant molds at about 0.66-0.70, most bacteria above about 0.95; (2) Organic food source: cellulose (drywall paper, wood, dust, carpet pad, insulation); (3) Suitable temperature: most indoor molds grow best between 68–86°F (20–30°C), though some can grow at lower or higher temperatures; (4) Time: spores need time to germinate and form colonies. Oxygen is also generally required, though some species tolerate low-oxygen environments.

water_activity.description: Water activity is the free water available for growth at the material surface, about the same as the equilibrium relative humidity there (a surface reading of 80 percent RH is aW 0.80). Most bacteria need aW above about 0.95. Many early molds need less, and dry-tolerant molds can grow at about 0.66 to 0.70. That is why a material can read 'dry' on a meter and still carry hidden growth.

growth_timeline.description: Under warm, wet conditions with organic material present, mold spores can begin germinating within 24–48 hours. Visible growth often appears between 48–72 hours. Significant colony formation and spore production typically accelerate after 72 hours and become well-established after 5–7+ days. These timelines are highly dependent on temperature, moisture availability, and substrate. Cooler or drier conditions can significantly slow or pause growth. The risk of problematic hidden amplification rises substantially after 48–72 hours in typical indoor environments.

hidden_mold_mechanisms.description: Mold commonly grows out of sight in wall cavities, behind baseboards, under flooring (especially LVP and sheet vinyl), inside cabinets, in interstitial spaces, and on the back side of drywall. Water wicks through materials via capillary action, carrying spores and nutrients into hidden areas. Vapor drive can move moisture into cavities even without liquid water intrusion. Once established behind finishes, mold can continue growing as long as moisture remains available, often undetected until demolition or odor complaints occur.

spore_production_and_dispersal.description: Mature mold colonies produce large numbers of spores. Disturbance (cutting drywall, pulling insulation, running high-velocity air movers, or even foot traffic) can aerosolize spores and fragments into the air. Without proper containment and negative pressure, these can spread throughout the building and HVAC system. Some species also produce mycotoxins and microbial volatile organic compounds (MVOCs) that contribute to odors and potential health effects.

category_and_dwell_time_interaction.term: Interaction with Water Category and Dwell Time
category_and_dwell_time_interaction.description: Category 1 water starts clean but can support mold growth once it contacts organic materials and sits long enough. Category 2 and 3 water carry higher initial microbial loads and accelerate risk. Dwell time is often a stronger predictor of hidden mold problems than the original water category. Warm temperatures significantly speed up microbial amplification in all categories.

key_relationships.time_and_risk: Time is one of the strongest multipliers of mold risk. The longer water remains in contact with organic building materials under warm conditions, the higher the probability of significant hidden mold growth, even if visible mold is not yet apparent on surfaces.
key_relationships.moisture_vs_visible_growth: Absence of visible mold on exposed surfaces does not equal absence of mold risk. Significant growth frequently occurs behind finishes, under flooring, and in cavities where it cannot be seen without opening assemblies.
key_relationships.temperature_acceleration: Higher temperatures accelerate both mold growth and the rate at which water can move through materials via vapor drive. Hot water line leaks in crawlspaces are particularly problematic because they combine sustained moisture with elevated temperature in a confined space.
key_relationships.material_type_matters: Porous, cellulose-based materials (drywall paper, OSB, particle board, fiberglass and cellulose insulation, carpet pad) are excellent substrates for mold. Dense or non-organic materials (dimensional lumber, concrete, closed-cell foam) support growth more slowly but can still harbor mold on surface dust or in checks and end grain.

field_implications.removal_decisions: On long-dwell losses (more than 48 hours in warm conditions, especially with Category 2/3 water), the probability of hidden mold behind finishes increases significantly. Visible growth often appearing between 48–72 hours is a hidden-growth caution, not a second definition of long dwell. This supports more aggressive selective removal of porous materials rather than attempting to dry them in place. This aligns with the principles of IICRC S500 and S520.
field_implications.containment_and_disturbance: Any job with suspected or confirmed mold growth requires proper engineering controls before aggressive demolition or disturbance. Running air movers directly on moldy materials without containment can spread spores and fragments throughout the structure and HVAC system.
field_implications.crawlspace_and_interstitial_risk: Crawlspaces, wall cavities, and areas behind cabinets or vanities are high-risk locations for hidden mold after water intrusion. Warm, moist air can migrate upward through gaps, plumbing penetrations, and HVAC returns, potentially affecting living spaces above.
field_implications.odors_as_indicators: Musty or earthy odors are often reliable indicators of hidden mold growth even when no visible mold is present on exposed surfaces. Odors should trigger investigation of concealed areas.
field_implications.drying_limits: Drying can stop active mold growth by removing moisture, but it does not kill existing mold colonies or remove spores and mycotoxins already present in materials. Materials that have developed significant mold growth are generally removed rather than dried.

common_misunderstandings.no_visible_mold_means_no_problem: A common and dangerous assumption is that if there is no visible black or green growth on exposed surfaces, mold is not an issue. In reality, significant hidden mold frequently exists behind drywall, under flooring, and in cavities with no visible signs until assemblies are opened.
common_misunderstandings.category_1_water_cannot_grow_mold: Category 1 water is initially clean, but once it sits and contacts organic materials (drywall paper, wood dust, insulation), it can readily support mold growth. Time and warmth turn many Category 1 losses into mold problems.
common_misunderstandings.drying_kills_mold: Drying removes the moisture mold needs to grow, but it does not kill existing mold or remove spores. Materials that have already developed colonies generally require removal because the mold structures and spores remain even after the material reaches dry standard. Drying stops the bloom; it does not clear the spore reservoir: mold goes dormant, not dead.
common_misunderstandings.only_black_mold_is_dangerous: While Stachybotrys (often called black mold) receives the most attention, many common species of Aspergillus, Penicillium, and others can produce mycotoxins and cause health effects. The quantity, species, and individual sensitivity matter more than color alone.
common_misunderstandings.surface_readings_detect_hidden_mold: Moisture meters and thermal cameras have limitations when mold is growing behind vapor barriers, under flooring, or deep in wall cavities. Physical investigation and odor assessment are often required to detect hidden issues.
common_misunderstandings.kill_equals_remove: Spraying a biocide or oxidizer on an exposed colony may kill live growth, but killing is not removal. Dead spores and fragments remain a reservoir and can still be allergenic. Physical removal is the primary means; a kill, coat, or fog without removal is a written deviation. If removal must wait, contain locally and keep it from spreading, then remove.

condition_vocabulary.condition_1: Normal fungal ecology for that kind of space.
condition_vocabulary.condition_2: Residue from a known Condition 3 source in the same building: spores, fragments, mycotoxins, MVOCs. Cannot be confirmed by eye; an assumed Condition 2 is written with the rationale.
condition_vocabulary.condition_3: Actual growth, active or dormant, visible or hidden. Visible growth is Condition 3.
condition_vocabulary.causal_path: Plain-words path: a Condition 3 source sheds Condition 2 residue around it; removal and detailed cleaning bring the area back to Condition 1. Drying alone stops growth but does not return anything to Condition 1.

test_intake_lines: Start mitigation as soon as it is safe. Most bacteria want water activity above 0.95. Some molds grow at 0.66 to 0.70. Musty odor is a growth sign. Do not treat sewage as a dry-out.

material_behavior.description: How different building materials interact with water: how they absorb it, transport it, hold it (free vs bound), release it during drying, and how they respond to contamination and time. This section explains the physical reasons why some materials can be dried while others should be removed, and why modern assemblies often behave differently than older ones.

free_vs_bound_moisture.description: Free moisture exists in pores, on surfaces, or between fibers and can usually be extracted or evaporated relatively easily. Bound moisture is held within the cellular structure of materials (especially wood) or tightly adsorbed to surfaces. Bound moisture requires more energy, time, and favorable vapor pressure gradients to release. This distinction is critical for setting realistic drying expectations and understanding why some materials dry slowly even with good airflow.

porosity_and_permeability.description: Porosity refers to the volume of empty space within a material. Permeability refers to how easily water (liquid or vapor) can move through those spaces. High-porosity, high-permeability materials (drywall paper, carpet pad, fiberglass insulation) absorb water quickly and can also release it relatively fast if airflow reaches them. Low-permeability materials (vinyl, closed-cell foam, some coatings) resist both absorption and drying.

wicking_and_capillary_action.description: Water is pulled through tiny pores and gaps by surface tension, often moving horizontally or upward against gravity. This allows water to travel far beyond the visible wet area: along baseplates, under vapor barriers, behind cabinets, and into wall cavities. Materials like drywall paper, wood, concrete, and some insulation are excellent wicking media.

drywall.description: Drywall consists of a gypsum core sandwiched between paper facings. The paper wicks water extremely well and serves as a primary food source for mold. Once the paper is wet, mold risk rises quickly. The gypsum core softens and loses structural integrity when saturated. Heavily wetted or mold-affected drywall is almost always removed rather than dried because the paper facing is difficult to salvage and hidden mold growth behind it is common.

dimensional_lumber.description: Solid wood framing can absorb significant amounts of water but is relatively resilient compared to engineered wood products. Water penetrates end grain and checks much faster than face grain. Dimensional lumber can often be dried successfully if addressed before significant swelling, checking, or mold colonization occurs. Hidden moisture in checks and end grain is commonly missed during assessment.

engineered_wood.term: Engineered Wood Products (Particle Board, MDF, OSB)
engineered_wood.description: Particle board, MDF, and OSB use wood particles or strands bonded with resins. They absorb water rapidly through exposed edges and swell or disintegrate when wet. Once significantly swollen or delaminated, they rarely return to structural integrity. These materials are almost always removed when substantially wetted, especially on Category 2/3 or long-dwell losses. Cabinet bottom panels are the part that holds the box. Category 1 with light exposure can look salvageable; meaningful dwell is what swells them and takes the strength. Those bottoms are cheap: prefer replace, same class of call as drywall or insulation. Solid-wood cabinet boxes can often dry in place on Category 1.

insulation_types.description: Fiberglass and cellulose insulation are highly absorbent and hold water like a sponge, losing R-value when wet. Wet cellulose comes out on any category. Fiberglass is usually removed, especially when contaminated or on long-dwell jobs; unfaced fiberglass wet only at the bottom can stay. Closed-cell spray foam is much more resistant to water absorption and can often be dried if not heavily saturated, but it slows the dry behind it. Open-cell foam behaves more like fiberglass and is typically removed when wet.

concrete_and_slabs.description: Concrete is porous but absorbs water slowly and releases it even more slowly. It can act as a moisture reservoir under flooring for extended periods. Moisture can also wick upward from below the slab through hydrostatic pressure or capillary rise. Good airflow, dehumidification, and sometimes controlled heat are required to dry concrete effectively. Surface moisture readings often understate the moisture content deeper in the slab.

modern_flooring_systems.term: Modern Flooring Systems (LVP, Sheet Vinyl, Tile)
modern_flooring_systems.description: Luxury Vinyl Plank (LVP), sheet vinyl, and many tile installations create effective vapor barriers. Water easily migrates underneath these systems (especially along baseplates or through perimeter gaps) and becomes trapped. Drying from above is often ineffective or extremely slow. Thinset + liner/uncoupling membrane systems can allow water to travel between layers, creating hidden moisture in the underlayment or subfloor. These assemblies frequently require lifting edges or selective removal to achieve proper drying.

carpet_and_pad.description: On Category 1, carpet itself can sometimes be cleaned and dried if extracted quickly. Category 2 defaults to removing carpet and pad; the customer may elect to keep and clean the carpet in certain instances by signing a release of procedure. Carpet pad is highly absorbent, wicks water laterally, and supports rapid mold growth. Saturated pad is almost always removed. Delamination and persistent odor issues are common when pad remains wet for more than 24–48 hours.

key_relationships.material_type_drives_decisions: The same amount of water can justify completely different responses depending on the material. Particle board or saturated fiberglass often requires removal where dimensional lumber in the same environment might be dried successfully.
key_relationships.time_changes_behavior: Materials that might be salvageable with rapid response frequently become unsalvageable after extended dwell time due to swelling, checking, deep penetration, or microbial growth. Time is a major variable in material fate.
key_relationships.vapor_barriers_create_traps: Modern flooring and some wall/floor assemblies that include vapor barriers protect from one direction but can trap liquid water that gets underneath them. This is one of the most common reasons hidden moisture persists in contemporary construction.
key_relationships.porosity_vs_drying_difficulty: Highly porous materials absorb water quickly and can also release it relatively quickly if airflow reaches the water. Low-permeability or layered assemblies often create situations where water is present but very difficult to remove without physical intervention.

field_implications.removal_vs_drying: Material behavior is one of the primary drivers of remove-versus-dry decisions. Porous, organic, or dimensionally unstable materials with significant dwell time or contamination are usually lower-risk to remove than to attempt drying in place.
field_implications.hidden_moisture_assessment: Surface moisture readings are often unreliable on materials with vapor barriers or layered construction (LVP, tile over thinset + liner, carpet over pad). Physical investigation or edge lifting is frequently required to confirm actual conditions.
field_implications.drying_strategy_adjustments: High-velocity air movement is often effective on open, porous materials. Lower-velocity, directed airflow or localized tenting is frequently more effective on wood with bound moisture or in confined cavities. Over-blasting some materials can create new boundary layers or uneven drying.
field_implications.modern_vs_traditional_assemblies: Older construction (plaster, dimensional lumber, no vapor barriers under flooring) generally dries differently than modern construction. LVP, engineered flooring, and thinset + membrane systems have changed the moisture dynamics on many jobs and require updated expectations.

common_misunderstandings.all_materials_dry_the_same: A frequent error is treating all wet materials with the same drying approach. Particle board, drywall, and fiberglass behave very differently from dimensional lumber or concrete, both in how they hold water and how readily they release it.
common_misunderstandings.surface_dry_means_dry: Materials can feel dry or read dry on the surface while still holding significant moisture deeper inside (especially wood and thick assemblies). Bound moisture and moisture behind vapor barriers are commonly missed.
common_misunderstandings.extraction_fixes_everything: Extraction removes free water effectively but does little for bound moisture or water that has wicked deep into materials or under vapor barriers. Proper airflow and time are still required after extraction.
common_misunderstandings.newer_materials_are_always_better: Some modern materials (certain LVP systems, thinset + liner assemblies) actually create more difficult hidden moisture situations than older construction because they trap water effectively once it gets underneath.
common_misunderstandings.closed_cell_foam_is_indestructible: While closed-cell spray foam is highly water-resistant, it is not immune. Heavy saturation, long dwell time, or contamination can still require removal or specialized drying techniques in some cases.

reference_lines: Category 3 gypsum board, mineral-fiber lay-in tile, cellulose, and particleboard cabinets are removals. Steel, plaster, and concrete can usually stay and be cleaned and dried. (informative)
Tile, vinyl, and coatings are lids. The dry is the cavity or substrate under them, not the surface reading. Intact asbestos-containing material stays intact.

Category 2 or 3 under a floating, sheet, or wood-backed floor is a removal. Swollen laminate is unrestorable. A slab under hardwood or vinyl is a long dry confirmed by the flooring warranty test methods, not a pin meter.

Physical removal is the mold remediation. A kill, a coat, or a fog without removal is a written deviation. Return to Condition 1 is written before containment comes down, and the moisture cause is corrected.
A coating waits until Condition 1 and a dry substrate, breathes at 2 perms or more, and never covers Condition 2 or 3. Knockdown residue is physically cleaned. Mycotoxins come off with the dust.

Wet carpet comes off the tack strip from the knees, not standing. No electric staple gun. Woven carpet is secured on all four edges and dried from the top. Wet cushion is bagged before it crosses a dry room. (informative)
Heat moves toward cold, moisture toward dry, high pressure toward low, unless the job is forcing it. A sudden loss that will not dry is often a chronic failure underneath.
Open-cell foam holds water. Closed-cell usually does not, but both slow the dry of whatever is behind them. Unfaced fiberglass wet only at the bottom can sometimes stay.
A falling concrete reading in the first weeks after a pour is hydration, not drying. Two coats of oil gloss can drop a wall board from about 34 perms to about 1: the paint is a vapor lid.

field_lessons.tile_thinset_liner: On tile floors with water intrusion, don't assume the water stopped between the thinset and the liner: check under the liner, on top of the underlayment. A tile floor can read mostly dry at the surface while real moisture sits underneath; tile is a lid, and the dry is the substrate under it. This is a situational call. Reasons to take the tile, thinset, and liner out: water got under the liner, moisture is hidden where you can't read it, or the assembly can't be reached to dry or verify. Reasons to leave it: tile is expensive to reinstall, and sometimes you can get airflow and access another way; for example, cut the drywall around a backsplash perimeter to open up behind it. Weigh it on the job and write down why.
field_lessons.electronics_and_appliances: High risk of hidden corrosion, especially after acidic smoke plus moisture. Many items fail weeks or months later even if they power on now. Electronics leave the humid room the same day; a wet TV, computer, or appliance gets a specialist evaluation.
field_lessons.fabrics_and_upholstery: Often cleanable and dryable if addressed quickly. Category 2/3 mattresses, box springs, pillows, and stuffed pieces are generally unrestorable.
field_lessons.documents_and_photos: Inks run and pages stick. Normal drying often adds damage. Freeze-drying or a document specialist is often worth it for irreplaceable items: a specialty line.

corrosion_and_degradation.description: Moisture plus contaminants, especially acidic smoke residue, speeds up damage to metals, electronics, and HVAC parts. It keeps going after the water and smoke are gone.
key_points: Fire jobs put out with water are the highest-risk setting: acidic residue + moisture + time.
Hidden corrosion inside electronics, appliances, and HVAC coils is not visible at inspection and can cause failure later.
Drain cleaners (caustic) and strong oxidizers as the cause of loss raise corrosion risk on pipes, fixtures, and appliances: flag metal components and document it.
If it powers on, it is not proven undamaged. Surface cleaning does not stop corrosion already started inside a component.
Be upfront with the customer and the adjuster about corrosion risk; document exposure and recommend specialist evaluation instead of promising a working unit.

vapor_drive_and_pressure.description: How vapor pressure differences drive moisture movement through materials and assemblies. This is the fundamental physics behind drying and why moisture moves the way it does.

core_concepts.vapor_pressure_gradient: Moisture always moves from areas of higher vapor pressure to areas of lower vapor pressure. Creating and maintaining this gradient is the core goal of drying.
core_concepts.temperature_effect_on_vapor_pressure: Warmer air can hold significantly more moisture. Raising temperature increases the vapor pressure of wet materials, which can help drive moisture out, but only if the moisture is being removed from the air.
core_concepts.vapor_barriers: Materials that stop vapor movement (LVP, sheet vinyl, some coatings, closed-cell foam) protect from one direction but can trap liquid water if it gets underneath them.
core_concepts.stack_effect_and_air_movement: Warm moist air rises. In buildings, this can move moisture from crawlspaces or basements into wall cavities and living spaces through gaps, HVAC, and penetrations.

field_implications.drying_strategy: Effective drying requires both airflow across wet surfaces (to disrupt the boundary layer) and continuous moisture removal from the air (dehumidification) to maintain the vapor pressure gradient.
field_implications.why_some_jobs_dry_slowly: If temperature is low or dehumidification is insufficient, the vapor pressure gradient stays weak even with air movers running. Small rooms can overheat quickly, reducing drying efficiency.
field_implications.hidden_moisture_movement: Vapor can move through materials even when liquid water cannot. This is why moisture can appear in unexpected places days after the initial loss.

wood_emc.description: Equilibrium Moisture Content (EMC) in wood: the moisture level wood naturally reaches based on surrounding temperature and humidity. Critical for setting realistic drying targets and understanding when wood is truly dry.

core_concepts.what_is_emc: EMC is the moisture content wood will eventually reach when left in a stable environment. It is determined by temperature and relative humidity. The standard working range for wood is 12–14% MC. The dry standard comes from unaffected wood in the same structure, not a chart number.
core_concepts.why_it_matters: You cannot dry wood below the EMC of its environment. Attempting to do so wastes time and energy. The 2–4 points from unaffected wood of the same species in the same building is the field check; the goal is a moisture reading that meets or is below the dry standard (Base Science: Dry Standards: Wood).
core_concepts.checking_vs_drying: Wood that has been wet for a long time often develops checking (cracks). Checking is permanent damage. Drying can stop further checking but will not repair existing checks.
core_concepts.seasonal_variation: EMC changes with the seasons. Wood is naturally drier in winter (heated homes) and higher in summer. Always compare affected wood to unaffected wood in the same environment rather than using a fixed chart number.

field_implications.target_setting: On wood floors and framing, establish the dry standard from unaffected wood in the same house under current conditions. 12–14% is the standard working range, not a substitute for that reading. Do not chase a number below the unaffected wood in this structure.
field_implications.monitoring: Pin readings on wood should be taken at consistent depth and location. Surface readings can be misleading on thick members: deeper readings are more reliable for structural wood.
field_implications.when_to_remove: If wood has significant checking, swelling, or has been wet long enough to support mold, removal is often more practical than attempting to dry it back to a stable condition.
